title: literary novel|an elderly translator finishing her last book
text:
The light in the study was thin and yellow, the kind that pooled like old honey on the surface of the desk—on the worn green felt, on the spine of the dictionary bound in cracked blue cloth, on the rim of the teacup where a single ring of tannin had dried into a perfect, fragile ellipse. Eleanor’s left hand rested palm-down on the page, her knuckles swollen, the skin translucent as rice paper stretched over river stones. Her right held the fountain pen—not the sleek modern one gifted by her publisher last spring, but the Parker 51 she’d bought in ’58, its black lacquer dulled to a soft, bruised sheen, its nib split slightly at the tip, leaving faint, deliberate ghosts of ink where she pressed too hard. She was translating a passage from a Lithuanian novella written in 1947, a story about a woman who mended fishing nets on the Curonian Spit while waiting for a letter that never came. The original text was spare, almost brittle: *Ji suplojo rankas į smėlį ir palaukė, kol vėjas nuplauna žodžius nuo liežuvio.* She’d written three versions already in the margin: *She clapped her hands into the sand and waited until the wind washed the words from her tongue.* Too literal. *She struck her palms against the sand and waited for the wind to scour the words from her mouth.* Too violent. *She slapped sand from her palms and waited for the wind to carry the words away, word by word, from her tongue.* Closer—but “slapped” implied dismissal, not surrender; “carry” suggested intention, not erosion. She circled *scour* again, then crossed it out with a single, slow line. Her wrist ached, a deep, familiar throb behind the ulna, the kind that flared when rain pressed low on the Baltic coast, though here in Oxford it was merely damp and grey, the kind that seeped through window frames and settled in the joints like cold ash.

A fly buzzed against the pane—insistent, futile. She watched it trace the same frantic arc between glass and frame, its wings catching the weak light like shards of mica. She remembered a similar fly in Vilnius, in the cramped apartment above the bookbinder’s shop where she’d lived for six months in ’63, translating a collection of folk songs rendered in dialect so archaic even the local scholars hesitated. That fly had landed on the open page of her notebook, its tiny legs gripping the inked Cyrillic of *žalčiai*, the word for grass snakes, which she’d rendered as *adders*, though the connotation was softer, more sinuous, less venomous—more like something coiled in warm hay than something striking from shadow. She’d left it there, watching the creature pulse, until the ink beneath it blurred faintly from the heat of its body. She hadn’t moved. Time had thickened, become viscous, like the honey in the jar beside her now, its amber depth holding suspended flecks of pollen, golden and inert.

Her glasses slid down her nose. She pushed them up with the side of her index finger, leaving a faint smudge of graphite near the bridge. The manuscript before her wasn’t typed; it was typeset on cream-coloured paper, the font Garamond, twelve-point, generous leading—her publisher’s final concession, after she’d refused digital proofs. She’d insisted on seeing the physical galleys, the weight of them in her lap, the slight give of the paper under her thumb as she turned each page. She liked the way the ink bled, just barely, into the fibres when she ran her fingertip along a line—proof it was real, not pixelated air. On page 42, she’d pencilled a question mark beside the phrase *tamsos švelnumas*. Darkness’s softness. It was grammatically odd, almost nonsensical in Lithuanian, yet the author—Dalia Vaitkevičiūtė, dead these thirty years—had repeated it twice, once at the beginning, once at the end, like a hinge. Eleanor had tried *the softness of darkness*, *darkness’s gentle hush*, *the yielding dark*. None held the paradox—the way velvet absorbs light, the way moss grows in shade not despite it but because of it, the way silence after a long illness isn’t empty but full of the body’s quiet labour. She dipped the pen, drew a single, wavering line beneath the phrase, then wrote, in her smallest, most precise hand: *the dark’s soft insistence*.

The clock on the mantel ticked—wooden, unhurried, its pendulum swinging with the steady, unblinking rhythm of a man counting breaths. She thought of her father’s watch, the one he’d given her at sixteen, its face cracked, its hands frozen at 3:17—the hour the train pulled out of Kaunas station in 1944, carrying him east, carrying him away. She still wore it, wound daily, though it kept no time. Its weight was familiar, a small, cold anchor against her wrist bone.

Outside, a bicycle bell chimed—two clear, bright notes—and then the soft hiss of tyres on wet gravel. A student, perhaps, hurrying to a tutorial, briefcase slung over one shoulder, scarf trailing. Eleanor watched the shadow pass the window, elongated and swift, then vanish. She lifted the teacup. The liquid inside was lukewarm, the dregs thick with sediment. She drank it anyway, the bitterness sharp on her tongue, the warmth spreading low in her belly like a slow ember.

She turned back to the page. The sentence demanded resolution. Not truth, not fidelity, but resonance—the echo that lingers after the sound has ceased. She uncapped the pen again, the metallic whisper loud in the quiet room. Her hand hovered. Not steady, not trembling—just present, suspended, like the fly, like the stopped watch, like the untranslated word waiting in the margin, breathing. She lowered the nib. The ink flowed, dark and certain, into the white space.

title: short story|a beekeeper's widow deciding whether to keep the hives
text:
The bees were always there, a constant hum in the background of our lives. Even before I met him, they were there, hovering around the edges of my consciousness like the quiet promise of something sweet and perilous. When he first took me to the hives, I remember the sun was setting, casting long shadows over the rows of white boxes. He moved with a grace that seemed almost otherworldly, his hands steady as he lifted the frames, pointing out the patterns of the comb, the way the workers clustered protectively around the queen. I felt a shiver run through me, not just from the cool evening air, but from the realization that this man, with his gentle strength and his deep knowledge, was someone I could love.

Now, standing in the same spot, the hives are silent. The sun is setting again, but it feels different, colder. The world has a way of shifting under your feet when you least expect it. He’s gone, taken by a heart that gave out too soon, leaving me with the weight of his absence and the responsibility of these hives. The bees, once a symbol of our life together, now feel like a burden I’m not sure I can bear.

I’ve been avoiding them, the hives. Every day, I tell myself I’ll go out, check on them, make sure they’re still thriving. But I can’t bring myself to do it. It’s not just the physical labor; it’s the emotional toll. Each hive, each frame, is a reminder of him. His laughter, his voice, the way he would talk about the bees as if they were old friends. I can hear his words echoing in my head, “They’re more than just insects, you know. They’re a community, a family. And we’re part of it.”

But what am I, without him? A solitary figure, adrift in a sea of memories. The neighbors have been kind, offering to help, to take over the hives if I can’t manage. Part of me wants to say yes, to let go of this responsibility and retreat into the comfort of solitude. But another part of me, a stubborn, aching part, resists. These hives are more than just a hobby or a business. They are a legacy, a connection to the man I loved, to the life we built together.

I finally gather the courage to approach the hives. The familiar scent of honey and wax fills my nostrils, and for a moment, I can almost feel his presence beside me. I lift the lid of the first hive, and the bees stir, their wings a soft, rustling symphony. The frames are heavy with honey, the combs full and golden. For a moment, I allow myself to be lost in the simple, soothing task of inspecting the hives, checking for signs of disease, making sure the queen is healthy.

As I work, I find myself talking to the bees, as he used to. I tell them about my day, about the empty house, about the silence that seems to fill every room. I tell them how much I miss him, how I’m not sure I can keep going without him. The bees, in their quiet, industrious way, seem to listen. They don’t judge, they don’t offer false comfort. They simply continue their work, a testament to the resilience of life, even in the face of loss.

When I finish, I step back and look at the hives. They are a part of me now, a part of us. I realize that I can’t give them up, not because I’m clinging to the past, but because they are a living, breathing reminder of the love we shared. The bees will go on, and so must I. I don’t know what the future holds, but I know that I will face it with the strength and determination that he taught me, with the knowledge that even in the darkest moments, there is still sweetness to be found.

The sun has set, and the sky is a deep, inky blue. The stars begin to twinkle, and I stand there, surrounded by the hives, feeling a strange, bittersweet peace. The bees will stay, and so will I. Not because I have all the answers, but because sometimes, the act of continuing, of tending to the small, everyday tasks, is enough. It’s a start, and maybe, just maybe, it’s enough to carry me forward.

title: short story|two sisters clearing out their mother's flat
text:
The rain in Glasgow had that particular grey insistence—cold, fine, and unrelenting—like breath fogging a window you never quite wiped clean. Fiona stood in the hallway of 3B, St. Vincent Street, her coat still damp at the shoulders, staring at the brass number screwed crookedly into the peeling paint. Beside her, Elara balanced a cardboard box stamped *Fragile – Do Not Stack* on one hip, her dark hair escaping its knot, strands clinging to her damp temple.

“Smells like lavender polish and damp wool,” Elara said, nudging the door open with her foot.

Fiona stepped inside. The flat hadn’t changed—not really. Same floral wallpaper in the hall, though the roses near the ceiling had faded to a bruised mauve. Same narrow staircase with its worn runner, frayed at the third step where Mum always stubbed her toe. She ran a finger along the banister. Dust rose in a soft, slow plume.

They worked in quiet sync for an hour: Fiona sorting the kitchen cupboards—tins of Robertson’s marmalade, three chipped *Glasgow Museums* mugs, a single wooden spoon with a hairline crack in the handle—while Elara tackled the spare room, now just a repository of decades: stacked National Geographics from ’87 to ’03, a broken typewriter with yellowed ribbon, a shoebox labelled *Elara’s First Teeth (??)* in Mum’s looping script.

It was in the wardrobe of the main bedroom—Mum’s bedroom—that Elara found the shoebox marked *Fiona’s Letters*. Not the one with the teeth. This one was smaller, bound with faded blue tape. Inside, not letters, but envelopes. All addressed to Fiona, all postmarked Glasgow, all returned. *Return to Sender. Addressee Unknown.* The earliest was 1998. The latest, 2005. Each bore Fiona’s old Edinburgh address—the flat off Leith Walk she’d shared with a violinist who vanished after six months and took half her teacups.

Fiona didn’t cry. She sat on the edge of the unmade bed, knees drawn up, and held the envelope from 2001. Her own handwriting, younger, sharper, on the front: *Mum — Please don’t call me at work. I’ll ring when I can.* She’d written it during a shift at the Royal Infirmary, ink slightly blurred where her thumb had smudged it.

Elara hovered in the doorway, arms crossed. “You never told me she kept them.”

“I didn’t know.” Fiona’s voice was flat, like stone warmed just enough to lose its chill. “I thought she stopped after the first few.”

“She didn’t stop. She just… filed them.” Elara picked up the box, turned it over. On the bottom, in ballpoint, Mum’s hand again: *For when she comes back. Or when I forget why she left.*

They moved to the living room. The bay window overlooked the tenement opposite, where Mrs. Carmichael still hung her washing on Tuesdays, even in this rain. Fiona lifted the lid of the piano stool—still the same chipped black lacquer—and pulled out sheet music: *Für Elise*, dog-eared at the coda; a beginner’s book titled *Piano for Grown-Ups*; and beneath it, a folded A4 page covered in Mum’s neat, slanting script.

*Dear Elara,* it began. *If you’re reading this, I’m gone, and Fiona is here—or she isn’t. If she is, tell her I listened to her play Chopin last summer, the one with the left-hand arpeggios, and I cried behind the kitchen door because it sounded like something breaking open and healing at the same time. Tell her I kept every programme from her student recitals—even the one where she forgot the middle section and bowed anyway. Tell her I knew she’d come back. I just didn’t know how long it would take me to stop waiting by the phone.*

Elara read it aloud, voice steady until the last line, then faltered. She looked at Fiona, who was staring at the rain-streaked glass, her reflection fractured by the droplets.

“Why didn’t she give it to me?” Fiona whispered.

“Because she knew you’d tear it up,” Elara said softly. She went to the bookshelf, pulled down the heavy, cloth-bound *Oxford Book of Scottish Verse*. From between *Burns* and *MacDiarmid*, she slid out a small, square photograph—Fiona, aged seven, grinning gap-toothed, holding a lopsided clay owl she’d made in primary school. On the back, in pencil: *Fiona’s owl. Still looks like it’s judging us.*

Fiona took it. Her thumb brushed the raised ridges of the clay captured in the photo. “She kept this. Not the letters. Not the programmes. This.”

Elara knelt beside her, not touching, just close. “She kept what fit in her hands.”

They carried boxes down to the van later—three trips, rain soaking their collars, the damp seeping into their shoes. At the foot of the stairs, Fiona paused, looking up at the landing light, its bulb long dead, the shade stained yellow at the edges. “Do you remember,” she said, “when we were twelve and thirteen, and we used to sit right here, eating custard creams, listening to her sing in the shower? Off-key. Always ‘Danny Boy’.”

Elara smiled, a real one this time, crinkling the corners of her eyes. “She’d belt it like she was at the Barrowlands. And you’d say, ‘She sounds like a goose being strangled,’ and I’d shush you, and then we’d both start giggling until we had to hold our stomachs.”

Fiona nodded. She didn’t say anything else. Just tucked the photograph into her coat pocket, next to the envelope from 2001. The rain softened, just slightly, as they loaded the last box—a wicker basket filled with tangled knitting needles, balls of grey wool, and a half-finished scarf, its stitches tight and even, stopping mid-row. Elara picked it up, felt the weight of the wool, the cool metal of the needles. She didn’t finish it. She just held it, for a moment, before placing it carefully in the van beside the piano stool and the shoebox of returned letters. Then she closed the doors. The latch clicked, sharp and final, in the wet Glasgow air.

title: literary novel|a sound archivist who finds a confession hidden on an old tape
text:
The tape smelled like burnt sugar and dust motes. Not metaphorically—*literally*. I held it up to the light in my cramped booth at the Northeastern Audio Archive, and a faint, caramelized tang rose off the oxide, sharp enough to make my sinuses twitch. Probably the acetate binder degrading. Or maybe just the ghost of someone’s forgotten cinnamon roll, left too long on the shelf beside the 1958 WGBH reel-to-reel cabinet.  

I’d pulled *Box 44-B: “Misc. Field Recordings – Unlabeled / Partially Catalogued”* on a whim. A Tuesday. Rain streaking the high windows like wet chalk. My coffee had gone cold, congealing into a skin that wrinkled when I stirred it with a bent paperclip. The kind of day where even silence feels heavy, thick with the weight of other people’s silences.  

The tape was unmarked. No spool label, no grease-pencil scrawl, just a single strip of masking tape near the hub, yellowed and peeling, with three shaky numbers inked in blue ballpoint: *7-12-53*. Not a date, not a track number—just… there. Like a secret whispered and then immediately regretted.  

I cleaned it first. Not just the surface—*deep* clean. Cotton swabs dipped in isopropyl, angled just so under the magnifier lamp. My left thumbnail had a crescent-shaped nick from last week’s broken stylus guard. I noticed it again. Always noticing things I shouldn’t.  

The playback deck was a Studer B67, temperamental as a retired opera singer. I threaded the tape by feel—thumb and forefinger tracing the edge, checking for stretch, for flaking oxide. It hissed when it engaged. Not the warm, analog *shhh* of good tape, but a dry, papery rasp, like dead leaves skittering across concrete. Then—silence. Five seconds. Ten. Just the hum of the machine and the distant, muffled *thump-thump-thump* of the HVAC kicking on in the basement.  

Then, a voice.  

Not loud. Not clear. A man’s voice, mid-fifties, maybe, voice frayed at the edges—not from age, but from holding something back. A cigarette cough, swallowed halfway. He didn’t say *hello*. Didn’t say *this is a confession*. He just began, mid-thought:  

*“…the lilac bush behind the old Miller place. You remember it? Purple, almost black in the rain. She liked to stand there, smelling it after storms. Said it smelled like ‘wet earth and forgetting.’ I never told her I hated that phrase. Too pretty. Too soft.”*  

I leaned in. My ear pressed against the headphone cup. The right one had a tiny tear in the leather—just a hairline split near the hinge—so every time I moved, it made a faint, sticky *shhk* sound. I didn’t pull away.  

He spoke for twelve minutes, seventeen seconds. No pauses longer than three breaths. No names—not hers, not his, not the town (though I recognized the cadence: that slow, gravelly New England lilt, the way *‘river’* becomes *‘rivver’*, the soft *d* in *‘dead’*). He described the rain that night—the kind that doesn’t fall so much as *settles*, low and grey, turning the pavement into a mirror. He described the wrench he used—not the big pipe wrench, but the small, adjustable one, the one with the chipped blue enamel on the handle. He described how the metal felt cold, then warm, then cold again in his hand.  

He didn’t say *I killed her*. He said, *“I held it. And then I didn’t let go.”*  

At 11:43, he stopped. Not abruptly. Just… tapered. His voice thinned, like smoke rising. A long inhale. A sigh that cracked at the end. Then, silence. Not empty silence—the kind that follows a slammed door—but the silence *after* someone stops breathing. Thick. Listening.  

I sat there. The headphones still on. My throat tight. My left hand, the one with the nicked thumbnail, resting flat on the console. The Studer’s red record light blinked, steady, oblivious.  

Later, I checked the box log. Box 44-B had been donated in 1982 by Eleanor Voss, widow of Harold Voss, longtime town historian and amateur recorder. Harold died in ’79. Heart. Quietly, in his study, slumped over a stack of transcribed oral histories.  

I went down to the basement archives—past the leaky boiler, past the box marked *“Unprocessed – Pre-1960: Fragile”*—and pulled Harold’s accession file. Inside, a faded Polaroid: Harold, balding, squinting in sunlight, holding a Nagra III like it was a newborn. On the back, in his looping script: *“Miller Lane, July ’53. Mrs. P. says the lilacs are ‘blacker than sin this year.’ Ha.”*  

No Mrs. P. listed anywhere in town records. No Miller Lane. Just Miller *Road*.  

I played the tape again. Not for content. For texture. That rasp wasn’t just degradation. There was a faint, rhythmic *tick-tick-tick* underneath—barely audible—like a clock wound too tight. I boosted the high-mids. It resolved: a metronome. Someone’s studio metronome, set to 60 bpm. Steady. Relentless.  

Harold recorded interviews with farmers, librarians, the last surviving mill worker. All logged. All accounted for. Except this.  

I haven’t logged it yet.  

It sits on my desk now, next to a half-eaten granola bar (oats, honey, one raisin stuck to the wrapper), a pen with dried blue ink on the cap, and a Post-it I wrote this morning: *“Call Marge re: the 1947 school play reels—she thinks they’re misfiled.”*  

The tape smells like burnt sugar.  

I keep thinking about the lilac bush. How something so purple could smell like forgetting. How easy it is to hold a wrench. How hard it is, sometimes, to let go—not of guilt, not of memory, but of the *sound* of someone’s last quiet breath, preserved in oxide and silence, waiting for the right pair of ears, the right Tuesday, the right kind of tired.  

I haven’t decided what to do with it.  

But tonight, I’ll listen again. With the lights off. Just me, the hum, and that terrible, beautiful, rasping voice—still speaking, still stopping, still holding on, long after the tape has run out.

title: memoir|learning to fish with a silent uncle on a Scottish loch
text:
...the loch spread out before us like a vast, unblemished mirror. The sun, still low in the sky, cast an orange glow across the water, and I could feel the chill of the morning air biting at my cheeks. Uncle Hamish, as always, was already knee-deep in the water, his waders blending seamlessly with the reeds and rushes. His back was to me, and even from this distance, I could see the rhythmic motion of his casting, the line arcing gracefully through the air.

I took a deep breath, trying to steady my nerves. Fishing had never come naturally to me, and the pressure of learning from someone as skilled and silent as Uncle Hamish only added to my anxiety. I waded in, the cold water seeping through my own waders, and felt a shiver run down my spine. The sensation was both invigorating and daunting.

Uncle Hamish turned slightly, his eyes meeting mine for a brief moment. There was no smile, no nod of encouragement, just a steady, unwavering gaze that seemed to say, "You know what to do." I nodded, though I wasn't entirely sure I did. I had watched him countless times, but the fluidity and precision of his movements always eluded me.

I began to cast, the line jerking awkwardly as it left the rod. It plopped into the water, sending ripples across the surface. I winced, knowing how clumsy it looked. Uncle Hamish didn't react, but I could feel his disapproval. He resumed his own casting, and I tried again, focusing on the smooth, sweeping motion he had demonstrated so many times. This time, the line sailed out more smoothly, landing with a gentle splash. It wasn't perfect, but it was better.

The hours passed slowly, each minute stretching out like the calm, undisturbed surface of the loch. We stood in silence, the only sounds the occasional call of a bird or the soft lapping of water against the shore. I found myself lost in thought, reflecting on the quiet strength of my uncle. He had been a fisherman all his life, and his connection to the water was almost spiritual. There was a peace about him, a sense of belonging, that I envied deeply.

As the sun climbed higher, the light shifted, and the loch seemed to come alive. The colors deepened, and the water took on a rich, emerald hue. I could see the shadows of fish moving beneath the surface, their forms ghostly and elusive. I cast again, and this time, the line landed perfectly, the fly settling gently on the water. I held my breath, watching, waiting.

Suddenly, there was a tug, and the line tightened. My heart leapt, and I felt a surge of adrenaline. I started to reel in, too quickly, and the fish fought back, thrashing wildly. Uncle Hamish's voice cut through the air, sharp and commanding. "Slow down, lad. Feel the fish."

I forced myself to slow, to focus on the tension in the line, to let the fish tire itself out. It was a battle of wills, and for a moment, I felt a deep connection to the creature on the other end. Finally, the resistance lessened, and I carefully guided the fish toward the shore. Uncle Hamish waded over, net in hand, and scooped up the trout. It was a beautiful specimen, its scales shimmering in the sunlight.

He held it up, and for the first time that day, I saw a hint of a smile. "Good catch," he said, his voice gruff but approving. I felt a rush of pride, and for a moment, the tension between us eased. We released the fish back into the loch, and it swam away, disappearing into the depths.

We fished for a few more hours, and I managed to land a couple more trout. Each time, Uncle Hamish's approval grew, and I could feel a bond forming between us, one that went beyond words. As the day wore on, the silence between us became less oppressive and more companionable. We were two men, sharing a simple, timeless activity, and in that, we found a common language.

By the time the sun began to set, painting the sky in shades of pink and gold, I felt a profound sense of accomplishment. I had not only caught fish, but I had also bridged a gap with my uncle. The loch, once a place of intimidation, now felt like a sanctuary, a place where I could find peace and connection.

As we packed up our gear, Uncle Hamish placed a hand on my shoulder. It was a rare gesture of affection, and I felt a warmth spread through me. "You're getting the hang of it, lad," he said. "You'll make a fine fisherman yet."

I smiled, feeling a newfound confidence. "Thanks, Uncle. I couldn't have done it without you."

He gave a small nod, and we made our way back to the car, the loch behind us growing dim in the fading light. The drive home was quiet, but the silence was different now. It was a comfortable, shared silence, the kind that comes from understanding and respect. And as I watched the landscape pass by, I knew that I would carry the lessons of that day, and the memory of fishing with my silent uncle, with me for the rest of my life.

title: personal essay|why I keep a notebook of overheard sentences
text:
The Notebook of Other People’s Air

I keep a notebook—not for my own thoughts, but for other people’s speech, caught mid-drift. It is not a journal, not a diary, not even a commonplace book in the old sense. It is a ledger of eavesdropping, bound in cracked black cloth, its spine held together with masking tape and time. Its pages are uneven: some entries inked in haste on damp subway platforms, others transcribed hours later from memory, already fraying at the edges—“the woman in the coat with the torn elbow said…” or “man at the bus stop, voice like gravel in a tin can…”

Why? Not because I believe language is precious in the abstract. I don’t. Language is often clumsy, redundant, weaponized, or just tired—like breath you’ve exhaled too many times. But when it slips free of intention—when someone says something not *for* anyone, not *to* anyone, but simply *into* the air—that’s when it acquires a strange, unvarnished weight. A weight that has nothing to do with truth or insight, and everything to do with presence.

I began this habit accidentally, ten years ago, after overhearing a man in a laundromat say, “My wife doesn’t like the way light falls on the toaster.” Not *the toaster*, not *the light*, but *the way light falls on the toaster*. The specificity was absurd, tender, devastating. It wasn’t metaphor. It wasn’t complaint. It was a fact he’d absorbed so deeply it had become part of his domestic weather. I wrote it down before I knew why. Later, I found myself listening differently—not for meaning, but for the particular gravity of a phrase that had landed just so, as if dropped from a height without warning.

There is no system. No categories. No index. Some entries are single sentences: *“I haven’t seen a pigeon since Tuesday.”* Others are fragments, almost illegible: *“—and then the cat looked up, not at me, but at the space where the ceiling fan used to be.”* (That one came from a hospice waiting room. The fan had been removed weeks earlier. The cat, newly adopted, still tracked the absence.)

I do not transcribe for accuracy’s sake—I’m terrible at that. My ear distorts vowels; my hand scrambles syntax. What I record is the residue: the rhythm, the hesitation, the odd preposition, the sudden shift in register—how a teenager switches from slang to formal diction mid-sentence when addressing an elderly neighbor. These aren’t quotes. They’re fossils of utterance, pressed flat between paper and time.

People ask if I feel guilty. I do, sometimes—briefly, like a flicker behind the ribs. But guilt implies violation, and what I’m doing feels less like intrusion than quiet witness to a kind of involuntary self-portraiture. Speech, unmonitored, reveals texture, not biography. You learn more about a person from how they say *“I guess”* than from what they guess. From whether *“maybe”* lands like a question or a door closing. From the pause before *“actually…”*, which is never about actuality, but about recalibration.

The notebook is full of banality. Pages dense with grocery lists overheard at checkout lines, weather observations delivered with existential finality (*“It’s not raining. It’s *waiting*.”*), declarations of minor defeat (*“The bread won again.”*). Yet these accumulate, not into wisdom, but into a low hum of shared human frequency—the sound of people trying, daily, to locate themselves in language that was never built for them.

I don’t reread it often. When I do, it’s rarely for comfort or inspiration. More often, it’s disorienting. A sentence from three years ago—*“She kept touching the locket, though it wasn’t there anymore”*—resurfaces, and I remember the woman’s hands, the tremor in her left thumb, the way she blinked slowly, as if surfacing from deep water. But I don’t know her name. I don’t know if the locket was lost, stolen, or given away. I only know that for twelve seconds, her grief lived in the air between us, unmoored and undeniable, and I caught it—not to keep, but because it startled me into attention.

There’s a superstition among writers that recording life preserves it. I don’t believe that. Nothing preserves. Everything leaks. The notebook doesn’t save anything. It doesn’t even archive. It simply holds, for a while, the echo of voices that have already dispersed—voices that were never mine to hold.

Sometimes, on slow afternoons, I’ll open it to a random page and read aloud—just once—my own imperfect transcription of someone else’s passing sound. My voice cracks on the consonants they didn’t stress. I misplace their pauses. It sounds wrong, hollow, like playing a record warped by heat. And yet, in that failure, something true emerges: the distance between hearing and holding, between speech and script, between one life brushing against another and vanishing into the ordinary noise of the world.

The notebook is nearly full. I will buy another soon. Not because I think the practice matters, exactly. But because, every now and then, I hear something—a phrase, a stumble, a laugh that breaks on the second syllable—and my hand moves before my mind catches up. Not toward understanding. Not toward art. Just toward the quiet, stubborn act of catching air.

title: fable|a crow who collects lost keys
text:
The crows of Blackwood Lane were known for their particular brand of thievery—not shiny coins or wedding rings, but keys. Not all crows, mind you. Just one: a female with left wing feathers slightly ruffled, as if perpetually caught in a crosswind, and eyes the colour of wet slate. Her name, according to Mrs. Elara Finch—who ran the secondhand bookshop on the corner and kept meticulous notes in a leather-bound ledger titled *Avian Anomalies*—was Cora. Not “Cora the Key-Crow,” though that’s what children whispered; just Cora, as if she’d once been human and forgotten her surname.

Blackwood Lane itself was a narrow, cobblestoned street in the old quarter of Bath, where Georgian facades leaned companionably toward one another and ivy grew thick enough to muffle footsteps. Rain fell often there—soft, persistent drizzle that turned the stones slick and made brass doorknobs gleam like submerged coins. It was in such weather, on a Tuesday in late October, that Cora first appeared at the wrought-iron gate of Number 17. The house belonged to Dr. Alistair Thorne, a retired orthopaedic surgeon who walked with a cane carved from yew and kept his keys on a heavy, tarnished fob shaped like a fox’s head.

He dropped them, of course. Not dramatically—no flailing arm, no startled cry—but simply as he fumbled with his umbrella and the latch of the gate. Three keys clinked onto the wet cobbles: the fox-head fob, a small Yale key for the study door, and a tiny, bent skeleton key that hadn’t opened anything in thirty years, kept only because it had belonged to his father. Cora watched from the lower branch of the copper beech across the street. She didn’t swoop. Didn’t even tilt her head. She waited until Dr. Thorne had hobbled inside, the front door clicking shut behind him, before dropping silently onto the stones.

She didn’t pick them up with her beak. That was the first thing Mrs. Finch noticed through her shop window. Cora nudged the fox-head fob with her foot, then tapped the Yale key twice with her beak—not to lift it, but to *test its weight*. Only then did she tuck the three keys beneath her left wing, where the feathers were longest and softest, and flew—not away, but diagonally across the lane, landing precisely on the rain-slicked windowsill of Mrs. Finch’s bookshop.

Mrs. Finch opened the sash window an inch. “Well,” she said, voice low and dry as pressed violets. “That’s new.”

Cora didn’t blink. She shifted her weight, and the fox-head fob slid out from beneath her wing, landing with a soft *clack* on the sill. Then the Yale key. Then, after a pause long enough for a sparrow to dart past, the bent skeleton key—placed deliberately beside the others, not dropped, but *laid down*, as if arranging a small, solemn offering.

“Not stealing,” Mrs. Finch murmured, pulling on her cardigan. “Returning. Or… curating.” She fetched a shallow porcelain dish—the kind used for holding paperclips—and placed it on the sill. Cora cocked her head. Mrs. Finch dropped in two sunflower seeds, one shelled, one unshelled. Cora ate the shelled one, ignored the other, and flew off without glancing back.

Word spread, as it does in places where people still leave letters in postboxes and remember neighbours’ birthdays. Mr. Henderson from the bakery lost his shop key while wrestling a sack of flour near the alley behind St. Swithin’s. He found it two days later, balanced atop the bell-pull of the church’s side door—dry, though it had rained all night. Miss Larkspur, who taught piano at the conservatory, misplaced her flat key during a recital intermission. She discovered it the next morning, resting on the open score of Chopin’s Nocturne in E-flat, page 3, exactly where her left hand would rest when reaching for the sustaining pedal.

No one saw Cora place them. But everyone knew. Children began leaving small offerings on sills and ledges—not food, but tokens: a smooth river stone, a blue glass marble, a single silver button from a coat that had long since been donated. Cora accepted none of these. She took only seeds, and only from Mrs. Finch. Once, when a boy named Leo tried to follow her—ducking under hedges, holding his breath behind dustbins—she led him not to a roost or nest, but to the crumbling brick wall behind the old gasworks, where a rusted iron grille covered a disused ventilation shaft. She landed there, tilted her head, and dropped a single key into the dark opening: a brass key stamped *H.M. Prison, Dartmoor, 1923*. Then she flew straight up, vanishing into the low cloud, leaving Leo standing alone, heart pounding, staring at the grille as if it might whisper back.

Dr. Thorne never retrieved his keys from Mrs. Finch’s dish. Instead, he polished the fox-head fob until it gleamed, hung it on a new ribbon, and wore it round his neck like a locket. “Some things,” he told Mrs. Finch over tea one afternoon, stirring honey into his cup with deliberate slowness, “aren’t meant to stay lost. Or found. They’re meant to be *held*, briefly, then passed on—like a note slipped under a door, or a sigh caught on the breeze.”

Cora still perches on the copper beech most mornings. She watches the lane—the postman’s cap bobbing, the baker’s van backing up with a soft *beep-beep*, the way light catches the raindrops on the shop windows. Sometimes she carries nothing. Sometimes she carries two keys, sometimes four. Last week, she dropped a single brass key into the gutter outside the library, where it lay until a woman in a grey coat paused, bent, and picked it up—not with surprise, but with recognition, as if she’d been expecting it. She held it in her palm for a long moment, then slipped it into her coat pocket without looking up. Cora watched her walk away, then preened a feather with slow, careful strokes, her eyes fixed on the damp, glistening cobbles, waiting—not for the next loss, but for the next quiet, necessary exchange.

title: myth retelling|the smith who forged the first bell
text:
In the hushed and misty valleys of a land long forgotten, there lived a smith named Goran. Not your everyday blacksmith, mind you, but one whose hands could shape metal as if it were soft clay. His forge was a simple place, a small wooden hut with an earthen floor and a great iron bellows that breathed life into the glowing embers. The air around him always smelled of soot and sweat, and his skin bore the marks of countless burns and scars, each telling a story of trials and triumphs.

Goran had a reputation that spread far and wide. They said he could make anything from a humble horseshoe to a mighty sword. But his true passion lay in creating something that would resonate with the very heartbeat of the earth. One night, as the moon hung low and heavy in the sky, Goran had a dream. In this dream, a figure, neither man nor beast, appeared to him. It spoke in a voice like thunder and whispered, "Forge the first bell, Goran. A bell that will call the spirits and unite the people."

The next morning, Goran woke up with a strange sense of purpose. He went about his day, tending to the usual tasks, but his mind was elsewhere. By midday, he had gathered all the materials he needed: copper, tin, and a rare ore that shimmered with an otherworldly light. This ore, he believed, would give the bell its unique resonance.

For days, Goran toiled at the forge, hammering and shaping the metal. The heat was intense, and the work was backbreaking, but he didn't falter. Sometimes, he would pause, lost in thought, staring at the half-formed bell, wondering if he was truly capable of such a task. His hands, though, never doubted; they moved with a sureness born of years of practice.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the valley, Goran finally finished the bell. It was a thing of beauty, with intricate engravings that seemed to dance in the firelight. The bell was large, too, nearly as tall as a man, and its surface gleamed with a deep, warm luster. Goran took a step back, wiping the sweat from his brow, and felt a surge of pride. He had done it.

But the real test was yet to come. Goran knew that the bell's true power lay not just in its form, but in its sound. With the help of his neighbors, he hoisted the bell onto a sturdy frame in the center of the village. The villagers gathered, their faces a mix of curiosity and skepticism. Goran, with a deep breath, struck the bell with a mallet.

The sound that rang out was unlike anything they had ever heard. It was a deep, resonant tone that seemed to vibrate through the very core of the earth. The villagers gasped, and for a moment, everything was still. Then, the sound began to change. It grew, filling the air with a melody that was both ancient and new. The wind picked up, and the leaves rustled as if the trees themselves were singing along.

And then, something extraordinary happened. From the edges of the village, figures began to emerge—spirits, old and wise, who had long been dormant. They were drawn by the bell's call, and as they approached, their forms became more solid, more real. The villagers, initially frightened, soon realized these were not malevolent beings but guardians of the land, awakened by the power of the bell.

Goran, standing beside the bell, felt a profound connection to the spirits. He understood now that the bell was not just a tool, but a bridge between the worlds of the living and the dead, a way to honor the past and embrace the future. The spirits, in turn, blessed the bell and the village, promising to watch over them and guide them through the ages.

From that day on, the bell became a sacred object, a symbol of unity and harmony. Every year, on the anniversary of its forging, the villagers would gather and ring the bell, listening to its haunting, beautiful song. And Goran, the humble smith, was remembered as the one who had brought the spirits and the people together, a hero in his own right.

Years passed, and the bell remained, a testament to Goran's skill and vision. The village flourished, and the stories of the first bell were told and retold, each version adding a little more magic and wonder. And somewhere, in the quiet corners of the world, the echoes of that first, magnificent toll still linger, a reminder of the power of creation and the enduring bond between the earth and its inhabitants.

title: nature essay|a winter of watching one heron on the same canal
text:
It is three minutes past seven, and the heron stands exactly where it stood yesterday, and the day before that—midway along the concrete bank where the canal narrows and the water slows into a silted eddy. Its left leg is bent at the knee, tucked tight against its belly like a folded letter; the right bears its weight, slender and grey as weathered iron. Frost feathers the reeds behind it, brittle and silvered, and the air holds that particular winter hush: not silence, but a thickened stillness, as if sound itself has congealed just short of the ear. I watch from the footpath, breath pluming, gloves stiff with cold, and think—not for the first time—that this bird does not wait. It occupies time. It *is* time, made visible in feather and bone.

I have learned its rhythms by subtraction. Not by counting seconds, but by noticing what is absent: no frantic pacing, no head-twitching scan, no restless shifting of weight. When sparrows explode from the alder in a brown panic, the heron does not flinch. When a dog barks three fields away, its neck remains a smooth, vertical curve. Even the wind, which rattles the last dry cattail heads and lifts fine powder from the frozen towpath, seems to part around it, leaving its crest feathers undisturbed. This stillness is not passive. It is calibrated, deliberate—a suspension of impulse so absolute it feels like resistance. Against the season’s hurry—the frantic caching of jays, the desperate pecking of starlings at frozen crumbs, the hurried, shivering flights of wrens between hedges—it is an act of quiet defiance. The heron does not adapt to winter; it presides over it.

Its fishing is a study in minimalism. It does not stalk, not really. It watches. Its eyes, large and amber-gold, are fixed on the water’s surface, unblinking, yet somehow not vacant. They hold a depth that makes my own gaze feel shallow, distracted. When a shadow flickers beneath the thin ice-skimmed film—a perch, perhaps, or a slow-moving roach—the heron’s strike is not a lunge but a *release*: the coiled neck unspooling with terrifying speed, the dagger-beak piercing the water not with splash, but with a single, dark ripple. Then stillness again. It lifts its head, the fish wriggling once, a flash of silver against the grey plumage, before vanishing down its throat. No triumph, no pause for digestion—just the slow, deliberate repositioning of the left foot onto the damp concrete, the resettling of balance. It eats not for hunger’s urgency, but as a necessary punctuation in its long, slow sentence.

I began coming here out of habit, then curiosity, then something quieter—recognition. At first, I assumed it was one of many, rotating through the stretch of water. But the markings held: a slight kink in the upper mandible, a patch of slightly paler grey on the inner primary feather of the left wing, a habit of tilting its head precisely thirty degrees left when scanning the far bank. These are not traits I catalogued with scientific intent, but with the slow, intimate attention one gives a neighbour whose face one sees daily—the kind of noticing that bypasses thought and settles directly into the body. My pulse slows when I see it standing there. My shoulders drop. The tight knot between my brows, the one that forms with emails and deadlines and the low thrum of urban anxiety, loosens, almost imperceptibly, as if the heron’s stillness is a physical pressure releasing against my own tension.

The canal itself changes with the cold, and the heron changes with it. When the first hard frost sealed the surface, it stood longer on the bank, its gaze dropping lower, searching the translucent ice for the slow, dim shapes moving beneath. When snow fell—not the wet, clinging kind, but the fine, crystalline dust that settled like powdered glass—it stood motionless in the white hush, a charcoal sketch against the blinding field, its breath steaming in small, rhythmic puffs. Once, after a thaw had left the towpath slick and treacherous, I slipped, landing hard on my hip. Before I could even wince, the heron turned its head fully towards me. Not with alarm, but with a slow, unhurried rotation, its golden eye fixing on mine. We held that gaze for perhaps ten seconds—no more. There was no judgment, no fear, no invitation. Just pure, unmediated *presence*. And in that look, stripped of all human projection—no ‘wise elder’, no ‘lonely sentinel’, no ‘stoic survivor’—there was only the simple, staggering fact of another creature, utterly itself, sharing this sliver of frozen world. It turned back to the water. I got up, brushed the grit from my coat, and felt, for the first time in months, genuinely unobserved. Which, paradoxically, felt like being seen.

This is the quiet revelation of the winter: the heron does not ask for witness. It does not perform its endurance. It simply *is*, with a consistency that feels ancient, pre-linguistic. Its constancy is not stubbornness, but a different kind of belonging—one rooted not in claim or conquest, but in deep, unspoken agreement with the rhythm of light, water, and cold. It knows the exact temperature at which the eddy thaws first; it knows the precise angle of the low sun that glints off the submerged branch where minnows gather; it knows the subtle shift in air pressure that precedes the thaw’s softening grip. Its knowledge is written in posture, in timing, in the minute calibration of a single, poised foot. Watching it, I begin to unlearn my own frantic metrics—the need to *do*, to *achieve*, to *move on*. Here, on this narrow strip of frozen earth, time is not a river rushing downstream, but a pool—deep, still, holding its reflection perfectly, waiting only for the next ripple, the next breath, the next slow, inevitable turn of the light. And the heron, standing in the centre of it, is not waiting for spring. It is holding winter, whole and complete, in the quiet architecture of its own bones.

title: nature essay|a winter of watching one heron on the same canal
text:
The canal holds its breath. Not frozen—not quite—but thick with cold, the water sluggish, a dull pewter under low sky, its surface stippled with rain that falls more like mist than drops, fine and persistent, blurring the edges of things. I walk the towpath most days, boots sinking slightly into the damp earth at the bank’s edge, and there it is: the heron, always in the same place, a grey sentinel on the far side, halfway between the old brick bridge and the rusted iron footbridge where the ivy has long since swallowed the railings whole. It stands motionless, one leg drawn up beneath its belly, the other planted deep in the shallows, knee bent at an angle that seems impossible for bone and tendon, yet perfectly still. Its neck coils like a spring wound too tight, head tilted, beak pointed downward, not toward the water but just above it, as if listening to the silence beneath the surface.

I have watched this bird through weeks of sleet that silvered the reeds and turned the towpath into a slick, treacherous ribbon of black ice; through days when the air smelled of wet stone and decaying cattails, and the only movement was the slow, reluctant drift of a single leaf caught in an eddy near the lock gate. It does not flinch when the wind lifts, rattling the brittle stalks of last summer’s flag iris, nor when the geese pass overhead in ragged V’s, their cries sharp and hollow against the muffled hush. Once, a fox trotted along the opposite bank, low and liquid, pausing to stare across the water—not at the heron, but past it—as if the bird were part of the landscape’s grammar, unremarkable as a snag or a submerged root. The heron did not blink. Its eyelids, pale and almost translucent, closed only in slow, deliberate blinks, each one lasting several seconds, like the shutter of an old camera.

Its plumage is not the clean, stark grey of illustrations, but layered—slate at the back, charcoal along the wings, with faint, dusty buff streaks down the throat, like smudges of old chalk. In certain lights—those rare, thin moments when the sun breaks through the cloud cover, casting long, weak shadows—the feathers catch a sheen, not of gloss, but of depth, as though the light sinks into them rather than bounces off. When it does move—and it moves rarely—it unfolds with a kind of reluctant grace: the lifted leg descending, the neck uncoiling not all at once but in three distinct, unhurried stages, the head swinging forward, then down, then still again. Its feet, scaled and yellow, settle into the mud with quiet finality, toes splaying slightly, anchoring it. I have seen it strike only twice. Both times, the motion was less a lunge than a collapse of stillness—a sudden, vertical drop of the head, a flash of white wing as it recoiled, a small, silvery fish thrashing once in its beak before vanishing down its throat. No triumph, no pause. Just the return to posture, the slow re-coiling, the resumption of waiting.

The canal itself changes with the season, though never dramatically. The water level rises after heavy rain, swallowing the lower rungs of the stone steps near the weir, turning the banks into soft, dark margins where water striders skitter in tight, nervous circles. In frost, the reeds bow under white weight, their feathery heads nodding, and the heron stands amid them like a figure carved from the same material—bone-dry, patient, indifferent to the cold that stiffens my fingers even inside gloves. One morning, a thin skin of ice had formed over a shallow pool just upstream, and the heron stepped onto it, testing, then settling, its weight held by the fragile film. It stood there for nearly an hour, reflected upside-down in the glassy surface, the two images—one real, one inverted—so perfectly aligned that for long stretches I could not tell which was which, nor whether the reflection was the truer version.

People pass. A woman with a terrier stops, points, says, “Look, a heron!” Her voice sounds loud, intrusive. The dog strains at the leash, whining. The heron does not turn its head. A boy on a bicycle slows, pedals idling, then speeds away, shouting something unintelligible. The heron remains. Even the ducks ignore it—mallards paddle past, bobbing, preening, utterly unconcerned, as if the heron were merely another piece of driftwood, another weathered post half-submerged in the murk.

At dusk, the light bleeds out of the sky in slow gradations—pearl, then ash, then indigo—and the heron becomes a darker shape against the darkening water, its outline softening until it is little more than a suggestion, a slight denser patch of shadow where the reeds meet the bank. I do not see it fly. It simply ceases to be visible, absorbed into the gathering dim. Sometimes, in the very last light, I glimpse the faintest tremor in its stance—not a shiver, but a minute adjustment, a shift of weight so subtle it might be imagined, a quiet recalibration of balance as the temperature drops further and the first true stars prick through the violet haze.

I do not know how long it has been here. Months, perhaps. Or longer. It does not appear to migrate, not this one. It does not seem to roost elsewhere; I have never seen it depart at dawn or arrive at dusk. It is simply *there*, as the bricks of the bridge are there, as the moss on the lock gate’s iron hinge is there—part of the canal’s slow, unspoken syntax. Its stillness is not absence, but presence refined to its essential frequency: a pulse measured not in beats, but in the space between them; a vigil kept not for something expected, but for the sheer, unadorned fact of being present, in this exact place, in this exact cold, in this exact light, watching the water watch itself, while the world walks past, barely glancing, and the canal flows on, indifferent, carrying nothing but its own slow, cold weight.

title: memoir|growing up above a family laundry in a northern English town
text:
In the heart of a northern English town, where the cobblestone streets whispered tales of yesteryears and the air carried the scent of coal and rain, I grew up above a family laundry. The sign, faded but still legible, read "Lancaster's Laundry" in bold, blue letters. It was a modest shop, tucked between a bakery that filled the morning with the aroma of fresh bread and a small, cluttered bookshop that seemed to hold more stories than it could possibly contain.

My father, John Lancaster, was a man of few words but many smiles. He had taken over the laundry from his own father, who had passed away when I was just a toddler. My mother, Margaret, was the warmth in our home, her laughter a melody that danced through the rooms. She worked alongside my father, her hands always busy, whether it was folding linens or tending to the customers who often lingered for a chat.

Our flat was on the second floor, a cozy space with wooden floors that creaked underfoot and walls that held the memories of generations. The kitchen, with its old gas stove and chipped porcelain sink, was the heart of our home. It was here that we gathered for meals, shared stories, and made plans for the future.

I remember one particular winter, when the snow fell thick and heavy, blanketing the town in a serene white. The laundry business was slow, and my parents worried about making ends meet. One evening, as the wind howled outside, my father sat at the kitchen table, poring over ledgers and bills. His brow was furrowed, and the lines on his face seemed deeper than usual.

"John, don't worry so much," my mother said, placing a steaming cup of tea in front of him. "We'll get through this, like we always do."

He looked up, his eyes meeting hers, and for a moment, the weight of the world seemed to lift. "You're right, Meg. We'll find a way."

I watched them, feeling a sense of security and love that only a child can feel. Despite the challenges, our home was a place of warmth and resilience.

The laundry itself was a maze of machines and baskets, each with its own purpose. There was the large, industrial washing machine that rumbled like an old train, the long, metal irons that heated on the stoves, and the racks where the freshly laundered clothes hung, swaying gently in the warm, humid air. I spent countless hours down there, helping my parents, learning the trade, and listening to the stories of the people who came through our doors.

One of our regulars was Mrs. Hargreaves, a widow who lived alone in a small cottage on the edge of town. She would come in every week, her arms laden with a basket of linens, and always with a smile. "Good afternoon, dear," she would say, her voice soft and kind. "How are you today?"

"I'm well, thank you, Mrs. Hargreaves," I would reply, taking the basket from her. "And how are you?"

"Oh, I'm just fine, dear. Just fine." She would then sit in one of the chairs by the window, watching the world go by, while my mother and I sorted and washed her linens.

Another customer was Mr. Thompson, a retired schoolteacher who had a penchant for tweed jackets and bow ties. He would bring in his suits and shirts, and we would have long conversations about history and literature. "You know, young man," he once told me, "books are the windows to the world. Never stop reading."

I took his advice to heart, and soon, the small library in our flat became my sanctuary. I devoured books, from classic novels to encyclopedias, and even the occasional romance novel that my mother kept hidden in a drawer.

As the years passed, the town changed, and so did our little laundry. New, modern laundromats opened, and the demand for our services dwindled. But my parents never lost their spirit. They adapted, offering dry cleaning and alterations, and the community continued to support us.

One summer, when I was seventeen, I decided to leave for university. It was a bittersweet moment, standing in the doorway of the laundry, saying goodbye to my parents and the life I had known. My father, his eyes glistening, handed me a small, wrapped package. "Something to remember us by," he said, his voice steady but full of emotion.

Inside was a photograph of the three of us, taken in front of the laundry, and a note from my mother. "Always follow your dreams, my son. We will always be here for you."

As I boarded the train, the familiar sights of the town receding into the distance, I felt a deep sense of gratitude. Growing up above a family laundry in a northern English town had given me more than just a roof over my head; it had given me a foundation of love, resilience, and the belief that no matter what, I could always find my way back home.

title: personal essay|why I keep a notebook of overheard sentences
text:
I keep a notebook—blue, spiral-bound, slightly warped from sitting in the rain once outside a café in Portland—that’s full of other people’s words. Not quotes from books. Not lyrics I love and scribble down like a teenager. Just… things overheard. Snippets. Fragments. The kind that land in your ear like a dropped earring: small, shiny, inexplicably significant.

Last Tuesday, at the bus stop near 23rd and Burnside, a woman in a mustard-yellow raincoat said to no one in particular, *“My therapist says I’m not wrong for wanting silence. Just inconvenient.”* I wrote it down before the bus came. My pen smudged because my thumb was damp and I hadn’t wiped it off after touching the wet bench slats. That sentence still hums in my head—not because it’s profound, but because of the way she paused after “silence,” like she’d just cracked open something heavy and let the air rush in.

Why do I do this? Not for research. Not for writing stories (though sometimes I steal them, shamelessly—I’ll admit it). It’s more like… listening with my hands. Like catching falling ash on paper before it vanishes.

I started in college, during a terrible poetry workshop where everyone kept saying “find your voice” like it was a lost set of keys under the couch. I kept trying—and failing—to sound like myself on the page. Then one afternoon, sitting on the floor of the library’s third-floor stacks, I heard two grad students arguing softly behind the philosophy section: *“You can’t cite Kant if you haven’t cried while reading him.”* I copied it into a margin. Didn’t even know who Kant was, really. But the sentence had weight. A kind of quiet, stubborn truth. And something clicked: maybe my voice wasn’t mine alone. Maybe it was all the voices I carried, half-remembered, half-stolen, folded into my own like origami cranes stuffed in a coat pocket.

The notebook isn’t neat. Pages are dog-eared, coffee-ringed. One entry is written in pencil, then smudged by a thumbprint—*“He didn’t leave. He just… unarrived.”* (Overheard at a funeral home, of all places. The woman speaking wore lavender gloves and kept adjusting her glasses. Her left lens was slightly fogged.) Another page has a grocery list scrawled sideways in the margin: *milk, kale, that weird pear-shaped soap*, then back to: *“I named my anxiety ‘Gary’ so I could yell at him in public and people just think I’m eccentric.”*

Sometimes I go weeks without adding anything. Other times, three entries in one day—like yesterday, when I caught a barista say *“This espresso shot tastes like a missed opportunity”* while steaming milk. I laughed out loud. She looked up, startled. I mumbled something about the weather. Wrote it down anyway.

People ask if it feels intrusive. Honestly? Sometimes. Once, at a hospital waiting room, an older man whispered to his wife, *“I forgot how soft your hand feels when you’re scared.”* I hesitated. Pen hovered. Then I wrote it—but I tore that page out later and folded it into a tiny square, slipped it into the pocket of my winter coat, and forgot about it until spring, when I found it again, brittle and faintly smelling of cedar.

I don’t transcribe full conversations. Never names. Rarely context. Just the line that sticks—the one that vibrates at the same frequency as something inside me I didn’t know was humming. Like last month, on the MAX train: a kid, maybe six, pointing at a pigeon on the tracks and declaring, *“That bird looks like he’s thinking about quitting.”* I snorted. The woman beside me smiled, then turned back to her crossword. I wrote it. Underlined *quitting*. Because yeah. Me too, buddy. Me too.

It’s not nostalgia. I don’t romanticize strangers. Some of these lines are sad, sure. Some are funny. Some are just… odd. Like the time I heard a man mutter, *“My socks are conspiring against me today”* while tying his shoes outside a laundromat. No deeper meaning. Just a perfect little absurdity, warm and human and utterly unrepeatable.

Maybe what I’m really collecting isn’t language—but evidence that we’re all stumbling through the same strange, tender, ridiculous mess, whispering truths into thin air, hoping someone hears them, or at least catches the echo.

The notebook’s getting full. The spine’s cracking. I’ll buy a new one soon. Same blue. Same spiral. Probably spill something on it within a week.

And I’ll keep listening. Not for wisdom. Not for material.

Just for the way a sentence lands—unexpected, unasked-for, real—as if the world leaned in, just once, and told me something true, in passing.

title: personal essay|living next to a railway line for twenty years
text:
The train hits the crossing bells just as I’m stirring the porridge—*clong, clong, clong*, low and insistent, vibrating the spoon handle against my palm. Steam rises in a slow, steady column from the pot; outside, the air shivers with the approaching rumble, a deep, guttural thrum that doesn’t so much arrive as *unfurl*, like a wave gathering beneath the floorboards. I don’t look up. My wrist moves in the same small clockwise circle it’s moved every weekday morning for nineteen years, seven months, and three days—long enough that the rhythm of the spoon matches the rhythm of the 7:42 express without conscious thought. The train doesn’t startle me anymore. It *anchors* me.

That’s the first thing people misunderstand: they assume it’s noise you learn to ignore. But you don’t ignore it. You absorb it. It becomes the bassline to your domestic symphony—the scrape of toast on plate, the hiss of the kettle, the muffled laughter from the neighbour’s garden two doors down—all layered over the constant, low-grade hum of the rails themselves, a vibration you feel more than hear, like the house breathing. On still nights, if the windows are open, you can feel the metallic sigh of the tracks cooling after a hot day, a faint, almost imperceptible contraction that sends a tremor up through the floorboards and into the soles of your bare feet. It’s not intrusion. It’s presence. A neighbour who never knocks but whose footsteps you know by heart.

I remember the first winter, twenty years ago, when the frost heaved the pavement along the fence line and the ground cracked like old pottery. We’d just moved in—a young couple with second-hand furniture and untested optimism—and the trains felt like violations. Not just the noise, but the *arrogance* of them: the sudden, blinding glare of headlights slicing through our bedroom window at 3:17 a.m., the way the whole house would shudder when a freight train, loaded with timber or grain or something nameless and heavy, ground past at walking pace. We’d lie awake, listening to the rhythmic *clack-clack-clack* of wheels over rail joints, counting them like sheep, each one a tiny indignity. We argued about soundproofing, about moving, about whether this was sustainable—or even sane. Then, one February morning, snow falling thick and silent, the world muffled under a white hush, the 6:58 commuter train came through, its engine a soft, muffled groan, its carriages trailing plumes of warm vapour into the frozen air. And for the first time, instead of flinching, I watched. Really watched. Saw how the snow settled differently on the warm metal of the overhead wires, how the conductor’s breath fogged the cab window, how the train itself seemed less like an intruder and more like a necessary artery, pulsing life through the sleeping town. That was the quiet pivot.

Over time, the railway taught me to listen differently. Not *past* the noise, but *into* it. There’s the language of the horns: the sharp, urgent double-blast for the level crossing, the longer, mournful single note for a station stop, the irregular, questioning toot of the shunter in the sidings behind the old goods yard. There’s the weather report in the rails: a high, thin whistle when cold air tightens the steel; a damp, sluggish groan when humidity hangs thick before rain; a bright, brittle rattle in the dry heat of August. Even the birds adapted. The sparrows learned to time their chattering bursts between the passing of trains, their songs stitching the silences like embroidery. We planted willows along the fence—not for privacy, but because their long, supple branches sway *with* the vibration, not against it, turning the tremor into a gentle, green rustle.

I’ve watched generations of commuters pass my kitchen window. Teenagers slumped in hoodies, earbuds in, eyes glazed, riding the same carriage every day until their faces softened into adulthood. Older men in raincoats, briefcases balanced on knees, reading newspapers that grew thinner, then vanished, replaced by tablets held at the same angle, the same weary tilt of the head. Once, during a prolonged strike, the silence was so profound it felt like pressure in the ears. No distant whistle, no rhythmic shudder, no sudden, familiar surge of acceleration. The garden birds sang too loudly. The wind sounded raw and unmoored. We missed the train. Not the convenience, but the *continuity*. Its absence left a hollow where rhythm used to live.

My daughter learned her numbers on the platform bench, counting carriages—“One blue, two red, three yellow!”—her small hand patting the warm metal pole beside her. She knew the 4:15 was the “mummy’s train,” the one that brought me home smelling of city rain and coffee, her small arms already reaching before the doors fully opened. When she was eight, she lay on the grass verge one summer evening, ear pressed to the rail, and whispered, “It sounds like a heartbeat. A really big, slow one.” She was right. It does. Steady. Unhurried. Enduring.

Now, the rails are quieter than they were. Diesel has given way to electric, smoother, quieter, less percussive. The freight traffic dwindled; the sidings stand mostly empty, overgrown with bindweed and self-seeded buddleia. Sometimes, I worry the rhythm is fading, that the anchor is loosening. But then a heritage steam train passes, its deep, resonant *chuff-chuff-chuff* rolling across the fields like thunder, and the whole neighbourhood leans out of windows, drawn by the sheer, visceral *weight* of the sound—the heat, the smoke, the raw, beautiful labour of it. And I feel it again: the deep, familiar throb in the floor, the vibration in the teacup on the sill, the unbroken thread connecting this quiet morning to all the others, stretching back two decades, a steady pulse beneath the surface of ordinary life—proof that some things don’t need to be loud to be essential, and some neighbours, though they never cross the fence, become the very ground you stand on.

title: personal essay|living next to a railway line for twenty years
text:
For twenty years, the railway line has been my neighbor, a constant presence that I’ve come to know as intimately as the lines on my own hands. It is not just a strip of metal and gravel, but a living, breathing entity that pulses with its own rhythm, day and night. The tracks run parallel to the back of our house, a mere stone’s throw away, close enough for me to feel the vibrations through the soles of my feet when a train passes by.

When we first moved in, the sound was jarring, a harsh intrusion into the quietude of our new home. The screech of metal wheels on steel, the deep, resonant hum of the engine, and the occasional whistle that pierced the air like a sharp cry—all of it felt like an assault on the senses. But over time, the noise became a part of the fabric of our lives, as familiar and unremarkable as the ticking of a clock or the creaking of floorboards underfoot.

The trains come at all hours, each one a different character in the ongoing narrative of the line. There are the freight trains, lumbering giants that rumble past in the dead of night, their cars filled with the raw materials of industry: coal, timber, and steel. They move slowly, almost reluctantly, as if burdened by the weight of their cargo. In the darkness, I can see the glow of their lights, a string of fireflies moving through the shadows, and I imagine the distant places these goods will travel, the factories and cities they will feed.

Then there are the passenger trains, sleek and swift, a blur of color and motion. They arrive and depart with a precision that is almost musical, their schedules as predictable as the tides. In the morning, they carry commuters to the city, faces pressed against the windows, lost in thought or buried in books. In the evening, they return, the carriages filled with the weary and the hopeful, the tired and the triumphant. I often wonder about the stories of the people inside, the lives they lead, the dreams they chase, and the homes they leave behind.

Living next to the railway has given me a unique perspective on the passage of time. The trains mark the hours, the days, and the seasons, each one a reminder of the relentless march of life. In the spring, the tracks are flanked by wildflowers, their colors bright against the dull gray of the gravel. In the summer, the heat makes the metal expand, and the rails sing a low, mournful song. In the fall, the leaves from the trees along the line scatter across the tracks, a confetti of gold and red. And in the winter, the snow mutes the sounds, turning the world into a hushed, white landscape, where the trains cut through the silence like knives.

There are moments, too, when the railway becomes a stage for unexpected drama. Once, during a fierce storm, a tree fell across the tracks, blocking the path of an oncoming train. The conductor, a man with a weathered face and a calm demeanor, emerged from the cab, his flashlight cutting through the rain. He worked methodically, clearing the debris, while the passengers waited, huddled together, their breath fogging the windows. It was a scene of quiet heroism, a small victory against the forces of nature.

Over the years, I have come to appreciate the railway not just as a means of transportation, but as a symbol of connection. It links us to the wider world, a lifeline that stretches out in both directions, binding us to the past and the future. The tracks are a thread that runs through the tapestry of our lives, a constant reminder of the journeys we take, both literal and metaphorical.

Sometimes, late at night, when the house is still and the world seems to hold its breath, I lie awake and listen to the trains. The sound is a lullaby, a soothing melody that carries me through the dark hours. Each train that passes is a promise, a whisper of the adventures yet to come, the possibilities that lie ahead. And in those moments, I am grateful for this strange and wonderful neighbor, this ever-present companion on the journey of my life.

title: memoir|working nights in a hospital kitchen at nineteen
text:
The Night Shift, 1998

I was nineteen and smelled of bleach and burnt sugar. Not the clean, sharp kind—the sour, clinging residue that seeped into the cuffs of my uniform, settled in the creases behind my ears, and lingered on my tongue like a bad aftertaste. My job was to run the night kitchen at St. Brigid’s, a crumbling brick hospital on the city’s western edge—less a culinary station, more a low-humming engine room for sustenance: trays for the unwell, coffee for the exhausted, toast for the newly bereaved.

The day shift left at six. By seven, the lights dimmed—not fully, but enough to flatten the colour from the linoleum, turning it the grey of old dishwater. The automatic doors hissed shut behind the last nurse, and the building exhaled: a slow, metallic sigh through vents, the groan of ancient pipes, the distant, rhythmic *thump-thump-thump* of the laundry chutes. Then silence, thick and watchful, broken only by the refrigerator’s bass drone and the scrape of my spoon against stainless steel.

My domain was a narrow corridor of stainless steel and steam: two convection ovens, a deep fryer that bubbled with quiet menace, a walk-in cooler where the air tasted of raw celery and damp concrete, and a prep table scarred with knife marks and dried gravy. I worked alone. No supervisor. No schedule beyond the handwritten list taped to the microwave: *7:30 – 20x oatmeal w/raisins; 10:00 – 45x toast (wheat, no butter); 1:15 – 12x broth (low-sodium, warmed, not boiled); 3:45 – 8x coffee (black, double-strength, carafe 3).*

The oatmeal was the worst. Not because it was hard, but because it was monotonous. A hundred and twenty cups of porridge, each portion measured by a dented aluminum scoop, each pot stirred with a wooden paddle that grew slick and heavy. Steam rose in veils, blurring the fluorescent tubes overhead until they bled into smudges of yellow light. My arms ached. My eyes watered—not from emotion, but from the alkaline sting of the industrial cleaner I used to scour the griddle between batches of toast. I’d wipe my face with the back of my wrist, leaving a faint, greasy smear.

People think night shifts are empty. They’re not. They’re full of different kinds of presence. There were the orderlies who drifted in around midnight, shoulders slumped, eyes hollowed out by the weight of bodies they’d moved—living, dying, already gone. They’d lean against the counter, silent, accepting a cup of coffee without thanks, staring past me at the wall clock, its second hand ticking with unnerving loudness. Sometimes, one would ask for an extra slice of toast, just the bread, no butter. He’d eat it slowly, methodically, as if chewing were the only thing anchoring him to the floor.

Then there were the patients who wandered. Not often, but sometimes—a woman in a faded floral gown, barefoot, holding a plastic cup of water she hadn’t touched, asking, “Is it morning yet?” Her voice thin, uncertain, like a radio signal fading in and out. I’d nod, pour her fresh water, point vaguely down the hall toward the nurses’ station. She’d drift away, her footsteps soft on the linoleum, and I’d watch her reflection in the darkened window above the sink until she vanished into the corridor’s gloom.

Once, at 2:30 a.m., a young man in a hospital gown stood before me, trembling. His IV pole leaned against the counter like a third limb. “They said I could have juice,” he whispered. “Apple. Just apple.” His hands shook so badly he couldn’t hold the cup. I poured it, steadied his wrist, held the cup while he drank. He didn’t look at me. He looked at the steam rising from the kettle behind me, as if it held some answer. When he finished, he murmured something I couldn’t catch, then turned and walked back down the hall, his bare feet making no sound.

I learned the architecture of exhaustion. How the body doesn’t just tire—it recalibrates. Your knees feel lighter, your thoughts slower, your sense of time dissolving into intervals measured not in hours, but in the cycle of the dishwasher’s rinse cycle, the hum of the freezer compressor, the exact number of seconds it takes for the toaster to pop. You stop noticing the cold until your fingers go numb gripping the metal handle of the walk-in door. You stop hearing the distant sirens until one stops outside, its red light pulsing silently against the high windows, painting the walls in fleeting, arterial streaks.

I never saw the sun rise from that kitchen. I’d finish at five-thirty, lock the doors, walk out into the city’s first grey light—streetlights still burning, buses idling, shopkeepers pulling down metal grilles. The air felt thin, brittle. I’d walk home past closed bakeries, their windows dark, past the all-night laundromat where a single man sat hunched over a folding chair, watching his clothes tumble. I’d pass my own apartment building, its lobby light flickering, and climb the stairs, my keys jingling too loudly in the stairwell’s hollow quiet.

Back then, I thought the work was about feeding people. It wasn’t. It was about bearing witness to the interstitial hours—the long, unremarkable stretches between crisis and care, between sleep and waking, between life and whatever comes next. We weren’t preparing meals. We were holding space for the body’s stubborn, quiet persistence: the need to swallow, to warm the throat, to hold something warm in cold hands.

I quit in March. Not dramatically. Just handed in my notice, collected my final pay in crumpled bills, wiped down the prep table one last time. The new kid was seventeen, wide-eyed, already smelling faintly of bleach and burnt sugar. I didn’t tell him anything useful. Just pointed to the list on the microwave, showed him where the spare spoons were kept, and walked out.

I don’t miss it. But sometimes, in the deep quiet before dawn—when the world is suspended, neither day nor night—I’ll catch the scent of overcooked oats, or hear the particular, resonant *ping* of a cooling metal pan, and for a fraction of a second, I’m back there: standing in the steam, listening to the building breathe, stirring porridge for people I’ll never know, waiting for a clock that never quite catches up.

title: literary essay|why old maps are more honest than new ones
text:
Old maps are more honest. Not *better*, mind you—God knows, they’ll get you lost in the North Sea if you trust them—but *honest*. There’s a difference.
