I say this standing in the Bodleian’s Weston Library, squinting at a 1584 Dutch portolan chart where the coast of Norway is drawn with such confident, looping curves it looks like someone traced the edge of a teacup. Greenland is labelled *Terra Incognita*, but not blank—oh no. It’s filled with three fat, snarling sea serpents, one with a single, lidless eye and what appears to be a tiny bishop’s mitre perched crookedly on its head. A marginal note, in spidery Latin, reads: *Hic sunt dracones. Et fortasse piscis bonus.* (“Here be dragons. And perhaps good fish.”)

That’s honesty.

Modern maps? They’re polite. Polished. Obsessively *correct*, down to the centimetre, yet utterly disingenuous. Google Maps tells me my walk to the chemist is “7 minutes, 520 metres”—as if time and distance were fixed things, not variables subject to rain-slicked pavements, a sudden memory of my father whistling off-key outside that same chemist in ’98, or the way the light hits the stained glass above the bakery door just past the bus stop at 4:17 p.m., every Tuesday. The app doesn’t know about the pause. Doesn’t care. It renders absence as silence, not as grief. It shows the footpath—but not the crack in the pavement where I dropped my mother’s locket in ’03, never found it, still look down there, every time.

Old maps admit their ignorance. They don’t hide it behind algorithms or “estimated times.” They draw blanks—and then fill them with whales wearing crowns, islands shaped like sleeping monks, rivers that flow *uphill* because, well, someone swore they did, and who was the cartographer to argue with a sailor who’d just survived six weeks of salt-rot and scurvy? He’d seen things. Or thought he had. Either way—the map says so. Loudly. In gold leaf, sometimes.

I remember holding a 1627 Mercator world map at the British Library, trembling slightly—not from awe, but from the sheer *weight* of its admission. South America is lopsided, bulging westward like a man holding his breath; Japan floats 500 miles east of where it should be; the Caspian Sea is drawn as a perfect oval, because that’s how Herodotus described it, and Herodotus, bless him, hadn’t been there either. But the map doesn’t pretend otherwise. It cites him. In the corner, a little vignette: a scholar in a velvet cap, pointing at a scroll. Caption: *Ex vetustis autoribus.* “From ancient authors.” No shame. No disclaimers. Just: *This is what we’ve been told. This is what we believe enough to draw.*

New maps erase the teller. They speak in the voice of the network, the satellite, the consensus algorithm—all disembodied, all certain. Even OpenStreetMap, which prides itself on being “human-powered,” smooths out the tremor in the hand. You submit a road edit; it gets validated, averaged, merged into the grid. Your doubt—“Wait, does that alley actually connect, or did Mrs. Gable just *think* it did?”—gets filtered out. Deleted. Polished into neutrality.

And the colours! Oh, the colours of old maps—ochre for deserts, lapis lazuli for oceans (ground from real stone, mixed with egg yolk), vermilion for royal domains. They’re not trying to replicate reality. They’re trying to *mean* something. That deep blue isn’t water—it’s mystery. That gold border isn’t decoration; it’s a warning: *You are approaching the edge of the known. Proceed with prayer.*

My neighbour, Elara, a retired geodesist, once showed me her GPS unit—a sleek, black thing that chirped cheerfully as it recalculated my route around a fallen branch. “It doesn’t know the branch is fallen,” she said, tapping the screen. “It only knows the branch *isn’t on the map anymore*.” She paused. “Old maps knew branches fell. They knew roads washed away. They knew people lied. So they drew the lie *and* the doubt—in the same stroke.”

Which brings me to the margins. Always the margins. That’s where the honesty lives. Not in the coastlines, but in the borders: the ink blots, the coffee stains, the tiny, scratched-in corrections (“*Non Sicilia sed Sardinia*”), the doodles of ships with absurdly long masts, the faint pencil sketch of a dog in the lower left corner—probably drawn by the apprentice while the master napped. Evidence of the human hand. The tired eye. The moment of hesitation.

We don’t make maps like that anymore. We make interfaces. Tools. Things that serve. Old maps *confess*. They say: *I am made by a man who feared God, loved wine, misheard a name, and once got very, very lost near the Azores.*  

That’s not accuracy.  
That’s truth.  
And truth, like a good map, doesn’t always point north.  
Sometimes it just points, unflinchingly, at the dragon.

title: creation myth|how the northern lights were woven
text:
...and so, the weaver of the skies, Aelara, found herself in a quandary. The heavens had been woven with such precision and beauty, yet something was amiss. The northern expanse of the sky remained unadorned, a vast, dark canvas that seemed to yearn for color and light. Aelara, whose fingers were as delicate as spider silk and as strong as the winds, knew that this task would be her greatest challenge.

She sought counsel from the ancient spirits, who resided in the shimmering mists of the celestial river. The spirits, wise and enigmatic, spoke in riddles and whispers. "To weave the northern lights, you must gather threads from the four corners of the world," they said. "Only then can you create a tapestry that will dance and sing with the very essence of life."

Aelara, undaunted, set forth on her journey. Her first destination was the fiery heart of the south, where the sun blazed with unrelenting heat. She descended through layers of scorching air, her eyes shielded by a veil of stardust. There, she met the Sun Guardian, a being of molten gold and searing light. The Guardian, impressed by Aelara's determination, gifted her a thread of pure, radiant fire. It burned with the intensity of a thousand suns, yet Aelara, with her deft touch, wove it into a strand that glowed softly, like the embers of a hearth.

Next, she traveled to the deep, icy waters of the north, where the moon cast its silvery glow upon the frozen waves. In the stillness of the night, Aelara encountered the Moon Weaver, a figure draped in robes of shimmering silver. The Moon Weaver, with a voice as gentle as the lapping of waves, presented Aelara with a thread of moonlight. This thread, cool and luminous, held the secrets of the tides and the mysteries of the night. Aelara, with great care, intertwined it with the fiery thread, creating a harmony of light and shadow.

Her third journey took her to the verdant forests of the east, where the trees whispered ancient secrets and the earth pulsed with life. Here, Aelara met the Earth Mother, a being of boundless wisdom and nurturing power. The Earth Mother, surrounded by a halo of green light, offered Aelara a thread of vibrant green, infused with the energy of the living world. This thread, rich and fertile, carried the essence of growth and renewal. Aelara, with a steady hand, wove it into the growing tapestry, adding a touch of life and vitality.

Finally, Aelara ventured to the stormy peaks of the west, where the winds howled and the clouds gathered. At the summit, she faced the Wind Spirit, a creature of swirling mist and crackling lightning. The Wind Spirit, with a voice that thundered like the storms, bestowed upon Aelara a thread of electric blue, charged with the raw power of the elements. This thread, wild and untamed, brought a sense of movement and dynamism to the tapestry. Aelara, with a masterful touch, wove it into the fabric, infusing it with the energy of the tempest.

With the four threads gathered, Aelara returned to the northern sky, ready to complete her masterpiece. She stood at the edge of the darkness, her loom set up before her. The threads, each unique and powerful, lay in her hands, waiting to be woven. Aelara began her work, her fingers moving with a grace and precision that only a weaver of the heavens could possess. The fiery thread danced across the sky, leaving trails of golden light. The moonlight thread wove in and out, creating patterns of silver and shadow. The green thread added a touch of life, while the electric blue thread brought a sense of movement and energy.

As Aelara wove, the northern sky came alive. The threads, once separate and distinct, now merged into a single, breathtaking tapestry. The colors swirled and danced, forming intricate patterns that shifted and changed with the wind. The northern lights, as they came to be known, were a symphony of light and color, a testament to the weaver's skill and the magic of the world.

The spirits, watching from the celestial river, marveled at Aelara's creation. They saw in the northern lights a reflection of the world's beauty and diversity, a reminder that even in the darkest of places, there is always the potential for light and wonder. And so, the northern lights became a beacon, a symbol of hope and enchantment, forever dancing in the sky, a gift from the weaver to all who looked up and beheld their splendor.

title: memoir|the year spent caring for a grandmother with dementia
text:
The year began with the smell of burnt toast and silence where laughter used to live. I moved into her house—small, clapboard, painted a faded sage that peeled at the eaves—on a Tuesday in late March, the air still holding winter’s damp breath. Her name was Eleanor, but I’d called her Nana since I could speak, and even then, she’d leaned close when I said it, as if catching a falling thing. By March, she no longer recognized the word. She’d tilt her head, blink slowly, and say, “That’s a nice name,” as though I’d introduced myself.

Her hands were always moving: smoothing tablecloths that hadn’t been disturbed, folding napkins into tight, useless triangles, patting the armrests of her chair like testing the temperature of water. Once, I found her in the pantry, standing barefoot on a stack of folded dish towels, reaching for the top shelf—not for anything, just reaching, her fingers brushing the dusty underside of the cabinet. When I asked what she was after, she whispered, “The blue box. The one with the little birds.” There was no blue box. There hadn’t been for thirty years. But I didn’t say that. I brought her a teacup instead, the one with the chipped robin’s-egg glaze, and she held it like something sacred, turning it slowly in her palms, her thumb tracing the chip as if reading Braille.

She still knew how to make tea—kettle whistling sharp and insistent, milk poured first, sugar stirred counterclockwise—but she’d forget to lift the spoon, leaving it clinking against the porcelain long after the tea had cooled. Sometimes she’d pour the tea into the sugar bowl, then stare at the amber liquid pooling around the granules, her expression unreadable. I learned not to correct, only to replace, to rinse and refill, to fold the towel again and again.

Her bedroom smelled of lavender sachets and something deeper, older—the faint, sweet decay of paperbacks stacked beside the bed, their spines cracked, pages yellowed at the edges. She kept a shoebox under the bed filled with buttons: mother-of-pearl, wood, brass, one shaped like a tiny anchor. She’d sit on the floor, cross-legged despite the ache in her knees, sorting them by size or color or weight, humming a tuneless melody I’d never heard before, yet somehow recognized—as if it lived in my bones before I knew her voice.

One afternoon, rain sheeting down the windows, she stood at the back door, hand pressed to the glass, watching the neighbor’s cat slink across the wet grass. “He’s waiting for me,” she said. “He always waits.” I didn’t ask who. I brought her a blanket and sat beside her on the cold linoleum, our shoulders almost touching. She didn’t shiver. Her skin was warm, dry, papery. After a while, she turned and looked at me—not through me, not past me, but *at* me—with such startling clarity that my breath caught. “You have your mother’s eyes,” she said, and then, softer, “I’m sorry I forgot your name.” I told her it was okay. She nodded, as if accepting a fact already known, and went back to watching the cat, which had vanished.

We walked every day, rain or shine, though she rarely made it past the oak at the end of the driveway. She’d stop there, place a palm flat against the bark, and whisper something low and rhythmic, like a prayer or a lullaby. Once, she pulled a single acorn from her coat pocket—how it got there, I never knew—and pressed it into my hand. It was cool, smooth, impossibly heavy. I kept it on my desk for months, rolling it between my fingers when the silence in the house grew too thick.

She stopped sleeping deeply. Nights were long stretches of quiet vigil: the creak of floorboards as she wandered, the soft thud of a book sliding off the nightstand, the sound of her humming in the bathroom, voice thin and wavering, like a radio tuned just shy of frequency. I’d find her sitting on the closed toilet lid, fully dressed, staring at her reflection in the medicine cabinet mirror. Not frightened. Not confused. Just… present, in a way that felt more absolute than anything I’d ever witnessed. I’d sit on the edge of the tub and talk—about the weather, about the sparrows nesting in the eaves, about nothing at all—until her eyelids grew heavy and she let me guide her back to bed.

There was no grand unraveling, no dramatic collapse. Just a slow, quiet dimming, like a bulb losing wattage, filament trembling before the final hush. One morning, she didn’t rise. She lay in bed, eyes open, watching dust motes drift in the sunbeam slicing through the curtains. Her breathing was shallow, regular. I sat beside her, holding her hand—not the frail, bird-boned thing it had become, but the hand I remembered from childhood: strong, capable, smelling faintly of yeast and garden soil. She turned her palm up, and I placed the acorn there. She closed her fingers around it. Her thumb moved once, twice, over its curve.

Later, I washed the teacup—the one with the robin’s-egg glaze—and set it on the draining board to dry. Outside, the oak rustled, leaves newly unfurled, green and urgent. A sparrow landed on the sill, cocked its head, and peered in. I watched it until it flew away. Then I picked up the cup, rinsed it again, and placed it carefully in the cupboard, facing forward, where it belonged.

title: memoir|a childhood split between two countries and two languages
text:
The Grammar of Absence  

I learned to say *goodbye* before I understood it was a word that could mean *not yet*, or *not ever*, or simply *the space between two rooms*.  

My childhood wasn’t divided—it bled. One year, I was seven, standing barefoot on cool linoleum in a Toronto apartment, watching rain streak the windowpane while my mother rehearsed English sentences aloud: *“The bus arrives at three forty-five. Not three forty-four. Not three forty-six.”* Her voice was careful, almost apologetic, as if English were a guest she’d invited but hadn’t quite learned to host. The next year, I was back in Oaxaca, sleeping on a cot in my abuela’s adobe house, where the floor smelled of dried chiles and damp earth, and the air hummed with Spanish so thick it felt like breathing soup. There, time didn’t arrive at precise minutes; it settled, lingered, evaporated. *“Ya viene,”* Abuela would say—*It’s coming*—and the bus might appear in ten minutes or forty-five. No one corrected her. No one needed to.  

Languages didn’t live side by side in me. They occupied different anatomies. English lived in my throat—tight, precise, a muscle I had to flex deliberately to produce consonants cleanly. Spanish lived lower, in the soft palate and the belly, vowels opening wide and warm, consonants rolling or dissolving like sugar in hot milk. When I switched, it wasn’t translation; it was relocation. My shoulders dropped in Spanish. In English, I held them higher, as if bracing for correction.  

School in Toronto was a series of small, repeated dislocations. I’d raise my hand, form the sentence carefully in my head—*“Can I go to the bathroom?”*—but when I spoke, the words came out flattened, syllables clipped, the *r* swallowed whole. Other children mimicked me, not cruelly, but with the casual mimicry of something unfamiliar made momentarily amusing. I stopped raising my hand. I held it instead, until the bell rang, until I could walk out without asking. In Oaxaca, no one asked me to speak slowly. My cousins teased me for my Canadian accent—the way I said *“pescado”* too crisply, like a fish filet laid flat on ice—but they never questioned whether I belonged. Belonging there wasn’t spoken; it was measured in how much tamarind candy you were given, how long you were allowed to sit beside Abuela while she shelled beans, how quickly your hands learned the rhythm of kneading masa.  

There was no grand rupture, no dramatic farewell scene at an airport gate. Just the slow, quiet erosion of continuity. I’d return to Toronto after summer and find my English sharper, colder, more efficient—but also thinner, like paper held up to light. My Spanish, meanwhile, grew looser, more idiomatic, but also more fragile, prone to sudden gaps: the name of a common kitchen tool, the correct preposition for *“waiting for the bus,”* the exact shade of blue in the ceramic tile behind the church altar. These weren’t failures of memory. They were absences that had taken root, hollows where meaning used to sit.  

I remember once, at nine, trying to describe the sound of cicadas to my teacher. In Spanish, it was easy: *el zumbido que no para nunca, como si el aire mismo estuviera hirviendo.* In English, I faltered. *Buzzing? Humming? A high-pitched whine?* None of it carried the weight—the insistence, the heat, the sheer *presence*—of the original phrase. I gave up. She marked my description “vague” and moved on. I didn’t correct her. What would I have said? That vagueness wasn’t laziness, but the residue of living in two grammars, neither of which could fully hold the thing I meant?  

We never called it bilingualism. That word sounded too neat, too institutional, like a certificate pinned to a wall. We called it *lo que se habla en casa* and *lo que se habla en la escuela*, and later, *lo que se dice cuando hay gente de afuera*. Language wasn’t identity; it was weather—something you adjusted to, something that changed the quality of light in a room, something you couldn’t control but had to navigate.  

There were no epiphanies, no moments where the two halves fused into some luminous synthesis. Instead, there were accumulations: the way I still count money in Spanish, even now, decades later, fingers moving instinctively over bills as if sorting seeds; the way I dream sometimes in one language, sometimes the other, and wake unsure which world I’ve left behind; the way I’ll catch myself using a Mexican idiom in a Toronto meeting—*“¡Qué va!”*—and watch the polite, baffled pause settle over the table like dust.  

What remains isn’t balance. It’s a kind of calibrated instability. A constant, low-grade recalibration. I don’t feel whole in either tongue, nor do I seek wholeness there. I feel most myself in the slippage—the moment a phrase refuses translation, the hesitation before choosing a word, the slight lag between thought and utterance where something unnameable lives. That space isn’t emptiness. It’s the only place where both countries, both languages, both versions of my younger self, can stand together—not reconciled, not merged, but quietly, stubbornly, present.  

I still don’t know how to say goodbye properly. Not in either language. So I don’t try. I just wait, and listen, and let the silence between the words hold what the words cannot.

title: nature essay|the life of an abandoned quarry
text:
In the heart of the Cotswolds, where the rolling hills cradle secrets of a bygone era, lies the forsaken quarry of Upper Slaughter. It was here, under the watchful eyes of an ancient yew, that I first met Tom Bailey, a local historian and a man whose life had become intertwined with the silent stones. The quarry, once a bustling hive of activity, now stood as a testament to the ebb and flow of human endeavor.

Tom, a wiry man in his late sixties, with a shock of white hair and eyes that sparkled with the stories he carried, led me down a narrow path. "This place," he began, his voice carrying the gentle lilt of the countryside, "has seen more than its fair share of history. When the quarry was still active, it provided limestone for some of the grandest buildings in the region."

We walked past the crumbling remnants of a stone wall, overgrown with ivy and wildflowers. The air was cool and damp, and the only sounds were the distant calls of birds and the occasional rustle of leaves. Tom pointed to a spot where the ground sloped sharply downwards, revealing layers of sedimentary rock, each one a chapter in the geological narrative of the land. "The quarry was abandoned in 1962," he continued, "when the demand for limestone dwindled, and cheaper alternatives became available. The workers left, and nature began to reclaim what was hers."

As we descended into the heart of the quarry, the walls rose around us like the sides of a great bowl, their surfaces etched with the marks of countless chisels. The bottom of the quarry was a small, secluded world, a patchwork of grass, wildflowers, and shallow pools of water. Here, the sunlight filtered through the trees, casting dappled shadows on the ground.

"Look there," Tom said, pointing to a cluster of old tools lying half-buried in the earth. "Those are the remains of the quarrymen's work. They left them behind, perhaps thinking they'd be back, but they never returned." He picked up a rusted pickaxe, its handle worn smooth by years of use. "Imagine the hands that held this, the sweat and toil, the dreams and disappointments. It's all part of the story."

I asked Tom about the people who had worked here, and he shared tales of the quarrymen, their families, and the community that had thrived around the industry. "There was a man named John Smith, a foreman, who lived just up the hill. He was known for his strength and his kindness. He would often bring extra food from home to share with the other workers. His son, Michael, used to play among the rocks, dreaming of following in his father's footsteps. But when the quarry closed, those dreams faded, and Michael eventually moved away to find work in the city."

As we explored further, we came across a small, weathered wooden bench, nestled against the side of the quarry. "This was a favorite spot for the workers during their breaks," Tom explained. "They would sit here, eat their sandwiches, and share stories. Sometimes, they'd sing songs, and the sound would echo off the walls, filling the quarry with music."

We sat on the bench, and Tom fell silent, lost in thought. The sun was beginning to set, casting a golden glow over the quarry. The light danced across the water, and the shadows grew longer. In the stillness, I could almost hear the echoes of the past, the laughter and the voices of the men who had toiled here.

After a while, Tom spoke again, his voice soft and reflective. "You know, it's not just the stones that tell the story. It's the people, the lives they led, and the memories they left behind. This quarry may be abandoned, but it's not empty. It's full of the spirits of those who once called it home."

As we made our way back up the path, the darkness began to fall, and the stars appeared in the sky. The quarry, now a shadowy silhouette against the night, seemed to hold its breath, waiting for the next chapter in its long and storied life. And I knew that, for Tom, and for anyone who cared to listen, the quarry would continue to speak, its silent stones whispering the tales of the past.

title: short story|a beekeeper's widow deciding whether to keep the hives
text:
The hive box trembled in her hands—not with the low, resonant hum of life within, but with the fine, insistent vibration of her own pulse against the worn cedar grain. Eleanor stood at the edge of the south meadow, the late afternoon sun slanting gold and long across the clover, already gone to seed and dusted with a faint, silver down. Behind her, the old stone cottage hunched its shoulders against the cooling air, smoke curling thin and grey from the chimney—her own small fire, lit not for warmth, but as a habit, a tether. She hadn’t meant to come out here. Had meant only to refill the kettle, to wipe the flour-dusted counter where Ben used to knead bread dough with strong, knuckle-ridged hands. But the silence in the kitchen had pressed in, thick and suffocating, until she’d found herself pulling on his old waxed canvas jacket—the one that still held the ghost of propolis and warm beeswax—and stepping into the yard.

She lowered the box gently onto the grass, its weight familiar and alien all at once. *Hive Three*, the faded chalk mark on the lid read. Ben’s script. She ran a thumb over the groove where his initials—*B.M.*—had been carved years ago, then smoothed over, almost erased, by weather and time and countless passes of his palm. Inside, through the screened observation port, the colony moved: a slow, purposeful river of amber and black, glistening under the low light. They were building comb, drawing fresh, pale wax across the empty frames she’d left last week—*her* frames, placed not with Ben’s quiet certainty, but with hesitant, almost apologetic precision. She’d done it because the bees needed it. Because the brood chamber was tight, the queen laying steadily, and the nectar flow from the late-blooming goldenrod was thick and sweet. She’d done it because stopping felt like betrayal—not just of Ben, but of the rhythm itself, the ancient, humming contract between keeper and kept.

But the contract had always been Ben’s. He spoke their language in murmurs and pauses, reading the tilt of a guard bee’s antennae, the pitch of the hive’s thrum, the subtle shift in the scent of the entrance—a blend of honey, wax, alarm pheromone, and something indefinable, like warm earth after rain. Eleanor understood the mechanics: the sugar syrup for spring feedings, the powdered sugar dusting for mite checks, the careful, gloveless inspection he insisted upon ("They know fear," he’d say, holding out a hand for a worker to land, "not your gloves"). But she’d never grasped the *conversation*. She’d been the listener, the note-taker, the one who brought the tea and the clean cloths, who watched his face soften, his shoulders drop, when he stood before a full, contented hive. His calm was her anchor. Now, standing alone, the anchor was gone, and the water felt deep and cold.

A breeze stirred, lifting the dry grass and carrying the sharp, green tang of crushed mint from the border. A single bee, disoriented or perhaps just curious, bumped softly against the mesh of the observation port. Eleanor didn’t flinch. She watched its tiny, iridescent wings catch the light, the frantic, precise movement of its legs cleaning itself. It wasn’t afraid. It wasn’t asking permission. It was simply *being*, following an imperative older than memory, older than grief. Her throat tightened. This wasn’t about courage or fear, not really. It was about stewardship. Ben hadn’t owned these bees; he’d tended them, honoured their wildness even as he coaxed honey from their labour. To walk away now wouldn’t be liberation—it would be abandonment. And abandonment, she realized with a quiet, hollow certainty, was the one thing Ben would never have countenanced. Not of the bees, not of her, not of the fragile, sun-warmed world he’d so carefully nurtured.

She thought of the neighbours. Old Mr. Hemlock from the next valley, who’d stopped by yesterday, his cap clutched awkwardly in his large, work-roughened hands. "Terrible business, Ellie," he’d rumbled, eyes avoiding hers, fixed instead on the hives gleaming dully in the distance. "Hard work, keeping 'em on your own. Lot of folk round here… well, they’d take 'em off your hands. Fair price. No trouble." His kindness was a stone in her chest. Taking the hives meant selling Ben’s life’s quiet work, parceling it out like firewood. It meant the end of the morning ritual—the smell of warm wax rising from the supers as she lifted them, the soft, heavy *thump* of honey-laden comb against the scale, the way the light caught the golden liquid dripping from the uncapping fork. It meant silencing the sound that had been the bass note of their shared years—the constant, living hum that vibrated up through the soles of her boots, a sound that wasn’t noise, but presence. A sound Ben had called the "earth’s own breathing."

Yet, the practicalities loomed, cold and unblinking. The ladder leaning against the shed wall looked steeper. The varroa mite counts, though low this season, required vigilance she wasn’t sure she possessed. The paperwork for the organic certification, the insurance, the sheer physicality of moving supers laden with fifty pounds of honey—Ben had always handled it, his movements economical, sure. Could she? Or would she become the widow who let the hives dwindle, who missed a critical treatment window, whose negligence led to a collapse? The thought was a physical chill. Failure wasn’t just financial loss; it was complicity in a silent, buzzing death.

She knelt, the damp grass cool through her trousers, and pressed her palm flat against the warm wood of Hive Three. Through the cedar, she felt it—not just the vibration, but a deeper resonance, a steady, insistent *thrum* that seemed to rise from the ground itself, meeting the hive’s song. It was the same thrum she felt in her own chest when she stood very still and listened, not with her ears, but with her bones. Ben had taught her that too, though he’d never named it. *Listen to the stillness beneath the buzz,* he’d said once, watching a swarm settle on a pear branch. *That’s where the true strength lives.*

Eleanor closed her eyes. She didn’t hear Ben’s voice. She heard the wind in the tall grass. She heard the distant, lonely call of a curlew. And beneath it all, woven through the air, steady and undeniable, the hum. Not loud, not demanding, but *there*. Persistent. Patient. Waiting, perhaps, not for instruction, but for acknowledgment. For the simple, daily act of showing up.

She opened her eyes. The bee had flown. The light was deepening, turning the clover heads a soft, bruised purple. She didn’t stand up. She stayed kneeling, her hand resting on the hive, feeling the warm, living pulse beneath her palm. The decision wasn’t made. Not yet. But the paralyzing weight of the *should* and *must* and *can’t* had shifted, just slightly, like comb settling in the heat. What remained was quieter, sharper: the weight of the cedar grain under her thumb, the golden light on the grass, the deep, resonant hum vibrating up her arm, and the simple, terrifying, necessary truth that the next frame needed checking tomorrow. Before the light failed. Before the dew fell. Before the world, indifferent and beautiful, turned again. She took a slow breath, the air tasting of dust and dying clover and something sweet, almost imperceptible, like the first promise of honey. Her hand didn’t move from the wood.

title: literary novel|a lighthouse keeper's daughter returning after the light is automated
text:
The salt had seeped into the floorboards long before she left, a slow, patient invasion that turned pine the colour of weak tea and made the grain swell in damp seasons until the doors stuck. Now, stepping across the threshold for the first time in seventeen years, Elara felt it beneath her boots—not the grit of wind-scoured sand, but the faint, damp give of wood that remembered water. The air inside was colder than the late October gale outside, not sharp with the old tang of lamp oil and beeswax, but stale, thick with the quiet accumulation of absence. A single cobweb trembled above the mantelpiece, suspended like a frayed nerve.

She’d been twelve when the last keeper—her father—had walked down the spiral stairs for the final time, his oilskin coat smelling of brine and pipe smoke, his hands already stiffening at the knuckles. She’d stood on the gallery rail, bare feet cold on iron, watching the launch bob away, her father’s hat a small, dark shape receding into the grey. The light had kept burning, of course. Just not by him. Not by anyone. A clockwork heart now, wound tight in the lantern room, its beam sweeping the black water with indifferent precision. No more midnight climbs with kerosene cans sloshing against her thighs, no more wiping soot from the glass with chamois leather softened by years of handling, no more the low, rhythmic groan of the Fresnel lens turning on its mercury bath—a sound that had lived in her bones, a lullaby and a warning both.

The kitchen held the ghosts most insistently. The cast-iron stove, cold and black, its enamel chipped near the damper. The cupboard where her mother’s blue-glazed mug still sat, handle slightly askew, as if waiting for a hand to right it. Elara ran a finger along the shelf’s edge: dust, yes, but also the faint, waxy residue of candle stubs melted and re-hardened over decades. She opened the drawer where her father kept his whittling knives. One remained—the smallest, its bone handle worn smooth and yellowed, the blade dulled but un-rusted. She held it, the weight familiar, the curve of the handle fitting her palm as though it had been shaped for her alone. Outside, the wind rose, rattling the loose pane in the east window—the one she’d cracked at fourteen, throwing a stone at a gull that had stolen her sandwich. She’d never told him. He’d just sighed, wiped his spectacles, and said, “Salt’ll seal it soon enough.”

Upstairs, her room. The bed was stripped, mattress bare and stained in the centre, the springs sagging like tired shoulders. The wallpaper—faded roses climbing a trellis—peeled at the ceiling corner, revealing layers beneath: older paper, then plaster, then the rough-hewn lath. She pressed her palm flat against the wall where her height had been marked in pencil, year after year, a crooked ladder ascending beside the window frame. Her name, scrawled in childish script beneath the highest line: *Elara, 12*. Below it, her father’s careful hand: *June ’78*. She traced the letters, the graphite cool and powdery under her thumb. The window looked out over the same stretch of sea, the same jagged teeth of black rock below. But the light itself was gone from the tower’s crown. The lantern room was shuttered, the great lens covered in heavy canvas tarps, tied with thick, tarred rope. From here, the tower looked less like a sentinel and more like a wound dressed in grey cloth.

She climbed the stairs anyway. Not to the lantern room—that door was padlocked—but to the watchroom, the narrow chamber where her father had spent hours, logbook open, binoculars resting on the sill, listening to the radio crackle with weather reports and ship-to-shore static. The brass telegraph key sat on the desk, its lever frozen mid-click. She lifted the receiver of the old wall phone; dead silence, not even the hum of a dial tone. On the desk, beneath a sheet of glass, lay his logbook. She didn’t open it. She knew its rhythms: *0300 hrs. Gale force 8. Sea breaking high over south rocks. Light steady.* Her own childhood scribbles filled the margins—crude drawings of ships, a starfish, the word *bored* written fifty times in looping, angry script. One page bore a single, smudged fingerprint, dark as ink, where he’d rested his thumb while writing *Fog bank thick. Visibility nil.*

Down in the boathouse, the air smelled of rotting cedar and dried kelp. The skiff, *The Marigold*, sat on its cradle, paint blistered, oarlocks rusted orange. A single barnacle, white and sharp, clung to the hull near the waterline—proof the tide still remembered this place, even if the light did not. She ran her hand along the gunwale. The wood was dry, brittle, yet still held the ghost of its shape, the curve meant for cutting through water. A gull screamed overhead, a raw, tearing sound that echoed off the cliffs and seemed to hang in the air, unresolved.

That night, she slept on the floor of the living room, wrapped in a blanket smelling faintly of mothballs and something deeper, older—the scent of wool soaked in salt air and forgotten time. The wind howled around the tower’s base, a sound she hadn’t heard in years, yet it settled into her ribs without surprise. She woke once, disoriented, certain she’d heard the deep, resonant *thunk* of the lens mechanism engaging, the slow, inevitable turn beginning its sweep. But there was only wind, and the drip of condensation from the ceiling into the bucket she’d placed beneath the leak in the corner. She listened to the steady *plink… plink… plink*, counting the seconds between drops, the rhythm irregular, human, flawed. She closed her eyes again, and the dark behind her lids wasn’t empty. It held the afterimage of light—not the clean, mechanical beam, but the warmer, trembling gold that had spilled from the lantern room windows onto the wet rocks, the light her father had coaxed, tended, loved, and finally let go.

title: narrative poem|a ferry crossing in a storm
text:
The Ferryman’s Lament

The rain began as a whisper, a soft susurrus against the windowpane of the ferry’s pilothouse. I was alone, save for the creaking hull and the steady hum of the engines, their thrumming like the heartbeat of some ancient beast. The sky was a bruised canvas, darkening with every passing moment, and the sea, once a gentle cradle, now rose in swells, each wave a restless sigh.

I had been at this for years, ferrying souls from one shore to another, my vessel a mere speck in the vast expanse of water. The passengers, usually a mix of weary travelers and those with destinations etched into their eyes, were few tonight. They huddled below, their murmurs blending with the storm's growing crescendo. I envied them, their ability to seek refuge, while I stood watch, a solitary figure at the helm.

The wind picked up, howling like a chorus of the damned, and the ferry shuddered, its timbers groaning under the strain. I gripped the wheel, my knuckles white, and steered through the tempest, the lights of the distant shore a faint promise, a beacon that seemed to mock me. The waves grew taller, their crests foaming and frothing, and I felt the weight of the storm pressing down, a relentless force intent on swallowing us whole.

Below, a child cried, a thin, piercing wail that cut through the din. I imagined a mother, her arms wrapped around the small body, her face a mask of fear and determination. I thought of my own daughter, long since grown and far away, and wondered if she ever thought of me, the father who spent his days and nights on the water, always returning but never truly present.

The storm intensified, and the ferry dipped and rolled, each movement a violent dance. The compass spun wildly, and I relied on instinct, the feel of the boat beneath my feet, the taste of salt on my lips. Lightning split the sky, a jagged scar, and thunder rumbled, a deep, resonant voice that seemed to speak directly to me, its words lost in the chaos.

I remembered another night, many years ago, when the sea had been kinder, and the stars had lit our path. My wife had stood beside me, her hand on my shoulder, her laughter a melody that still echoed in my mind. She had loved the water, its endless possibilities, its mysteries. But she was gone now, taken by a different kind of storm, one that no man could navigate. The memory stung, a sharp pain that mingled with the cold and the wet.

The ferry groaned again, and I felt a jolt, a sudden lurch that sent me stumbling. The engine sputtered, and for a moment, all was silence, save for the roar of the wind and the crash of the waves. Panic surged, a cold, hard knot in my chest, and I fumbled with the controls, my hands shaking. The engine caught, a rough, uneven purr, and I breathed a sigh of relief, though it was fleeting.

The passengers below must have sensed the danger, for their murmurs grew louder, more urgent. I heard the sound of footsteps, the creak of the stairs, and then, a figure appeared at the door, a woman, her face pale and drawn. She clutched a small, sleeping child, her eyes wide with fear. "Are we going to make it?" she asked, her voice barely audible over the storm.

I met her gaze, and for a moment, I saw myself, a man adrift, navigating the tides of life and loss. "We’ll do our best," I said, and she nodded, a silent understanding passing between us. She turned and went back below, her steps slow and deliberate, and I was left alone once more, the weight of responsibility heavy on my shoulders.

The storm raged on, a symphony of fury, and I fought to keep the ferry on course, my muscles aching, my mind a whirlwind of thoughts and memories. The lights of the shore grew closer, a dim, flickering hope, and I pushed the engines harder, the boat straining against the waves. The wind howled, a mournful dirge, and the rain beat down, a relentless drumbeat.

Finally, the ferry reached the safety of the harbor, the water calmer, the storm receding. I guided the vessel to the dock, my hands steady, my heart still racing. The passengers emerged, their faces a mix of relief and exhaustion, and they thanked me, their voices quiet, their gratitude palpable. I nodded, a silent acknowledgment, and watched as they disembarked, their figures disappearing into the night.

Alone once more, I stood at the helm, the storm’s remnants a distant echo. The ferry, battered but resilient, rocked gently in the calm waters, and I felt a strange sense of peace, a fleeting respite from the turmoil. The night was not yet over, and there would be other storms, other crossings, but for now, in this moment, I was at rest, a ferryman in the eye of the storm, a solitary soul on the vast, unending sea.

title: memoir|working nights in a hospital kitchen at nineteen
text:
The fluorescent lights in the basement kitchen of St. Brigid’s Hospital in South Bend, Indiana, didn’t hum—they *thrummed*, a low, persistent vibration that settled behind my molars and made my fillings ache. I was nineteen, newly arrived from Warsaw, Indiana, with a duffel bag, a GED, and a letter from the county social worker that said, “This young man is reliable and needs work.” Reliable. That word tasted like cold oatmeal.

My shift began at 10:45 p.m., and by 11:02, I was already peeling fifty pounds of russet potatoes in the walk-in cooler—its steel door sweating condensation onto my forearms, the air thick with the damp, earthy smell of raw tubers and the faint, sour tang of yesterday’s boiled cabbage clinging to the drain grate. My fingers went numb after twenty minutes, then stiffened into clumsy hooks. Mrs. Lefebvre, the night supervisor, would glide past in her orthopedic sandals, smelling of peppermint gum and lavender hand sanitizer, and say, without breaking stride, “Danny, the mashed spuds need to be smooth—not lumpy like regret.” She’d been at St. Brigid’s since ’63, she told me once while scraping burnt-on macaroni off a steam table, and had watched three generations of night cooks age out, burn out, or get transferred upstairs to dietary administration, where they wore cardigans and stopped knowing the weight of a full stainless-steel pan.

I learned the rhythm: the clatter of aluminum trays on the conveyor belt at 2:17 a.m., when the first wave of overnight labs came down for coffee and toast; the soft, insistent *beep-beep-beep* of the dish machine alarm when the rinse temperature dropped below 180°F; the way the steam from the soup kettles rose in slow, translucent veils, catching the light like heat-haze over a cornfield. At 3:48, I’d slide two fresh loaves of rye bread—still warm from the bakery’s midnight delivery—into the slicer. The blade whirred, sharp and precise, and the scent of caraway and yeast would bloom, sudden and startling, cutting through the grease and disinfectant.

One Tuesday in late October, the power went out. Not the whole hospital—the backup generator kicked in for life support and ER lights—but our basement died. The freezers groaned, the exhaust fans stuttered and fell silent, and the only light came from the red EXIT sign above the swinging doors, casting long, trembling shadows across the floor tiles. We stood in the dark, breathing steam and silence. Then, from the far corner, Old Man Rizzo—sixty-eight, retired but still showing up three nights a week because, he said, “the daytime cooks don’t know how to season a broth without crying”—struck a match. He held it to the pilot light on the old gas-fired convection oven. A blue flame flared, then steadied. In its glow, his face looked carved from walnut, his knuckles swollen and veined like tree roots.

“Light’s not just electricity, Danny,” he said, his voice gravel wrapped in smoke. He pulled a dented thermos from his coat pocket and unscrewed the cap. “It’s intention. You want light? You strike the match *toward* the wick—not away.” He poured steaming black coffee into two chipped mugs—mine had a hairline crack near the handle, the one with the faded green St. Brigid’s logo. “Drink slow. This batch’s got chicory. Makes it honest.”

We sat on overturned milk crates beside the oven, the warmth radiating against our thighs. Outside, an ambulance siren rose and fell, distant and mournful. Inside, the only sounds were the drip-drip-drip of condensation from the ceiling pipes and the low, rhythmic *shush-shush* of Rizzo stirring a pot of barley soup he’d started hours before, just in case. He never measured. “Eyes and wrist,” he’d tell me. “Soup remembers kindness. Or neglect. Doesn’t lie.”

At 5:13 a.m., the lights surged back on—harsh, white, unforgiving. The freezer compressor roared to life. Someone cursed softly in Spanish near the dish station. Rizzo blew out the pilot light, then wiped his thumb across the brass knob. “There,” he said. “Now you know what the dark feels like—and what it costs to hold it off.”

I walked home at dawn, past the closed laundromat on Western Avenue, past the boarded-up storefront where the neon “OPEN” sign still blinked erratically, its wires frayed and bare. My boots scuffed wet pavement. My hands smelled of onions and lye soap and something deeper—sweat, yes, but also the faint, metallic whisper of blood from the surgical trays we washed, the ghost of antiseptic, the warm, yeasty breath of rising dough. I passed the bus stop bench where a nurse named Marisol used to sit, head tilted back, eyes closed, waiting for the 5:45 to Mishawaka. Sometimes she’d wave, sometimes not. Once, she handed me a single caramel, unwrapped, saying, “For the sugar crash you haven’t felt yet.” I kept the wrapper in my wallet for six months.

The sun hadn’t cleared the rooftops yet, but the sky was the color of weak tea—pale gold bleeding into dove gray. I could hear the first birds, tentative, testing the air. My left shoulder ached where I’d strained it lifting the industrial mixer the week before. My right thumb bore a fresh, shallow cut from the slicer blade—a thin red line, already crusting over. I touched it, then kept walking. My breath fogged, brief and gone. The city exhaled around me, slow and heavy, still half-asleep, still holding its breath.

title: elegy in free verse|a closed coal mine and the men who worked it
text:
Elegy for the Black Diamond Shaft  

It’s quiet now. Not peaceful—*quiet*. Like the kind of silence that settles after someone stops breathing but before you’ve quite registered it. The headframe’s still there, rust bleeding down its steel ribs like old blood under thin skin. They didn’t tear it down. Too expensive, they said. Or maybe just too tired.  

I walked past yesterday—just me and a stray terrier with one ear folded sideways, like it was listening to something I couldn’t hear. The dog sniffed at the chain-link fence, whined once, then trotted off toward the slag heap where fireweed’s pushing up through cracked concrete, purple and stubborn as hell.  

Used to be three shifts: dawn, day, swing. Now it’s just pigeons nesting in the hoist house rafters, cooing like they’re rehearsing a hymn no one taught them. Their droppings stain the brickwork—white smears on red brick, like chalk marks left by children who forgot what they meant to write.  

My uncle Len worked here thirty-eight years. Died last March, lungs full of coal dust and quiet. His funeral was in St. Brigid’s, same church where he got married, same pews where he’d sat with his cap still on, hands blackened even after scrubbing, knuckles split and crusted at the edges. He never wore gloves—not really. Said they made him clumsy. “You feel the seam *in your fingers*,” he told me once, holding out his palm, turning it slowly under the kitchen light. “Not with your eyes. With your *bones*.”  

The seam was called the Black Diamond. Thick, clean, low-sulfur. They used to say it sang when you tapped it right—low hum, like a cello string wound too tight. I never heard it sing. But I saw the men come up at shift’s end, faces washed raw, hair matted with sweat and grit, shirts dark at the armpits and down the spine, stiff with salt and coal. Some carried thermoses wrapped in frayed dish towels. One—old Mr. Hargrove—always had a tin of mints in his pocket, spearmint, because “it cuts the taste of the dark.” He’d offer one, breath sharp and cool, and you’d suck it while watching the sun hit the tipple for the first time that day, blinding off the wet rails.  

They closed it in ’09. Not with fanfare. Not with speeches. Just a notice tacked to the bulletin board beside the time clock: *Operations suspended indefinitely.* Someone had drawn a tiny coffin in the margin, in blue ballpoint. No name. No date. Just the box.  

After that, the machines went silent—the draglines, the continuous miners, the roaring belt conveyors that used to shake the windows in the company houses on Sycamore Street. Even the rats stopped scurrying. Or maybe they just got quieter. Hard to say.  

I found a hard hat last week behind the old tool shed. Paint chipped, liner frayed, stamped *J. MURPHY – 1974*. Inside, scribbled in pencil, faint as a sigh: *Maeve’s birthday. Got her the blue dress.* No year. Just that. Blue dress. Maeve.  

There’s a bench welded to the ground near the gate—concrete base, iron frame, bolted down so it wouldn’t blow away in the wind. It wasn’t there when the mine was open. Must’ve been put up later. By who? No plaque. Just two names scratched into the armrest, deep: *Dale & Ray*. And below, smaller: *2nd shift, ’83.*  

Sometimes, on cold mornings, steam still rises from the vent shaft—thin, ghostly, almost invisible unless the light hits it just right. Geothermal, they say. Residual heat. But the men called it *the mine’s last breath*. And if you stand close enough, you can smell it—not smoke, not sulfur, but damp earth and something metallic, like licking a battery wrapped in wet cloth.  

The union hall’s boarded up now. The sign’s half-gone: *U__n H__l*. Rain’s eaten the letters. A squirrel’s built a nest in the hollow where the “A” used to be.  

I think about the boys—teenagers, really—who started at sixteen, sent down with a lunch pail and a lamp they weren’t supposed to use anymore, but did anyway, because the electric ones flickered, and flickering made men nervous. One boy—Danny Varga—fell down the skip shaft in ’76. They pulled him out whole, but he never spoke again. Just sat on his porch every evening, staring at the headframe, rocking slow, hands folded in his lap like he was praying to something buried.  

No one talks much about the mine anymore. Not the young ones. They say *coal’s dead*, like it was a person who finally gave up. But it wasn’t dead down there. It was *alive*. Breathing slow. Waiting.  

I keep a piece of Black Diamond in my desk drawer. Not polished. Just a jagged lump, cold and heavy, about the size of a clenched fist. When I hold it, my palm goes numb. Not from cold—from weight. From memory.  

The fence is sagging now. Wire loose at the bottom. Kids crawl under it sometimes. Leave soda cans, cigarette butts, once—a single red high-heeled shoe, heel snapped off. Who knows why.  

The mine didn’t die. It just stopped answering.  

And the men? They’re in the houses with the peeling paint, watching TV with the sound off. Or sitting at the VFW, stirring coffee long after it’s gone cold. Or lying in graves marked with simple stones, no dates carved yet—just names, and underneath, always, *Miner*.  

That’s enough.  

That’s all it ever needed to be.

title: narrative poem|a ferry crossing in a storm
text:
Beneath a sky that roared with thunder's might,
A ferry, small and worn, set sail at night.
The captain, grizzled, stood with steadfast gaze,
His weathered hands upon the helm, a maze
Of scars and calluses, each one a tale
Of battles fought against the tempest's gale.

The passengers, a motley crew of souls,
Huddled in fear, their hearts like frozen coals.
A young girl clung to her mother's dress,
While whispers of the storm grew more distress.
An old man, eyes like faded parchment, sighed,
And wrapped his cloak around his frame, as if to hide
From the fury of the elements, unkind,
That raged and howled, a force most undefined.

The waves, like mountains, rose and fell,
Each crest a challenge, each trough a spell.
The wind, a banshee's shriek, tore through the air,
And lightning split the heavens, stark and bare.
The ferry rocked, a fragile leaf adrift,
In waters that could crush it with a single shift.

The captain's voice, a bellow over sound,
Called out commands, his presence strong and bound.
"Hold fast!" he cried, "This storm will pass!
Trust in the vessel, trust in the mass
Of wood and steel, and in the skill of those
Who guide you through the darkness, who oppose
The wrath of nature, and who stand as shields
Against the chaos, as the tide yields."

Yet doubt crept in, like shadows in the night,
As bolts of lightning pierced the gloom, a sight
That filled the hearts of all with dread and fear.
The young girl wept, and even the old man's ear
Trembled at the roar, the crash, the scream
Of wind and wave, a monstrous, ghastly team.

A sailor, lean and lanky, with a face
Carved by the sea, took up his place
At the prow, his eyes fixed on the squall,
His grip on the rope, a lifeline for them all.
He sang a shanty, rough and raw, a song
Of sailors bold, of storms they faced, and long
Voyages through the dark, where hope was thin,
But courage, like a beacon, burned within.

The ferry creaked and groaned, its timbers strained,
As if the very soul of the ship complained.
The captain, resolute, steered through the fray,
His mind a compass, guiding them this way
And that, a dance with death, a gamble cast
On fate and skill, and on the strength that lasts
When all else fails, when hope is but a spark,
And every moment seems the last, the dark.

The storm, relentless, battered on and on,
Until, at last, the first pale light of dawn
Crept over the horizon, a glimmer faint,
A promise of the calm that would acquaint
The weary travelers with the world anew,
A world washed clean, and skies of azure hue.

The ferry, battered, bruised, but still afloat,
Rode the waves, now gentle, to a remote
And sheltered cove, where silence reigned supreme,
And peace, like a balm, soothed every dream.
The passengers, relieved, stepped onto land,
Their journey done, the storm behind, a strand
Of memory, a tale to tell, a bond
Forged in the fire, and in the deep beyond.

title: historical novel|a cartographer's apprentice in eighteenth-century Lisbon
text:
The Ink and the Uncharted

I am seventeen, and my fingers smell of iron gall and salt. Not the clean salt of the Tagus at low tide, but the sour, metallic tang that rises from the damp stone of the *Casa dos Mapas*, where I spend my days bent over vellum so thin it breathes under the nib. My master, Senhor Valente, is not cruel—only precise, as a compass needle is precise—and his silence is a kind of weather: cold, still, liable to shift without warning.

Lisbon in 1754 is a city of surfaces. Gilded churches rise above narrow alleys where laundry drips like slow tears. The sea glitters, indifferent. And everywhere, maps—on walls, in merchants’ ledgers, pinned to the backs of tavern doors—each one a small, confident lie. They show coastlines drawn with certainty, rivers named with authority, blank spaces labelled *Terra Incognita* in elegant, untroubled script. As if ignorance could be framed.

My task is not grand discovery. It is the grinding work of fidelity: tracing the contours of Madeira’s western cliffs from Captain Almeida’s logbook, correcting the latitude of the Azores by cross-referencing three separate navigators’ journals (two of whom contradict each other, and the third writes in Latin so florid it borders on prayer), transcribing the names of fishing coves near Sesimbra—*Praia do Castelo*, *Angra do Sino*—names whispered by old men who’ve never seen a printed map, let alone held one. Their voices are gravel and brine; their geography is memory, not measurement. I write them down. Valente approves the orthography. He does not ask whether *Sino* means bell or sorrow—or whether the bell they mean is one that rings for ships lost, or for saints forgotten.

One Tuesday, a chest arrives from Bahia. Not gold, not sugar, but paper—reams of it, wrapped in oiled cloth, smelling faintly of tobacco and river mud. Inside, a single folio, water-stained at the edges, bearing the seal of the Royal Society of Rio de Janeiro. It is a sketch-map of the interior, drawn by Father Estêvão, a Jesuit who vanished two years prior while attempting to trace the source of the Paraguaçu. His hand is shaky, urgent. Rivers fork and rejoin like nervous veins. A cluster of symbols—a circle, three crosses, a crude depiction of a jaguar’s head—is annotated only: *“Here the words of God do not travel well.”*

Valente studies it for ten minutes, then slides it across the desk. “Redraw it. Clean lines. Standard scale. Omit the symbols. Label the river *Rio Paraguaçu*. Mark the settlement *Aldeia de São Francisco*—though no such place exists on any Admiralty chart. Do not speculate.”

I do as instructed. My hand moves smoothly. The jaguar vanishes. The crosses become neat black dots. The circle becomes a star—the conventional mark for a mission station. I even add a tiny, invented chapel roof, rendered in perfect perspective. When I finish, Valente nods once. “Good. Now burn the original.”

I light the candle. Watch the ink curl, the vellum blacken and curl inward, the jaguar’s head shrinking to ash before it vanishes entirely. The heat stings my eyes. I think not of heresy or censorship, but of the weight of that single word—*omit*—and how easily it becomes *erase*, then *never was*.

Later, walking home past the Ribeira das Naus, I see a boy—no older than twelve—kneeling in the wet sand, drawing with a stick. Not a ship, not a fish, but a tangle of lines, intersecting, overlapping, looping back on themselves. No coast, no horizon, just the pattern, repeated, insistent. I stop. He looks up, unafraid. “My father drew this,” he says, tapping the centre. “Before the earth shook.”

I don’t correct him. There was no earthquake here—not yet. But I know what he means. In November ’55, the ground will shudder, the river will boil, the churches will fall like rotten fruit. Maps will be useless then. Not because they’re wrong, but because the land itself will refuse its own name.

Back in the *Casa*, I am copying the new hydrographic survey of the Algarve coast. The line of the shore is jagged, precise. I dip my pen. The ink flows—thick, black, certain. Yet my wrist hesitates, almost imperceptibly, at the point where the cliff drops sheer into the sea. A flaw? A tremor? Or simply the body remembering, before the mind does, that all lines end somewhere—and that ending is rarely marked on the page.

Valente enters, places a fresh sheet before me. “The Cape Verde corrections. Use the blue ink this time. The Admiralty prefers it for deep-water soundings.”

I nod. Uncap the bottle. The blue is colder than the black, sharper. It smells of lapis and distance.

I begin. The line starts true. Then, halfway down the page, my hand slips—not much, just a hair’s breadth. A slight, unintended swell in the contour. I could scrape it away with the pumice stone. Start again. Valente would expect it.

But I leave it. Just a whisper of deviation. A breath held too long. A coastline that remembers, however faintly, the shape of its own uncertainty.

The map will go to Lisbon’s port authority. It will hang in the custom house. No one will notice the flaw. No one will need to. It is, after all, only ink on vellum. A record of what was seen, not what was felt. Not what was feared. Not what, in the quiet dark between measurements, might still be moving beneath us—unmapped, unnamed, and wholly, stubbornly, real.

I cap the bottle. The blue stain on my thumb dries slowly, a faint, fading bruise.

title: prose poem|a kitchen at four in the morning
text:
The refrigerator hums—not a steady drone, but a low, intermittent throb, like a tired heart remembering its rhythm. Four a.m. in the apartment above La Boulangerie du Pont on Rue Saint-Dominique, Paris. Rain slicks the cobblestones below, catching the sodium-orange glow of the streetlamp outside the window, painting a trembling rectangle across the worn oak floorboards. Inside, the air smells of yesterday’s espresso grounds, faint yeast from the brioche dough left to rise in a ceramic bowl covered with damp linen, and the ghost of garlic—Léa’s garlic, minced too finely three hours ago while arguing with her sister over the phone about their mother’s will.

Léa stands at the sink, barefoot, wearing her father’s old navy-blue cardigan, sleeves pushed past her elbows. Her hair is knotted loosely at her nape, strands escaping like frayed thread. She holds a paring knife—not the Japanese one she keeps sharpened for tomatoes, but the stubby, slightly bent stainless-steel blade her grandfather used to peel apples for tarte tatin in Montmartre. She’s not cutting anything. Just turning it, slowly, in her left hand, the cool metal catching the dim light from the stove’s digital clock: 4:03. The numbers blink, steady as a metronome counting down to something unnamed.

A kettle whistles—not sharply, but with a thin, reedy insistence, like a child holding a single note too long. She doesn’t move. Not yet. Instead, she watches the condensation crawl down the inside of the windowpane, tracing slow, branching paths toward the sill where a single dried lavender sprig lies beside a chipped blue mug stamped *Café de Flore, 1987*. That mug belonged to Étienne, who died last November, two days after his seventy-second birthday, in a room three floors down, breathing shallowly while Léa read aloud from *Le Petit Prince*, her voice cracking on the line *“Ce qui est essentiel est invisible pour les yeux.”* He’d smiled, just once, and squeezed her wrist with surprising strength.

She finally lifts the kettle, pours water into the French press—coarse-ground beans from the roaster near Bastille, dark as burnt sugar. As the water blooms the grounds, releasing that deep, almost animal scent of roasted earth and bitter chocolate, the door creaks open. Not the front door. The pantry door. Small, narrow, lined with shelves of glass jars: lentils from Le Puy, mustard seeds from Dijon, dried figs from Provence, all labeled in Léa’s looping script. And there, standing in the doorway in striped pajamas and slippers shaped like hedgehogs, is Julien, eight years old, clutching a stuffed badger named Monsieur Gris.

“Maman?” His voice is thick with sleep, eyes half-lidded, one sock missing.

She doesn’t say *What are you doing up?* or *Go back to bed.* She says, “The water’s just right,” and lifts the press gently. “Want to pour?”

He pads across the floor, bare feet silent on the wood, and stands on tiptoe, small hands gripping the handle beside hers. They tilt it together. The coffee pours—rich, viscous, almost black—into two mismatched cups: hers, the blue Flore mug; his, a chipped white one with a cartoon snail crawling up the side, a gift from his teacher, Madame Dubois, who always smells of violet water and chalk dust.

He sips, winces, then takes another sip, slower this time. “It tastes like… wet stones and warm bread.”

She smiles. “That’s because it is. Roasted beans, hot water, and the memory of bread baking at dawn.”

He nods seriously, as if this explanation settles something fundamental. Then he points to the counter, where a sheet of parchment paper holds three perfect, golden-brown madeleines, still warm, their scalloped edges glistening faintly with butter. “You made them?”

“I did. While you were dreaming about dinosaurs.”

He picks one up, breaks it carefully in half, peers inside at the soft, honeycombed crumb. “Did Papa ever eat madeleines at four a.m.?”

She pauses. Swallows. The question lands like a stone in still water. “Yes,” she says quietly. “Every Tuesday. After his night shift at the hospital. He’d come in quiet as smoke, wash his hands three times, then sit right there”—she nods to the stool by the window—“and eat one slowly, watching the sky turn grey.”

Julien climbs onto the stool, tucks his legs beneath him, and takes another bite. Crumbs scatter like tiny constellations onto the counter. Outside, a delivery van rumbles past, its engine groaning, then fading. A dog barks once, far away, near the Seine. The refrigerator hums again—louder now, insistent—and the light flickers, just once, casting their shadows large and wavering on the wall: mother and son, bent over steaming cups, the badger tucked under Julien’s arm, the lavender sprig trembling as a gust slips under the window frame.

Léa reaches across and brushes a crumb from his cheek. Her thumb lingers, warm and dry. He leans into it, just slightly. Neither speaks. The clock blinks: 4:17. Somewhere, a church bell begins to toll—not for mass, not yet—but for the hour, low and resonant, vibrating through the floorboards, through the soles of their feet, through the porcelain of the cups, through the very marrow of the silence between them. The coffee cools. The madeleines soften at the edges. The rain slows to a hush. And the kitchen, at four in the morning, holds its breath—not waiting for day, not mourning the night, but simply being: warm, imperfect, humming with the quiet, stubborn alchemy of presence—of flour and fire, of grief and milk, of a child’s sockless foot resting against a mother’s ankle, of time measured not in minutes, but in shared sips, in broken pastries, in the weight of a badger’s stitched eye against a small, sleeping temple. The light from the streetlamp shifts, just perceptibly, as the clouds thin. Not daylight yet. But the dark, for now, is no longer absolute. It is merely the space between one breath and the next—full, and held.

title: memoir|a father's ledger found after his death
text:
It was a cold, rainy afternoon when we finally got around to sorting through Dad's things. The house, once so full of life and warmth, now felt like an echo chamber, each step resonating with the weight of memories. Mom had insisted on waiting, saying she needed time, but I think it was more about not wanting to face the finality of it all. So, there we were, my siblings and I, gathered in the living room, surrounded by boxes and piles of papers, trying to make sense of a lifetime.

I remember the smell of old books and the faint scent of his cologne still lingering in the air, as if he might walk in at any moment, asking what we were up to. It was hard, really hard, to go through his belongings, to touch the things he had touched, to see the world through his eyes. But we did it, one box at a time, one memory at a time.

In the back of his closet, behind a stack of old coats and a faded blue sweater, I found it: a small, leather-bound ledger. It was unassuming, almost hidden, as if it had been placed there deliberately, away from prying eyes. The cover was worn, the edges frayed, and the pages yellowed with age. I opened it, and a wave of nostalgia hit me. It was Dad's handwriting, neat and precise, each entry meticulously recorded.

The first few pages were filled with dates and amounts, a record of expenses and income, the kind of thing you'd expect in a household ledger. But as I flipped through, the entries became more personal, more intimate. There were notes about our birthdays, anniversaries, and other milestones. He had written down the exact times we were born, the names of the doctors, even the weather on those days. It was like a secret diary, a chronicle of our lives, seen through his meticulous lens.

One entry caught my eye, dated a few months before I left for college. "Paid tuition, $12,000. Bought new laptop, $800. Packed bags, 3 hours. Drove to campus, 4 hours. Hugged, 5 seconds. Missed, forever." The words were simple, but they cut deep. I could almost hear his voice, feel the weight of his love, and the ache of letting go.

There were other entries that made me smile, like the one about the time we went on a family vacation to the beach. "Bought ice cream, 4 cones, $6. Built sandcastle, 2 hours. Watched sunset, 30 minutes. Laughed, countless times." It was a reminder of the joy we shared, the moments that seemed so ordinary at the time but were now precious treasures.

But it wasn't all happy memories. There were entries that spoke of struggles, of financial hardships and health scares. "Hospital bill, $3,000. Prayed, all night. Relief, morning." These were the moments he never talked about, the burdens he carried silently, shielding us from the weight of the world.

As I read on, I realized that this ledger was more than just a record of transactions; it was a map of his heart, a testament to his love and sacrifice. Each entry, no matter how small, was a piece of him, a glimpse into the man who had always put his family first.

I closed the ledger, feeling a mix of emotions. Sadness, of course, but also gratitude. Gratitude for the life he gave us, for the lessons he taught, and for the love he showed, even in the smallest of ways. I held the book close, as if I could somehow hold onto him, just a little longer.

We finished sorting through his things that day, but the ledger stayed with me. I took it home, placing it on my bookshelf, where I could see it every day. It's a reminder, a tangible connection to the man who shaped me, who loved me, and who, in his own way, left a piece of himself behind.

Sometimes, I open it and read a random entry, and it feels like he's right there, telling me a story, sharing a memory. And in those moments, I can almost hear his laughter, see his smile, and feel his embrace. It's a bittersweet comfort, but a comfort nonetheless. 

That ledger, that unassuming little book, has become one of my most cherished possessions. It's a legacy, a gift, and a reminder that even in death, love endures.

title: creation myth|how the northern lights were woven
text:
The loom was already trembling.

Not with the shuddering of earth or the groan of ice, but with a deep, resonant *hum*, like the lowest note of a whale-song vibrating up through the frozen sea floor. The Weaver—whose name was not spoken aloud but carried in the hush between breaths, in the way frost feathered across obsidian—stood barefoot on the ledge of the World’s Rim, where sky bled into void and the air tasted of ozone and star-dust. Her fingers, long and knotted with the calluses of millennia, were already deep in the warp: threads spun not from wool or flax, but from the cooled breath of dying stars, the sigh of glaciers calving into silent seas, the slow, silver pulse of auroral rivers buried deep beneath the tundra’s skin. These were the foundational strands—cold, strong, unyielding—and they stretched taut across the chasm, anchored to two jagged monoliths that rose like broken teeth from the ice: one carved from black basalt, the other from milky quartz veined with gold.

She did not begin with light. She began with *silence*.

With a single, deliberate motion, she drew her left hand down the central warp thread—the one spun from the last sigh of the First Comet—and pulled. Not to tighten, but to *listen*. The hum deepened. A vibration travelled up her arm, settled behind her eyes. In that resonance, she felt the ache of the long winter: the fox’s hollow belly, the caribou’s stiff joints, the child’s small hands pressed to frosted glass, searching for something *more* than grey. She felt the weight of memory too—the stories told in smoke-hazed tents, of ancestors who walked under skies so dark they swallowed stars, of elders who whispered that the heavens were not empty, only waiting. This silence was not absence. It was a held breath. A loom primed.

Then came the weft.

She reached—not to the basket at her feet, but *inward*, past bone and blood, past the steady drum of her own heart, into the quiet furnace where her own warmth lived. From that core, she drew forth a filament: not fire, not flame, but *intention* made visible—a strand of pure, liquid gold, warm as sun-warmed stone, humming with quiet certainty. She laid it across the cold warp. Where it touched, the black thread *glowed*, not with heat, but with a soft, internal luminescence, like bioluminescent plankton stirring in midnight water. The loom sighed.

But gold alone was too singular. Too certain. It spoke of noon, not night.

So she turned. With her right hand, she dipped her fingertips into the swirling, slow-moving river of the Sky-Current—a ribbon of charged particles the ancients called the Breath of the Sky-Fox—that flowed just beyond the Rim’s edge. It was raw, untamed, electric. She gathered a coil of its violet-blue essence, cool as glacial melt, crackling with potential. She wove it *over* the gold, then *under* the next black warp strand, then *over* again, her fingers moving with the unconscious grace of tide meeting shore. Where the violet crossed the gold, the light didn’t mix—it *bloomed*. A sudden, startling flare of emerald, sharp and clean as crushed pine needles, pulsed once, then softened into a gentle, breathing green. The loom shivered, and a low, melodic chime echoed off the monoliths, like ice singing in the wind.

This was the first true stitch.

She worked faster now, not with haste, but with the deep rhythm of a heartbeat finding its pace. She wove in threads of the Moon’s reflected silver—thin, cool, and precise—laying them diagonally to catch the eye and guide the gaze upward. She added filaments spun from the laughter of children playing on snow-dusted ice, a shimmering, almost imperceptible pink that bloomed at the edges of the green, softening its sharpness, lending it tenderness. She wove in the deep, resonant indigo of the raven’s wing at twilight, a grounding shadow that gave the light its depth, its mystery, its sense of vast, watchful presence.

Each thread was chosen, each pass deliberate. She did not force the pattern. She *listened* to the tension in the warp, the resistance of the weft, the subtle shift in the Sky-Current’s flow. When the violet thread grew too restless, sparking erratically, she soothed it with a whisper-thin strand of the northern wind’s patience, spun from the stillness between gusts. When the gold threatened to overwhelm, she introduced a sliver of the bear’s deep, slow hibernation sleep—a rich, velvety brown that didn’t extinguish the light, but cradled it, giving it weight and rest.

The fabric grew—not as cloth, but as *presence*. It hung suspended in the void, a vast, shimmering tapestry woven from the very substance of the world’s quietest truths: the endurance of ice, the resilience of life beneath snow, the fierce, tender spark of memory, the ancient, patient watchfulness of the land itself. It was alive. It breathed. It *pulsed*.

And then, the first tear fell.

Not from sorrow, but from the sheer, overwhelming fullness of it—the beauty of the interwoven threads, the profound rightness of the pattern emerging, the weight of the responsibility she held. It fell from her cheek, clear and cold, and struck the central warp thread just as the emerald-green weft passed over it. Where the tear met the light, it didn’t vanish. It *fractured*—shattering into a thousand tiny, perfect points of pure, crystalline white light. They didn’t fall. They *rose*, spiralling upwards, catching the violet, the gold, the silver, the pink, the indigo, and scattering them in a sudden, breathtaking cascade. A wave of colour surged across the nascent fabric—not a uniform wash, but a living ripple, a sigh made visible, a breath drawn across the face of the sky. Green rippled into violet, which bled into rose, which deepened into sapphire, all held together by that constant, grounding thread of black star-breath.

The loom stopped humming. It began to *sing*.

A low, complex chord, woven from the vibrations of the monoliths, the sigh of the Current, the echo of the Weaver’s own breath. The tapestry responded. It didn’t hang still. It *danced*. It billowed like a vast, celestial sail catching an unseen wind. It folded and unfolded, revealing new constellations within its weave—patterns that shifted with the observer’s gaze, holding the shape of a leaping caribou for one heartbeat, the curve of a mother’s arm cradling a child the next, the intricate, branching fractal of frost on a windowpane the moment after. It was never static. It was conversation. It was memory given form. It was the world’s quiet, persistent answer to the question asked every long, dark night: *Are we seen? Are we remembered?*

The Weaver stepped back, her bare feet numb on the ice, her hands trembling not with fatigue, but with awe. She looked upon the living light—not as a finished thing, but as a beginning. A covenant. A promise woven not in permanence, but in perpetual becoming. She knew then, with absolute certainty, that this was not a gift bestowed, but a dialogue invited. The lights would dance only when the land was listened to, when the silence was honoured, when the cold was met not with fear, but with the quiet, fierce warmth of enduring life. They were the sky’s breath, caught and coloured by the earth’s deep, slow song—and they would shimmer, ripple, and sing as long as the loom, the Rim, and the Weaver’s quiet, unwavering attention remained. The first true aurora hung, luminous and alive, above the sleeping world, a bridge of light spun from breath, memory, and the profound, necessary magic of paying attention.

title: personal essay|the last video rental shop in town
text:
The Last Shelf

I don’t go in for nostalgia. Not the kind that softens edges, not the kind that wraps memory in amber light and calls it truth. So when I say the last video rental shop in town—*Reel Time*, a narrow storefront wedged between a shuttered laundromat and a vape shop with perpetually fogged windows—still holds something real for me, it isn’t because I miss the smell of plastic cases or the clink of rewinding tapes. It’s because it’s stubbornly, awkwardly *there*, like a single tooth left after extraction: not beautiful, not symbolic, just persisting.

I walk past it most days. Not to rent. I haven’t rented anything in three years—not since my daughter stopped asking for *Finding Nemo* on loop, not since streaming algorithms learned to anticipate my restlessness before I do.
