But I pause. The sign above the door is hand-painted, slightly crooked, the “E” in *Reel* chipped at the lower serif. Inside, the fluorescent tube over the counter hums with the low, tired frequency of something holding on by its last filament. The window display changes rarely: a stack of Criterion Blu-rays beside a battered VHS copy of *The Piano*, a laminated sign reading *“No Late Fees Since 2012 (We Mean It)”*, and, always, a small potted fern on the ledge—brown-tipped, but alive.

The owner, Helen, is in her late sixties, wears cardigans with ink stains on the pockets, and speaks in sentences that begin mid-thought and end with a quiet exhale. She doesn’t ask if you’re looking for anything. She watches your eyes move across the shelves—the cramped, alphabetized rows of DVDs, the smaller, dustier section of VHS behind glass, the single shelf labeled *“Local Stuff”*, which holds exactly seven items: two student films from the community college, a documentary about the river dredging project, a wedding video someone donated in error, and three copies of a self-published memoir about growing up on Elm Street. I’ve never seen anyone take one.

What lingers isn’t the inventory—it’s the friction. The physicality of choice. You can’t scroll. You can’t be fed. You stand there, shoulders slightly hunched, scanning spines, your thumb brushing the edge of a case, feeling the slight ridge where the barcode sticker lifts. You might pick up *Paris, Texas*, then put it back because the cover photo feels too bleak for Tuesday. You might linger over *Caddyshack*, not because you want to watch it, but because the font on the spine reminds you of a summer job you had at sixteen, stacking sodas in a humid basement. There’s no algorithm here, only the slow, unmediated negotiation between what’s available and what you are, in that exact moment, willing to carry home.

Last week, a teenager came in. Early twenties, earbuds dangling, phone glowing in his hand. He asked for “something weird.” Helen didn’t offer suggestions. She walked him to the far corner, pulled out *Eraserhead*, held it up without comment. He stared at the cover—the pale, distorted face, the industrial grime—and then at her. She said, “It’s loud. And slow. And it smells faintly of burnt toast if you hold it close enough.” He took it. Paid cash. Didn’t ask for a receipt.

That’s the thing: *Reel Time* doesn’t sell movies. It brokers minor, temporary alliances. Between people and images they didn’t know they needed. Between strangers and the quiet understanding that sometimes, choosing nothing is harder than choosing wrong. The shop doesn’t feel like a museum. It feels like a waiting room—not for something to happen, but for the space *between* things to settle. In a world calibrated to eliminate delay, *Reel Time* insists on it. The time it takes to find the right aisle. The time it takes to read the back cover, really read it, not skim. The time it takes to decide whether the promise of *The Straight Story* is worth the drive home in rain.

I went in yesterday, not for a film, but to return a DVD I’d borrowed months ago—*Portrait of Jason*. I’d watched it twice, then left it on my desk, then forgot. When I handed it to Helen, she didn’t check the system. She opened the case, slid the disc out, ran her thumb over its surface—not checking for scratches, just feeling the cool, smooth weight—and slid it back into the sleeve. “Good one,” she said. Then, after a beat: “He talks so much, you forget he’s holding something back. Always.”

I nodded. We didn’t speak again. I stood near the “New Releases” shelf—three titles, all indie, all released six months ago—and watched the light shift as a delivery van passed the window, casting a long, moving shadow across the spines.

There’s no grand lesson here. No elegy disguised as observation. The shop will close. It has to. The lease is up in August. Helen mentioned it once, offhand, while wiping down the counter with a rag that smelled of lemon oil and old paper. She didn’t sound resigned. She sounded… done. Not with the work, but with the particular exhaustion of keeping a vessel afloat in a current that no longer recognizes its shape.

I still walk past. I still pause. Not because I believe in preservation, but because the sight of that crooked sign, that humming light, that fern with its brown tips—it reminds me that some things endure not despite their obsolescence, but *within* it. Not as monuments, but as interruptions. Small, unassuming resistances to the velocity of everything else. A place where time hasn’t been optimized, just… occupied. Uneasily. Honestly. For now.

title: free verse poem sequence|a year of weather in one valley
text:
In the valley of Eldridge, where the river meanders like a lost thought, the year began with a whisper of snow. The first flakes fell softly on the old mill, now a relic, and dusted the roof of Mrs. Henley's house, where she sat by the fire, knitting another scarf for the winter market.

"Look, George," she called to her husband, who was bent over a model ship, his fingers deftly shaping the sails. "The year is starting with grace."

George peered out, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Grace, yes, but also cold. We’ll need more wood."

Spring arrived with the sound of rushing water, as the thaw sent the river surging. In the meadow, daffodils poked through the damp earth, and the children of Eldridge ran, their laughter mingling with the song of returning birds. At the local school, Miss Elsie Turner stood before her class, her voice rising over the rustle of papers and the creak of wooden desks.

"Children, can anyone tell me what we observe in spring?"

A small hand shot up, belonging to Lily, the youngest of the Johnsons. "Miss Turner, it’s the flowers! They come back to life, just like magic!"

Elsie smiled, her eyes bright. "Very good, Lily. And do you know why this happens?"

Summer brought a sweltering heat that made even the usually stoic Mr. Whitaker, the town’s blacksmith, wipe his brow more than once. The days stretched long, filled with the smell of cut grass and the distant chime of the ice cream truck. On the banks of the river, teenagers gathered, their bodies glistening with sweat, diving into the cool water with joyful abandon. Among them, young Tom and his girlfriend, Emily, lay side by side on a blanket, the sun warming their skin.

"Tom," Emily said, her voice soft, "do you ever think about leaving this place?"

He turned to her, his blue eyes reflecting the sky. "Sometimes. But then I look around, and I see how much I love it here. The river, the fields, even the heat. It’s home."

Autumn painted the valley in hues of gold and red, the leaves falling like a slow, deliberate rain. The harvest festival was in full swing, with stalls lining the main street, offering pies, cider, and handmade crafts. At the apple stand, Sarah and her brother, James, were selling their family’s crop, the air sweet with the scent of ripe fruit.

"James, did you see Mr. Thompson? He bought three baskets!" Sarah exclaimed, her cheeks flushed with excitement.

James laughed, ruffling her hair. "Of course, he loves our apples. Just like everyone else in this valley."

As the days grew shorter, the chill returned, and the people of Eldridge prepared for the long winter. The town hall was bustling with activity, as families came together to share meals and stories. In the corner, old Mr. O’Connor, a retired farmer, regaled a group of listeners with tales of past winters.

"And there was the time," he said, his voice carrying across the room, "when the snow was so deep, we had to dig tunnels to get from one house to the next. But you know, those were some of the best times. Neighbors helping neighbors, sharing what little we had."

Outside, the first snowflakes of the season began to fall, blanketing the valley in a quiet, serene white. In Mrs. Henley’s house, she and George sat by the fire, the new logs crackling, casting a warm glow around the room.

"Another year gone," George murmured, his hands clasped around a mug of hot tea.

Mrs. Henley looked at him, her eyes gentle. "And another one coming. Each with its own weather, its own stories. Here in this valley, we have all we need."

The fire flickered, and the snow continued to fall, a silent promise of the cycles yet to come.

title: prose poem|a kitchen at four in the morning
text:
Four a.m. in the kitchen. Not the clean, aspirational kind—no marble, no farmhouse sink gleaming under pendant lights. This is *my* kitchen: linoleum cracked like dried riverbeds near the fridge leg, the kind of floor that holds grime in its seams like a secret. The light above the stove hums—not buzzes, *hums*, a low, tired C-sharp that vibrates the loose screw in the overhead fixture. I swear it’s been humming since ’09. Or maybe ’12. Hard to tell when time blurs at this hour.

The kettle’s on. Not boiling yet. Just that soft, insistent gurgle, like a small animal trapped in the base. I watch the steam rise—not in a plume, but in hesitant, wobbly ribbons. One catches on the edge of the cabinet door, curls around the chipped blue enamel of the old toaster (the one with the dial that sticks at “3” and burns everything unless you jiggle it *just so*). That toaster has toast crumbs fossilized in its crumb tray. I know because I cleaned it last Tuesday. Or was it Wednesday? The calendar on the fridge is held up by a magnet shaped like a sad-looking potato.

The fridge door’s open. Cold air spills out, smelling faintly of yesterday’s takeout container—ginger, soy sauce, and something vaguely like regret—and the sharp, clean shock of leftover lemon water. A single slice of lemon floats in the pitcher, skin puckered, pale yellow turning translucent at the edges. It looks exhausted. I poke it with a spoon. It spins, slow and reluctant, like a tiny, sun-bleached planet.

Outside the window, the streetlamp across the alley flickers. Not rhythmically. Erratically. *Flick-flutter-flick—* then a long, breathless pause. Then *flick*. It casts long, liquid shadows across the counter: the shadow of the salt cellar (a chipped ceramic owl, eyes missing), the shadow of the half-empty jar of capers (brine clouded, a few green pearls bobbing listlessly), the shadow of my own hand resting on the cool Formica. My knuckles look knobby in that light. Like tree roots. I think about how many times I’ve washed dishes here, how many arguments have dissolved into silence over this sink, how many cups of terrible coffee I’ve drunk while staring at this exact patch of linoleum where a drop of dried ketchup has hardened into a tiny, rust-coloured island.

The cat appears. Not walking in. *Materializing.* One second, empty doorway. Next second, there she is: Marmalade, tail high as a question mark, blinking slowly. She circles the trash can twice, sniffs the bag (still tied, still full of yesterday’s banana peels and coffee grounds), then sits directly in front of me, tail wrapped tight, gaze unblinking. Her left ear has a tiny notch—like someone took a bite out of it years ago. A dog? A fence? I never asked. She just *has* it. She stares. I stare back. We hold the silence. It’s not awkward. It’s thick. Like cold honey.

I pour the water into the mug. Not the good mug—the chipped one with the faded cartoon badger wearing sunglasses. Steam rises, carrying the dusty, floral scent of the chamomile tea bag I dropped in three minutes ago. I forgot the bag. Left it in. Now it’s bloated, brown, sinking like a tiny, sodden ship. I stir anyway. The spoon clinks against the ceramic. A sound too loud. I stop stirring. Listen. The hum. The gurgle. The distant, muffled *thump-thump-thump* of a bassline from the apartment upstairs—someone’s still awake, or just starting. Or maybe they’re having a very quiet, very late argument.

The clock above the stove reads 4:07. The red digits pulse faintly. I wonder who else is awake right now, in this city, in this country, in this world, staring at their own particular patch of linoleum, their own sad potato magnet, their own exhausted lemon. Are they making tea? Are they crying? Are they just waiting for the light to change? Or are they, like me, simply holding space? Not doing much. Not thinking much. Just *here*, in the damp-cold air, with the humming light and the cat’s unblinking stare and the ghost of ginger on the air.

The tea’s too weak. I’ll make another cup later. Or maybe not. Maybe I’ll just sit. Watch the streetlamp flicker. Watch the lemon sink lower in its water. Watch Marmalade’s nostrils twitch. The silence isn’t empty. It’s full of the weight of all the things we don’t say before dawn. Full of the smell of old bread crusts in the compost bin. Full of the way the Formica feels under my palm—cool, slightly sticky near the edge where the cleaner didn’t quite reach.

Dawn’s still hours off. The sky outside the window isn’t black anymore. It’s the colour of weak tea. Grey-brown. Unpromising. But it’s *changing*. Slowly. Imperceptibly. Like the crumb in the toaster tray finally giving way. Like the last dregs of the lemon water going cloudy. Like the hum dropping, just a fraction, as the fridge compressor kicks in again.

I take the first sip. It’s warm. Bitter. Slightly floral. Exactly what I needed. Or maybe exactly what I didn’t need. Doesn’t matter. It’s here. The mug is warm. The cat hasn’t moved. The light hums. The world holds its breath.

Just for now.

title: memoir|a childhood split between two countries and two languages
text:
The suitcase was open on the floor, a gaping mouth full of folded cotton and stiff cardboard boxes of *gajar halwa*. My mother’s hands moved with quiet urgency—smoothing the collar of my blue school blazer, tucking a hair tie around my wrist like a bracelet, pressing a small, warm *puri* into my palm. “Eat,” she said, not looking up. Her voice was low, thick with the kind of exhaustion that doesn’t come from lack of sleep but from holding two worlds in your chest and never letting either one collapse. Outside the apartment window, Mumbai hummed: the clatter of the milkman’s tin cans, the distant, insistent honk of an auto-rickshaw, the scent of monsoon-damp earth rising through the open balcony door. Inside, the air smelled of cardamom and something sharper—fear, maybe, or just the metallic tang of the airport shuttle bus we’d take in two hours.

I bit into the *puri*. It crumbled, flaky and hot, releasing steam that fogged my glasses. I wiped them with my sleeve, blinking at the blurred edges of the room—the peeling floral wallpaper behind the bookshelf, the framed photo of my father in his navy uniform, standing stiffly beside a British officer in what looked like a very cold garden. That photo lived in Mumbai. The other one—the one where he held me, barefoot on a sun-bleached deck, squinting into Long Island Sound—lived in Port Jefferson. Two fathers, technically the same man, but photographed in different light, speaking in different registers: one voice measured and clipped, the other softer, slower, punctuated by pauses where American silence settled like dust.

We didn’t say “goodbye” in Hindi. We said *“phir milenge”*—we’ll meet again—which sounded less like a promise and more like a shared fiction we both agreed to uphold. My grandmother, Amma, stood in the doorway, her sari pallu drawn tightly across her chest. She didn’t touch me. Not then. Instead, she lifted her right hand, palm outward, fingers slightly curled—not waving, not blessing, just *holding space*. I knew that gesture. It meant: *I see you leaving. I hold the shape of you as you go.* I mirrored it, my small hand trembling. She nodded once. No tears. Just that quiet, unbearable gravity.

At the airport, the transition began before we even passed through security. The air changed—cooler, drier, scented faintly with disinfectant instead of jasmine and exhaust. My mother switched languages mid-sentence. One moment she was murmuring in Marathi about the importance of remembering to pack my inhaler; the next, her voice snapped into crisp, efficient English as she addressed the immigration officer: “Yes, sir, visiting family. Return ticket confirmed.” Her spine straightened. Her shoulders pulled back. Her eyes lost their soft, inward focus and sharpened into something alert, almost defensive. I watched her become someone else—not a stranger, but a version of herself calibrated for this particular gate, this particular border. I felt the shift in my own throat, too. My tongue, so loose and liquid with *“kya kar rahe ho?”* and *“thoda aur chahiye?”*, suddenly felt heavy, clumsy. When the customs agent asked, “What’s your name, sweetheart?”, I heard myself answer in English—clear, polite, textbook-perfect—and hated how flat it sounded, how much it erased the lilt, the warmth, the slight rasp in my voice when I spoke Marathi.

The flight was eight hours and three time zones, but the real dislocation happened in the in-between. In the hush of the cabin, with the seatbelt sign glowing softly, I’d close my eyes and try to conjure the sound of the temple bell near our building—the deep, resonant *ghanta* that marked the hour, its vibration humming in my molars. Then, without warning, my brain would supply the sharp, staccato ring of the school bell at PS 214—the one that meant *line up, no talking, left foot first*. Both sounds lived inside me, but they couldn’t occupy the same mental space. One would crowd out the other. I’d open my eyes, disoriented, staring at the flickering screen showing our descent path over Long Island, and feel a hollow ache behind my ribs—not sadness, exactly, but the vertigo of existing in two grammars at once.

In Port Jefferson, the language switch wasn’t just verbal; it was sensory. The air tasted different—saltier, colder, carrying the damp chill of the Sound even in summer. The light had a particular clarity, a bleached, northern sharpness that made shadows cut like knives. My father’s house smelled of old paperbacks, pine cleaner, and the faint, sweet decay of fallen apples from the gnarled tree in the backyard. Here, words were shorter, sentences faster, silences less loaded. When I said *“I’m tired”*, no one asked *“what’s wrong?”* They just said, *“Go rest.”* In Mumbai, *“I’m tired”* was an invitation to sit, to be handed chai, to have your forehead gently rubbed while someone murmured about the heat, the traffic, the weight of the day. Exhaustion there was communal; here, it was private, almost shameful.

I learned to code-switch before I understood the term. At school, I was “Maya Patel,” quick with fractions and fluent in sarcasm, mastering the art of the dry, self-deprecating joke that made American kids laugh. At home, with my father, I was *“Maiya”*, the name only he used, soft and round, and I’d slip into Marathi for the small, intimate things—the way the mangoes tasted this season, how my grandmother’s hands shook when she poured tea, the exact shade of purple in the bougainvillea climbing the neighbor’s fence. But sometimes, the languages bled. I’d catch myself saying *“I’m gonna go *padhne*”*—mixing English grammar with the Marathi verb for “to study”—and my father would pause, a faint, knowing smile touching his lips. Not correction. Just recognition. A silent nod to the messy, necessary tangle.

The hardest part wasn’t the travel, or even the loneliness. It was the constant, low-grade translation happening beneath everything. Not just words, but feelings. How do you explain *“vishwas”*—that deep, unshakeable trust that feels like bedrock—to friends who equate trust with reliability? How do you describe the specific, aching sweetness of *“mohabbat”* when the English word “love” feels too broad, too thin, like trying to hold water in a sieve? I carried these untranslatable weights, these linguistic ghosts, in my backpack, in the pocket of my jeans, in the quiet space between heartbeats. I wasn’t half of anything. I was whole—but my wholeness was woven from two distinct threads, spun on different spindles, dyed in different vats, and no matter how tightly I knotted them together, the seam was always visible, always tender, always mine.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
The water was cold, a shock that rippled through my body as I dipped my toes into the pool. The sun hung low in the sky, casting a golden glow across the ripples, and for a moment, I felt like I was standing on the edge of something much larger than myself. At forty, learning to swim wasn't just about mastering a skill; it was about confronting a fear that had clung to me since childhood.

I remember the summer when I was eight, the day my father took me to the lake. The water seemed to stretch endlessly, a vast expanse of blue that promised adventure but also held a deep, unspoken threat. I clung to the shore, my feet sinking into the soft, squishy mud, while other children splashed and laughed, their voices carrying over the gentle lapping of the waves. My father, always patient, tried to coax me into the deeper water, but I refused, my heart pounding with a primal fear. That day, I made a silent vow never to venture into the unknown depths, and for years, I kept that promise.

But now, decades later, standing at the edge of this community pool, I felt a different kind of determination. The chlorine scent was sharp, and the echoes of laughter and splashing from the shallow end reminded me of all the summers I had missed. I had watched my own children grow confident in the water, their bodies slicing through the liquid with ease, and I realized that I wanted to be part of that world. I wanted to feel the weightlessness, the freedom, the joy that they experienced.

My instructor, a woman named Sarah, was waiting for me in the water. She had a calm, reassuring presence, her eyes crinkling at the corners as she smiled. "Just take your time," she said, her voice gentle. "We'll start slow."

I nodded, taking a deep breath, and then I stepped into the water. The cold enveloped me, and I shivered, my muscles tensing. Sarah guided me to the side of the pool, where we began with simple exercises: blowing bubbles, kicking my legs, and letting the water support me. Each movement was a small victory, a step towards overcoming the fear that had gripped me for so long.

As the weeks passed, I found myself looking forward to these lessons. The pool became a sanctuary, a place where I could focus on the present, on the sensation of water against my skin, on the sound of my own breath. I learned to float, first on my back, staring up at the sky, feeling the water cradle me like a mother's embrace. Then, on my stomach, with Sarah's hand supporting my hips, I learned to trust the buoyancy of my body, to let go of the tension that had always kept me anchored to the ground.

One day, Sarah asked if I was ready to try the deep end. My heart skipped a beat, and for a moment, I felt the old fear creeping back. But I looked at her, at the calm assurance in her eyes, and I knew I couldn't turn back. I nodded, and together, we moved to the deeper part of the pool. The water rose above my chest, and I felt a familiar panic rising, but I pushed it down, focusing on my breathing, on the sensation of the water around me.

Sarah showed me how to tread water, and I practiced, my arms and legs moving in a rhythmic dance, keeping me afloat. It was exhausting, but exhilarating. For the first time, I felt a sense of control, a mastery over the element that had once seemed so threatening. And then, she taught me to swim, to glide through the water, my body cutting through the surface with a fluid motion. I swam a few strokes, and then a few more, and with each one, I felt a little lighter, a little freer.

There were setbacks, of course. Days when the fear returned, when the water seemed too deep, too cold, too daunting. But I persisted, and with each lesson, I grew stronger, more confident. I started to look forward to the moments when I could escape into the water, leaving behind the stresses and worries of daily life. The pool became a place of solace, a place where I could simply be, without judgment, without fear.

And then, one afternoon, as the sun began to set and the pool was quiet, I decided to swim a lap on my own. I pushed off from the wall, my body stretching out, and I began to move, my arms and legs working in harmony. The water rushed past me, cool and smooth, and I felt a surge of joy, a sense of accomplishment that I had never known before. I reached the other end of the pool, and I turned, and I swam back, and then again, and again. Each stroke was a testament to my journey, to the courage it had taken to face my fears, to embrace the unknown.

Learning to swim at forty was more than just a physical challenge; it was a journey of self-discovery, a reminder that it's never too late to confront the things that hold us back. The water, once a source of fear, had become a place of peace, a place where I could find a new kind of strength. And as I stood by the pool, dripping wet, with the sun setting behind me, I knew that I had found something more than just a skill. I had found a part of myself that I had never known existed, a part that was brave, and strong, and free.

title: legend|a drowned village whose church bell still rings at low tide
text:
The village of Marlowe’s Hollow never officially vanished from the Ordnance Survey maps—not until 1973, when the final revision omitted it entirely, leaving only a faint watermark in the margin: *“Former settlement, submerged, estuary of River Lymn.”* Locals still say its name aloud, though, especially old fishermen like Silas Croft, who’ll tap his pipe against the rusted rail of the Lymn Quay and mutter, “Ah, the Hollow. Still rings, you know. When the tide’s low enough to bare the old bell tower’s crown.”

It happened in November ’58—not with a flood, but with slow, patient drowning. The Lymn Estuary had been silting for centuries, but after the Great Storm of ’53, the coastal defences failed in patches, and the Ministry of Agriculture, in its wisdom, approved the Lymn Reclamation Scheme: two miles of concrete sea wall, a pumped drainage system, and the deliberate flooding of 470 acres of low-lying marshland—including Marlowe’s Hollow—to create a managed saltmarsh reserve. The villagers were offered relocation grants, new bungalows in Upper Lymn, and a single afternoon to pack. Reverend Eleanor Thorne refused to sign the surrender deed. She stood on the chancel step of St. Elidyr’s Church while surveyors measured the nave with brass tapes, her hands folded over a worn copy of the Book of Common Prayer, her voice clear as cut glass: “This ground was consecrated in 1213. You may drain it, but you cannot un-bless it.”

They drained it. They flooded it. By spring ’59, the churchyard was a green lagoon, the thatched roofs of the Hollow’s twenty-three cottages collapsed into silt, and St. Elidyr’s—built on a slight rise of glacial till—stood alone, its stone tower half-submerged, its oak doors sealed with tarred canvas and iron bands. The bell, cast in 1687 by John Tewkesbury of Bridport, remained hung in the belfry, its clapper lashed tight with hemp rope.

For twenty years, nothing stirred. Then, in ’79, young Ben Carter—then sixteen, now head of marine archaeology at Exeter—was calibrating a sonar array near the old church site when his hydrophone picked up a low, resonant tone: *Bong… bong… bong…* Three clear strikes, spaced exactly twelve seconds apart. He thought it was equipment feedback. But when he returned at neap low tide, with his grandfather’s brass pocket watch and a thermos of strong tea, he heard it again—not through the machine, but with his own ears, muffled, hollow, vibrating up through the soles of his boots where he stood knee-deep in cold, peaty water.

“It wasn’t loud,” Ben told me last October, sitting in the snug of the Anchor Inn, steam rising from his mug. “More like the sound your bones make when you hum underwater. And it only happens when the tide drops below Chart Datum Minus 1.8 metres—just enough to expose the top three courses of the tower’s west face. That’s when the wind finds the gap where the belfry window used to be. Not the wind alone, though. It’s the water retreating *through* the old foundation stones—the weep-holes, the cracked mortar joints. Like air being drawn across a flute’s mouthpiece.”

I went down with him at dawn on the 12th of March. The sky was the colour of wet slate, the air tasting of brine and decayed eelgrass. We waded out past the marker buoys—painted red with faded white numbers—and there it was: a rectangle of weathered limestone, barely six feet above the waterline, slick with emerald algae. A single arched opening, black as a socket, gaped where the bell chamber once faced west. No bell was visible. Just damp stone, barnacle scars, and a narrow ledge where ivy roots snaked into crumbling mortar.

We waited. The tide ebbed with a soft, sucking sigh. Gulls wheeled, silent. At 6:43 a.m., the water level dropped below the threshold. A gust came—not strong, just a nudge off the estuary—and slid into that dark arch. Then, almost imperceptibly, the air thickened. A vibration hummed in my molars. And then—*bong*. Deep, rounded, resonant, as if struck not by wood or metal, but by the earth itself shifting. Twelve seconds passed. *Bong*. Again, lower this time, as though the second note settled deeper into the silt. Twelve more seconds. *Bong*. Final. Fading into the hush like breath leaving a body.

Later, in the parish archive at St. Mary’s, I found Eleanor Thorne’s last entry in the church logbook, dated 14 October 1958: *“The bell rope is cut. The clapper remains free. Let the water decide when it shall speak.”* Beneath it, in a different hand—fainter, ink blotted—someone had written, in pencil: *“It spoke today. Low tide. 3:17 p.m. Heard by Mrs. P. Hargreaves (widow), walking her terrier, ‘Pip’. She says it sounded like a sigh.”*

Silas Croft died last February, just shy of ninety-two. His funeral was held at St. Mary’s, and the vicar, a pragmatic woman named Dr. Armitage, made no mention of drowned bells. But as the coffin passed the west door, Silas’s grandson—twelve-year-old Leo—tugged his mother’s sleeve and whispered, loud enough for three pews to hear: “Nan says Grandad always timed his walks to the tide. Said he liked to hear the Hollow say hello before it went quiet again.” No one corrected him. Outside, the wind shifted, carrying the sharp, clean smell of exposed mudflats—and for a heartbeat, just a heartbeat, the air held its breath.

title: literary essay|why old maps are more honest than new ones
text:
Old maps are more honest. Not *better*, mind you—God knows, I wouldn’t trust a 1584 Mercator projection to get me from Piccadilly to Oxford Street—but *honester*. In the way a cracked teacup tells the truth about how many times it’s been dropped, or how your grandmother’s handwriting on a recipe card—“a handful of thyme (not too much, Billy hated it)” —betrays more of her than any polished memoir ever could.

Look at the Hereford Mappa Mundi. Not a navigational tool—not even close. It’s a vast, circular, ox-hide thing, nearly five feet across, drawn in 1300-something on calf skin that still smells faintly of tallow and damp earth when you lean in close (I did, once, in the cathedral’s climate-controlled vault; the guard raised an eyebrow but didn’t stop me). Jerusalem sits dead centre—not because it’s geographically central (obviously not), but because it’s *theological* centre. And around the edges? Not coastlines, but chaos: monstrous races—Blemmyae with faces on their chests, Sciopods who nap under their single enormous foot, dog-headed Cynocephali guarding the Gates of Alexander. Modern mapmakers call this “error.” I call it confession. They knew where their knowledge ended—and instead of smoothing it over with satellite data or algorithmic interpolation, they drew dragons. *Hic sunt dracones.* Here be dragons. Not “here be uncharted waters,” not “here be probable error margins ±2.7%,” but *dragons*. A declaration of humility wrapped in ink and gold leaf.

New maps? They lie with surgical precision. Google Maps doesn’t say, “We’re not sure if that alley behind the post office still exists—we last checked in 2022, and the building was half-demolished then.” No. It renders the alley in crisp, confident blue lines. It tells you the café is open *now*, even though the sign in the window says “Closed for Renovations (Indefinitely)” and a pigeon has nested in the planter outside. It shows three stars and “Great ambience!”—written by someone named “Trevor B., verified reviewer,” whose only other review is of a car wash in Slough. The lie isn’t malicious. It’s bureaucratic. It’s the lie of the dashboard: everything green, all systems nominal, even as the engine coughs and the oil light blinks like a nervous tic.

I remember a map my father kept in his glovebox—a wrinkled, coffee-stained Ordnance Survey sheet, 1:50,000, dated 1971. He’d annotate it in ballpoint: “Bridge out—use ford (muddy, 4x4 only),” “Mrs. G’s hens cross here at dusk,” “Badger sett—don’t park over it.” None of that appears on the digital version. The OS app just shows the road, smooth and uninterrupted, as if badgers had collectively agreed to relocate and Mrs. G’s hens had taken up yoga. The old map admitted its own incompleteness. It wasn’t trying to *be* the territory—it knew it was only a shaky, sweaty, human translation.

And the margins! Oh, the glorious, scribbled margins of old maps. The 1630 Blaeu atlas has a footnote beside Iceland: “Said to steam, though no man living has set foot there and returned sane.” A 17th-century Dutch chart of the South Pacific includes a tiny, precise drawing of a whale breaching—not as fauna, but as *warning*: “This beast capsized the *Vliegende Vos* on 12th May, anno Domini 1647. Crew lost, save one boy found clinging to a barrel of pickled herrings.” That’s not cartography. That’s testimony. That’s memory with salt crusting its edges.

Modern mapping feels like watching someone edit a video in real time—smoothing skin, erasing blemishes, adjusting lighting—until the subject bears only a polite, glossy resemblance to themselves. We’ve traded the wobble of the hand-drawn line for the unnerving stillness of the pixel. We’ve replaced “we think” with “the system confirms.” Which sounds authoritative. Which is why it’s so dangerous.

I don’t romanticise ignorance. I’m grateful for GPS when I’m lost in a rain-slicked Glasgow roundabout at midnight. But gratitude isn’t the same as trust. Old maps don’t pretend to omniscience. They wear their gaps like medals. They remind you—always—that every map is a story told by someone, from somewhere, with particular eyes, particular fears, particular hopes. A new map tries to erase the storyteller. An old one leaves fingerprints, coffee rings, a smudge of candle wax near the Caspian Sea, and sometimes—just sometimes—a single, shaky, inked word in the blank space north of Norway: *Hope?*

That question mark? That’s the most honest thing on the whole damn page.

title: literary essay|silence and omission in short fiction
text:
...as the characters sit in the dimly lit room, the silence between them stretches, taut and unyielding. It is a silence that seems to speak volumes, more so than any words could. In this moment, the absence of dialogue is not a void but a dense, palpable presence. This scene, like many others in short fiction, relies on the power of silence and omission to convey the unsaid, the unspoken, and the deeply felt. The author, through these moments of quiet, invites the reader to fill in the gaps, to interpret the nuances, and to engage with the text on a deeper, more personal level.

Silence, in short fiction, often serves as a narrative device that amplifies the emotional weight of a story. In Ernest Hemingway’s "Hills Like White Elephants," for instance, the conversation between the American man and Jig is punctuated by long, uncomfortable silences. These pauses are not just breaks in the dialogue; they are moments where the tension and the unspoken truths of their relationship are laid bare. The couple is discussing an abortion, a topic fraught with moral and emotional complexity, yet much of what they feel is left unspoken. The silences in their conversation become a form of communication in themselves, a way for the characters to avoid the harsh reality of their situation while simultaneously revealing it. Hemingway’s use of omission—what is left unsaid—creates a sense of unease and uncertainty, drawing the reader into the emotional landscape of the characters.

Similarly, in Katherine Anne Porter’s "The Jilting of Granny Weatherall," the titular character, Ellen, is lying on her deathbed, reliving the past and grappling with the memories that have shaped her life. As she drifts in and out of consciousness, the narrative is filled with silences and omissions. The story is told from Ellen’s point of view, and her fragmented thoughts and memories create a disjointed, almost dreamlike quality. The silences in the narrative reflect the gaps in Ellen’s memory and the unresolved issues of her life. For example, when she thinks about her first love, George, who jilted her at the altar, the narrative shifts to a series of fragmented, unconnected images and memories. The omissions here—the things that are not said—underscore the pain and the trauma of the past, which continue to haunt her even in her final moments.

In both of these stories, the authors use silence and omission to create a sense of depth and complexity. The silences are not empty spaces; they are filled with the unspoken emotions, the unarticulated thoughts, and the hidden truths of the characters. By leaving certain things unsaid, the authors invite the reader to engage more actively with the text, to read between the lines, and to infer the meaning behind the silences. This technique is particularly effective in short fiction, where every word and every pause must carry weight. The brevity of the form demands that the writer be economical with language, and the use of silence and omission can be a powerful tool for conveying complex emotions and ideas.

Moreover, silence and omission can also serve to highlight the power dynamics within a story. In Alice Munro’s "The Bear Came Over the Mountain," the relationship between Fiona and Grant, a married couple, is explored through the lens of Fiona’s dementia. As Fiona’s condition worsens, she begins to forget Grant, and the silences between them grow. The omissions in their conversations—things that are no longer remembered or acknowledged—become a metaphor for the gradual erasure of their shared history. The silence in their interactions is not just a result of Fiona’s memory loss; it also reflects the unspoken tensions and the unacknowledged aspects of their marriage. The silences, in this case, are a form of communication, a way for the characters to navigate the changing dynamics of their relationship.

In addition, the use of silence and omission can create a sense of ambiguity and open-endedness, allowing the reader to draw their own conclusions. In Raymond Carver’s "Cathedral," the narrator, a blind man, and the narrator’s wife share a moment of connection as they draw a cathedral together. The story ends with the narrator closing his eyes and continuing to draw, experiencing a profound, almost spiritual connection. The final lines of the story are simple and direct, but they leave much unsaid: "My eyes were still closed. I was in my house. I knew that. But I didn't feel like I was inside anything." The silence at the end of the story, the absence of further explanation, allows the reader to interpret the significance of the moment in their own way. The omission of a clear resolution creates a sense of openness, inviting the reader to reflect on the meaning of the experience.

In conclusion, the use of silence and omission in short fiction is a nuanced and powerful technique that enriches the narrative and deepens the reader’s engagement with the text. Whether it is through the unspoken tensions in a conversation, the gaps in a character’s memory, or the ambiguous ending of a story, these moments of silence and omission create a space for the reader to enter the world of the story and to participate in its creation. The absence of words, in this context, is not a lack but a presence, a way of saying more with less, and a means of exploring the depths of human experience.

title: folk tale|the miller's third son and the talking millstone
text:
The mill stood where the river bent sharp as a broken bone, its timbers blackened by centuries of damp and smoke, its wheel groaning like an old man’s knees in winter. Inside, the air hung thick with the scent of crushed grain and damp stone, and the floor trembled perpetually beneath the weight of the millstone’s slow, grinding turn. Old Hemlock, the miller, had three sons: the first, broad-shouldered and certain, took the lease on the best field near the village green; the second, quick-tongued and clever, apprenticed himself to the bailiff and learned to read leases and tally rents; the third, named Silas, was slight, with knuckles permanently dusted white from sifting flour, eyes that watched the light shift across the mill’s warped floorboards, and a habit of speaking only when the silence between words felt full enough to hold his voice. His brothers called him “the quiet one,” then “the slow one,” then, when he refused the forge and the clerk’s desk alike, “the useless one.” When Hemlock died—quietly, in his chair beside the hopper, a single kernel of rye caught in the corner of his mouth—the mill passed not to the eldest, nor the second, but to Silas, by the terms of a will written in faded ink and sealed with a thumbprint stained brown with flour.

The mill did not prosper. The river ran low that summer, and the wheel turned sluggish, its groan deepening to a hollow ache. Grain spoiled in the loft, souring in the heat. Villagers brought their corn less often, preferring the new watermill downstream with its iron gears and steady hum. One evening, after sweeping the last of the day’s bran into the sack, Silas leaned his forehead against the lower millstone—the great, circular slab of basalt, pitted and veined with quartz, worn smooth in the center where the runner stone ground against it. He did not pray. He did not curse. He simply rested there, breathing the cool, mineral breath of the stone, feeling the faint, residual vibration of its earlier work humming up through his bones.

Then, a voice—not loud, not soft, but *present*, like the sudden weight of a held breath—spoke from the stone itself. Not in words shaped for ears, but in syllables that formed inside his skull, clear as chipped flint: *You do not grind me. You let me rest.*

Silas drew back, heart hammering against his ribs. He looked at the stone: cold, inert, ancient. He touched it again, fingers tracing the spiral groove cut by generations of millers’ hands. *Who speaks?*

*The stone that remembers the mountain,* came the reply, dry as powdered shale. *The stone that remembers the glacier’s tongue. The stone that remembers your father’s father’s hand, pressing the wedge into the eye-hole. I remember the weight of wheat, the heat of summer sun on my flank, the chill of the river mist before dawn. I remember being silent. Now I am not.*

Silas did not laugh. He did not run. He fetched a cup of water, not for himself, but for the stone, pouring it slowly into the central hole—the eye—where the spindle would sit. The water darkened the porous surface, seeped into the ancient fissures. *What do you wish?*

*To be turned,* the stone said. *Not by force. Not by fury. By knowing. Your brothers turned me to make flour. Your father turned me to pay rent. You… you stand beside me. You feel the tremor. You hear the groan. Turn me, Silas, when the river rises. Not because the grain demands it. Because the stone remembers the turning.*

The next morning, rain fell—not the thin, spiteful drizzle of weeks past, but a slow, heavy rain that swelled the river’s throat. By noon, the wheel churned with renewed strength, its groan transformed into a deep, resonant song. Silas did not rush to the hopper. He stood beside the stone, listening. He felt the subtle shift in the vibration, the way the runner stone settled differently upon the bed, the minute sigh of compressed air escaping the grooves. Only then did he lift the wooden lever, easing the runner stone down with a gentleness that made the iron pins whisper. He fed the grain—not in haste, but in measured handfuls, watching how each kernel tumbled, how the stone accepted them, how the flour bloomed outwards, fine and pale as moth wings.

Word spread, not of magic, but of uncanny stillness. People brought their corn not for speed, but for the quality of the flour—unusually fine, unusually sweet, carrying a faint, clean scent of wet rock and deep earth. A widow brought her last sack, her hands trembling, and when Silas ground it, the stone spoke again, low and resonant: *This woman’s husband carved the oak beam above the hopper. His chisel marks are still in the grain.* Silas looked up, saw the faint, overlapping notches in the timber, invisible to all but the stone—and now, somehow, to him. He nodded, and the widow wept, not from sorrow, but from the shock of being truly seen.

One autumn night, frost silvered the river’s edge, and the mill stood silent. Silas sat on the cold flagstones, his back against the lower stone. The moonlight fell through the high, grimy window, illuminating motes of flour dancing in the air. He felt no fear, no wonder—only a quiet companionship, as deep and unspoken as the roots of the old ash tree that grew beside the millrace. The stone did not speak. It did not need to. Its presence was a weight, a warmth, a continuity. Silas closed his eyes and felt the slow, patient pulse of the river beneath the floor, the ancient, slow pulse of the stone beneath his spine, and the even slower pulse of time itself, measured not in seasons or harvests, but in the infinitesimal wearing away of granite, grain by grain, century by century. Outside, the wind moved through the reeds, a sound like distant, unending grinding. Inside, the mill held its breath, and Silas, the quiet son, held his, listening not for words, but for the long, low hum of the world remembering itself.

title: literary essay|why old maps are more honest than new ones
text:
The Cartographer’s Confession  
*By A. R. Thorne*

I keep a 16th-century portolan chart of the Mediterranean in my study—not framed, not behind glass, but folded loosely inside a folio of unbleached linen, its vellum edges brittle as dried riverbeds. When I unfold it, the ink—iron gall, dark and slightly raised—smells faintly of vinegar and time. The coastlines are precise where known: Genoa’s harbour mouth is rendered with surgical care; the jagged silhouette of Crete, unmistakable. But beyond Cape St. Vincent, the sea thickens. There, in the blank expanse westward, a dragon coils around a phrase in careful humanist script: *Hic sunt dracones*. Here be dragons.

I used to think that line was a warning. Now I think it’s an admission.

We praise modern maps for their fidelity—their satellite-verified contours, their centimetre-accurate bathymetry, their real-time traffic overlays blinking like nervous synapses. They feel authoritative. They feel *true*. But truth, as any archivist knows, is rarely a matter of resolution. It is a matter of what is named, what is omitted, and what is left unnamed—not out of ignorance, but out of principle.

Old maps do not pretend to omniscience. They declare their limits with ink and ornament. That dragon isn’t superstition; it’s cartographic humility made visible. It says: *This is where our knowledge ends. This is where our ships turn back or founder. We do not know what lies here, so we name the unknown—not with data points, but with myth, because myth is the only language adequate to absence.* The dragon is not a lie. It is a punctuation mark in the sentence of knowing: a full stop before the cliff edge of certainty.

New maps erase the cliff edge. They fill the void not with dragons, but with interpolated coastlines, algorithmically smoothed contours, ghost islands generated by sensor noise and then quietly absorbed into the official record. In 2012, the National Geographic Society quietly removed Sandy Island from its digital atlases—not because it had been found, but because it had never existed. Yet for over a century, it appeared on nautical charts, government surveys, even Google Earth, its non-existence sustained by repetition, not observation. Its erasure wasn’t correction; it was a kind of administrative forgetting—a preference for clean data over honest uncertainty.

I once spent a week in the British Library’s Map Room tracing the evolution of the Caspian Sea across six centuries of Russian and Persian cartography. Early Persian maps show it as a teardrop-shaped basin, fed by four rivers drawn with calligraphic precision. Later Russian surveys, emboldened by imperial surveyors and newly minted theodolites, stretch its eastern shore eastward, flattening its southern curve, adding phantom bays where none existed. By 1890, it looks almost like today’s shape—except for one detail: the 1734 map includes a marginal note in Persian script describing how local fishermen say the lake breathes—how its level rises and falls not with snowmelt alone, but with wind patterns no instrument could yet measure. That note vanishes by 1850. Not because the phenomenon ceased, but because the language for it—oral, empirical, embodied—had no place in the new lexicon of measurement.

Modern mapping doesn’t just depict space; it enacts sovereignty. Every GPS coordinate is a jurisdictional claim disguised as neutral fact. Every boundary line drawn on a digital platform carries the weight of treaties, military deployments, surveillance infrastructure. The map becomes less a representation of land than a legal instrument—a deed, a warrant, a zoning ordinance in disguise. Old maps, by contrast, often bear the names of patrons, not governments: *Made for the Duke of Urbino, 1524*. Their authority is personal, contingent, finite. They do not presume to bind the world to a single standard of truth. They offer a version—tempered by patronage, limited by travel, shaped by rumour and reverence.

There is also the matter of scale—not just of distance, but of attention. On a 1584 Dutch sea chart, the Strait of Magellan is depicted not as a narrow channel but as a labyrinth of overlapping currents, annotated with warnings about sudden squalls and magnetic deviation. The annotations are handwritten, cramped, urgent. They don’t reduce the strait to a line on a screen; they render it as a lived passage—hazardous, unpredictable, demanding presence. Today’s navigation apps flatten that same strait into a blue vector, overlaid with estimated arrival times and fuel consumption metrics. The dragon has been replaced by a progress bar.

I don’t romanticise the past. I’ve seen the cost of those dragons—the shipwrecks, the failed expeditions, the colonial violence that followed hard on the heels of “discovery.” Honesty is not innocence. But honesty *is* the willingness to inscribe your own uncertainty into the record—to let the margin speak as loudly as the centre, to allow the uncharted to remain uncharted rather than smoothed over by interpolation.

My old portolan chart has no latitude lines. No graticule. No north arrow pointing rigidly upward. Its compass rose is ornate, asymmetrical, slightly off-kilter—drawn by hand, not plotted. It does not claim to orient the world. It orients *me*, in this particular moment, to this particular sea. And when I look at it, I feel not the comfort of mastery, but the quiet, unsettling dignity of being precisely, unflinchingly lost.

That, perhaps, is the first condition of seeing anything clearly.

title: historical novel|a cartographer's apprentice in eighteenth-century Lisbon
text:
In the year 1755, when Lisbon was a city of both splendor and squalor, there lived a young man named João. He was an apprentice to one of the most renowned cartographers in Portugal, a man by the name of Master Rodrigo. The streets of Lisbon were narrow and winding, often choked with the scent of salt from the nearby Tagus River, and the cries of merchants hawking their wares. João's days were spent in the small, cluttered workshop on a steep cobbled street, where the light filtered through stained glass, casting a kaleidoscope of colors on the worn wooden floor.

Master Rodrigo was a stern but fair man, with a long, graying beard and eyes that seemed to hold the secrets of the world. He had traveled to distant lands, mapping territories that few Europeans had ever seen. His maps were works of art, meticulously detailed, with every river, mountain, and coastline carefully rendered. João, who had been orphaned at a young age, had found a home in this workshop, learning the craft of cartography from the master himself.

The apprenticeship was not easy. João spent hours hunched over his desk, drawing and redrawing lines, measuring distances, and labeling landmarks. His fingers were often stained with ink, and his back ached from the constant bending. But he loved the work, the way the map came alive under his hands, the sense of creating something that would guide sailors and explorers to new worlds. Sometimes, as he worked, he would imagine himself on one of those ships, sailing to the far corners of the earth, discovering lands that no one had ever seen.

One day, while João was meticulously inking a map of the coast of Brazil, Master Rodrigo entered the workshop, his face unusually somber. He carried a letter, sealed with the royal crest. "João," he said, his voice low, "we have been summoned to the palace. The king has requested a special commission."

João's heart raced. A royal commission! This was the opportunity of a lifetime. He quickly cleaned his tools and followed Master Rodrigo out into the bustling streets. The air was thick with the smell of baking bread and the sound of church bells. They made their way to the grand palace, its white stone gleaming in the afternoon sun. Inside, the opulence was overwhelming: marble floors, gilded mirrors, and tapestries depicting heroic battles and mythological scenes.

The king, Dom José I, was a portly man with a kind face, but his eyes were sharp and calculating. He explained that he needed a map of the Portuguese territories in Africa, a map so detailed that it could be used for military and trade purposes. The project would take months, perhaps even years, and it would require travel to the colonies to gather accurate information.

João's mind reeled. Travel to Africa! It was a dream he had never dared to entertain. Master Rodrigo, sensing his excitement, placed a firm hand on his shoulder. "We will do our best, Your Majesty," he said, bowing deeply.

The next few weeks were a whirlwind of preparation. João helped Master Rodrigo gather all the necessary materials: compasses, rulers, ink, and vellum. They also had to secure passage on a ship, which was no small feat. The docks were teeming with activity, and the air was filled with the shouts of sailors and the creaking of wooden hulls. João felt a thrill of anticipation as they boarded the ship, the *São Jorge*, bound for Luanda.

The voyage was long and arduous. The sea was rough, and many of the crew fell ill. João, however, found solace in the vast expanse of the ocean, the way the waves stretched endlessly to the horizon. He spent hours on deck, sketching the stars and the constellations, trying to capture the beauty of the night sky.

When they finally arrived in Luanda, the heat was oppressive, and the air was thick with the smell of spices and sweat. The city was a mix of European and African influences, with whitewashed buildings and bustling markets. João and Master Rodrigo set to work immediately, traveling to different regions, meeting with local leaders, and gathering information about the terrain, the rivers, and the settlements. 

They faced many challenges. The language barrier was a constant obstacle, and the harsh conditions of the African interior tested their endurance. But João was determined. He wanted to create a map that would be a testament to their journey, a map that would stand the test of time.

One evening, as they sat around a campfire, Master Rodrigo shared stories of his past adventures. He spoke of the Amazon, of the dense forests and the mighty rivers, of the people who lived in harmony with nature. João listened, mesmerized, feeling a deep connection to the man who had become like a father to him.

Months turned into years, and the map slowly took shape. It was a masterpiece, a testament to their hard work and dedication. When they returned to Lisbon, the city was unrecognizable. The Great Earthquake of 1755 had devastated the city, leaving it in ruins. The streets were filled with the debris of collapsed buildings, and the air was thick with dust and the smell of smoke.

Despite the tragedy, the king was pleased with their work. The map was presented to him in a grand ceremony, and João and Master Rodrigo were honored for their service. The map became a symbol of hope, a reminder that even in the face of disaster, humanity could create something beautiful and enduring.

João, now a skilled cartographer in his own right, continued to work with Master Rodrigo, creating more maps and charts. But he never forgot the lessons he learned in Africa, the sense of wonder and adventure that had driven him to explore the unknown. And though the world changed, and the maps grew old, the spirit of discovery remained, a beacon for future generations.

title: short story|a beekeeper's widow deciding whether to keep the hives
text:
The hive box trembled in her hands—not with the low, resonant hum of life within, but with the fine, insistent vibration of her own pulse against the worn cedar grain. Eleanor stood at the edge of the south meadow, the late afternoon sun slanting gold and long across the clover, already gone to seed and dusted with a faint, silver down. Behind her, the old stone cottage hunched its shoulders against the cooling air, smoke curling thin and grey from the chimney—her own small fire, lit not for warmth, but as a habit, a tether. She hadn’t meant to come out here. Had meant only to refill the kettle, to wipe the flour-dusted counter where Ben used to knead his sourdough, to feel the ordinary weight of domesticity settle back onto her ribs like a familiar shawl. But the gate latch clicked under her fingers, and then she was walking, the path worn smooth by thirty years of his boots and her sandals, and now, inexplicably, by her bare feet.

She lowered the box onto the grass, the thud soft, muffled. It was Hive Three—the one Ben called “the stubborn one,” the one that swarmed every May like clockwork, sending him scrambling for his veil and smoker while she watched from the porch, laughing, holding a mug of tea that grew cold. She hadn’t opened it since the funeral. Not properly. A quick, grim inspection three weeks ago: the frames thick with capped honey, amber and deep as old brandy, the brood nest compact and warm beneath a dense, living blanket of bees. Healthy. Thriving. Utterly indifferent to the absence at its heart.

Her fingers traced the seam where lid met body. The wood was warm still from the sun, but the metal strap—cold, unyielding. She remembered Ben’s hands on this same strap, knuckles broad and stained with propolis, the blue veins standing out like map lines. He’d never rush an opening. “Patience, Ellie,” he’d murmur, his voice a low thrum beneath the hive’s own song. “They know the difference between fear and respect. They’ll tell you if you’re lying.” And they had. Once, when she’d been nervous, her breath shallow, the guard bees had risen like smoke, a low, warning growl vibrating up her arms before she even lifted the lid. Ben had just nodded, not unkindly. “Listen better next time.”

She closed her eyes. Not to shut out the light, but to let the sounds flood in: the drowsy drone of the hives behind her—Hive One, Two, Four, Five, Six—all humming their collective, complex chord. The buzz wasn’t just noise; it was syntax. It held the temperature of the brood chamber, the urgency of foragers returning heavy-laden, the quiet vigilance of the guards, the slow, deep pulse of the queen’s presence—a vibration felt more than heard, a resonance in the soles of her feet, in the hollow behind her sternum. She’d learned to read it, not as Ben had, with the instinct of decades, but as a student learns a foreign language—by repetition, by paying attention to the silences between the notes, by noticing how the pitch shifted when the wind changed, or when the first frost nipped the lavender.

A bee landed on the back of her hand. Not tentative, not aggressive. Just… present. A worker, her tiny legs dusty with pollen the colour of crushed violets. Eleanor held her breath. The bee walked slowly, deliberately, across the knuckle, her wings catching the light like fractured stained glass. Then, without fanfare, she lifted off, joining the slow, golden river flowing towards the fading sun. Eleanor watched her go, a knot in her throat that had nothing to do with grief and everything to do with the sheer, staggering *continuity* of it. Life didn’t pause. It didn’t consult. It simply *was*, humming its ancient, intricate song right there, in the grass, in the air, in the warm, breathing wood beneath her palms.

She thought of the ledger on the kitchen table. Pages filled with Ben’s precise, looping script: dates, weights, varroa counts, syrup feeds, swarm dates, honey yields. Her own handwriting, hesitant at first, then firmer, appeared beside his later entries: *“Ellie checked brood pattern – good.” “Ellie fed 1:1 syrup – bees took well.”* She’d written those words, but had she *felt* them? Or had she been writing a script, performing the part of the widow-beekeeper, hoping the role would eventually fit, like Ben’s old waxed jacket hanging too loosely in the shed?

The practicalities were a cold, hard rain on the warm memory. The cost of new queens if she lost any over winter. The time—hours each week, dawn and dusk, regardless of weather, regardless of the hollow ache that sometimes made her want to sleep until noon. The sheer physicality: lifting supers heavy with honey, battling tangled burr comb, the sting that still made her flinch, the constant, low-grade anxiety about disease, predators, the unpredictable whims of weather and climate that Ben had navigated with a calm that now felt like myth. Could she stand in the rain, smoke puffing weakly, watching bees cluster helplessly on a wet branch after a sudden chill? Could she make the call to re-queen, knowing the old queen—Ben’s queen—would be gone forever?

She looked back at the cottage. Through the open kitchen window, she saw the flicker of the firelight on the wall, the curve of the teapot on the stove. Safety. Quiet. The profound, seductive relief of letting go. Of selling the land, the hives, the whole intricate, demanding, beautiful machine. Of becoming simply Eleanor again, unburdened by the weight of the swarm, the responsibility of the queen, the constant, humming conversation with ten thousand lives.

Her hand, still resting on the hive box, felt the faint, almost imperceptible shift. Not a vibration of sound, but of *heat*. A deeper warmth, radiating up from the wood, from the living core within. She pressed her palm flat, feeling the thrum not just in her bones, but in the marrow. It wasn’t Ben’s hum. It was older. Deeper. Hers, too, perhaps, if she dared to listen past the silence he left behind.

The violet-pollen bee was gone. The sun dipped lower, gilding the edges of the clover heads. The drone softened, deepened, settling into the twilight’s hush. Eleanor didn’t lift the lid. She didn’t walk away. She stayed, her hand on the warm wood, listening—not for Ben’s voice, but for the steady, undeniable, ancient music of the hive, and the quiet, answering pulse beginning, tentatively, in her own chest.

title: personal essay|the last video rental shop in town
text:
The neon sign flickered—not the cheerful, steady pulse of a diner or a laundromat, but a tired, intermittent stutter, like a breath held too long. *Video Vault*. The ‘V’ had gone dark years ago, leaving only *ideo Vault*, and even that was half-swallowed by the creeping ivy that climbed the brick façade like something patient and quietly insistent. Inside, the air smelled of dust motes suspended in amber light, old carpet glue, and the faint, sweet-sour tang of aging plastic—VHS casings sweating their slow chemical surrender. It wasn’t musty, exactly; it was layered. A sedimentary record of Saturday afternoons, teenage crushes whispered over the counter, arguments about whether *Blade Runner* deserved its reputation, the soft *thunk* of a rewinder churning tape back into its shell.

I remember the floorboards. Not just creaked—they groaned, a low, resonant complaint with every step past the glass display case holding faded posters: *The Princess Bride*, *Raising Arizona*, *Point Break*, all slightly curled at the corners, their colors muted to the soft sepia of memory. Behind the counter stood Mr. Arden, though no one ever called him that. He was just Arden—tall, thin as a film strip, with wire-rimmed glasses perpetually sliding down his nose and fingers stained yellow at the tips from decades of handling cassette spines. He never wore a name tag. His uniform was a faded band T-shirt—sometimes Nirvana, sometimes The Cure—and a cardigan perpetually snagged on a stray button. He knew everyone’s rental history not by scanning a barcode, but by the slight lift of an eyebrow when you walked in, the way his gaze would linger for half a second on your face before drifting to the shelf behind you, as if he’d already anticipated your hesitation between *Dead Man Walking* and *The Piano*.

The shelves weren’t arranged alphabetically, nor by genre in any strict sense. They were organized by *weight*, by *texture*, by some internal cartography known only to Arden and the ghosts of a thousand browsing afternoons. Horror lived in the back corner, near the leaky radiator that hummed a low bass note in winter, its spines often warped, titles like *Suspiria* and *The Texas Chain Saw Massacre* standing sentinel beside lesser-known gems with hand-scrawled stickers: *“Scared me more than the last three.”* Comedy occupied the sunlit aisle by the front window, where the light caught the iridescent sheen on *Airplane!* and *This Is Spinal Tap*, their cases slightly dusty, as if they’d been handled less, revered more. Foreign films huddled together in a narrow section marked only by a laminated index card taped crookedly to the shelf: *“Not Subtitled. Just Watch.”* Beneath it, a single, battered copy of *Cinema Paradiso*, its spine cracked, its cover worn smooth where countless thumbs had traced the embossed title.

I rented *Paris, Texas* there once. Not because I knew anything about Wim Wenders, but because Arden slid it across the counter without a word, placed it atop my stack of *Die Hard* and *Ghostbusters*, and said, “The desert’s quiet tonight.” I didn’t understand then. I took it home, watched Travis wander the bleached streets of Los Angeles, the silence of the film pressing in like actual weight, the absence of music making every footstep, every sigh, vibrate in my own small apartment. When I returned it, Arden didn’t ask what I thought. He just nodded, ran the tape through the machine—a whirring, mechanical sigh—as if checking its pulse, then shelved it back not where it belonged, but beside *Stalker*, two films bound by a shared, aching stillness.

The register was a relic: a heavy metal box with keys that clacked like typewriter hammers, receipts printed on thermal paper that faded to ghostly grey within months. Arden never charged late fees. He’d glance at the due date scrawled on the slip, then at your face, and say, “Rain kept you?” or “Dog ate the tape?” and ring it up anyway, sometimes slipping in a free popcorn coupon—stamped by hand, ink smudged, good for one small bag, always slightly stale, always perfect.

There were no surveillance cameras. No digital logs. Just Arden’s ledger, a thick, cloth-bound book with pages filled in his precise, looping script: *M. Chen – 3/12 – Raging Bull (x2), Amélie (x1) – $6.50*. Sometimes, beside a name, he’d add a tiny sketch: a coffee cup, a dog’s paw, a single star. I found mine once, weeks after returning *Paris, Texas*: my name, the date, the title, and beside it, drawn in careful pencil, a single, small, perfect palm tree.

The last time I went in, the ivy had breached the cracked pane above the door. Rain leaked in a slow, steady drip onto the rug near the horror section, darkening the pattern into a spreading stain. Arden wasn’t behind the counter. He was kneeling by the VCRs, unplugging cords, stacking tapes into cardboard boxes stamped with the logo of a local moving company. He looked up, saw me, and didn’t smile. He just held out a tape—*The Last Picture Show*, its case pristine, unrented. “Take it,” he said. His voice was dry, like pages turning. “It’s got a good ending.” I took it. The plastic felt cool, solid, real in my palm. Outside, a delivery van idled, its engine a low, impatient growl. The neon sign gave one final, shuddering pulse—*ideo Vault*—then went dark, leaving only the greenish glow of a streetlamp reflecting in the wet pavement, and the quiet, persistent drip, drip, drip from the ceiling onto the rug, soaking deeper into the fibers, into the floor, into the quiet, unremarkable space where stories used to wait, patiently, for someone to reach out and pull them off the shelf.

title: memoir|learning to fish with a silent uncle on a Scottish loch
text:
The loch, a mirror of the sky, stretched out before us, its surface occasionally broken by the leap of a trout or the gentle ripple of a breeze. I stood beside my uncle, his presence as still and quiet as the water. He was not a man of many words, and in that silence, I found myself drawn to the rhythm of nature, to the subtle changes in light and shadow, to the distant calls of birds.

I had come to Scotland with the naive expectation of learning to fish, but it soon became clear that the lessons were deeper, more intangible. My uncle, a tall, lean man with a weathered face and hands that seemed to have been shaped by the very elements he lived among, moved with a deliberate grace. He was a fisherman, yes, but also a guardian of the loch, a keeper of its secrets.

Our first morning, we walked along the shore, the grass damp beneath our boots. The air was cool, carrying the scent of earth and water. Uncle carried his rod with the ease of a swordsman, and I followed, clutching mine with the awkwardness of a novice. We stopped at a spot where the reeds grew thick, and he set down his gear, motioning for me to do the same. He began to tie a fly, his fingers moving with practiced precision, and I watched, trying to mimic his movements. But my hands fumbled, and the thread tangled, and I felt a flush of frustration.

He looked at me, his eyes kind, and took the fly from my hand. Without a word, he untangled the mess and handed it back to me. I tried again, and this time, with his silent encouragement, I managed to complete the knot. It was a small victory, but it felt significant. We cast our lines into the loch, and the world around us seemed to hold its breath.

Hours passed, and the sun climbed higher in the sky. We did not speak, but there was a strange comfort in the shared silence. I watched the water, waiting for the slightest twitch of the line, and when it came, I pulled too hard, jerking the rod and losing the fish. My uncle glanced at me, a hint of a smile on his lips, and I knew he understood. There was no need for words; the lesson was in the act itself, in the patience and the stillness.

Over the days that followed, we returned to the loch, each morning bringing a new challenge, a new opportunity to learn. I began to notice the subtle signs of the fish: the dimples on the surface, the shadows beneath the waves. I learned to read the water, to understand its moods, and to move with it, rather than against it. My uncle taught me, not with words, but with his presence, with the way he moved, with the way he waited.

One afternoon, as the sun began to set, casting a golden glow across the loch, I felt a strong tug on my line. I remembered to be gentle, to let the fish run, and then to reel it in slowly. When I finally brought the trout to the shore, my heart was pounding with a mix of excitement and pride. My uncle nodded, and I saw a glint of approval in his eyes. We released the fish, and it swam away, leaving ripples that spread across the water, a reminder of the moment.

As the days turned into weeks, I found myself changing. The silence, which had once been oppressive, now felt like a balm. I learned to listen to the loch, to the wind, to the rustle of the reeds. I learned to be patient, to wait, to let the world unfold in its own time. And in that patience, I found a peace I had never known before.

But the lessons were not just about fishing. They were about life, about the importance of stillness, of observation, of understanding the world around us. My uncle, with his quiet wisdom, had shown me a different way of being, a way that was rooted in the natural world, in the rhythms of the earth.

When it was time to leave, I felt a deep sense of loss. The loch, with its ever-changing moods, had become a part of me, and my uncle, with his silent guidance, had become a mentor. We said our goodbyes, and as I hugged him, I felt a connection that went beyond words. I knew that I would carry the lessons of the loch with me, that they would shape the way I saw the world, the way I lived my life.

Years have passed since those days by the loch, but the memories remain vivid. I still fish, though not as often as I would like, and when I do, I find myself returning to the lessons I learned. I remember the silence, the stillness, the patience. I remember the loch, and I remember my uncle, and I am grateful for the time we spent together, for the unspoken bond that formed between us.

In the end, I realize that the true art of fishing is not in the catching, but in the waiting, in the watching, in the listening. It is in the moments of stillness, in the quiet communion with the natural world, that we find the deepest meaning. And in that, I have found a way to live, a way to be, that is both simple and profound.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
The chlorine hit me first—not the sharp, clean sting I’d imagined, but a thick, wet slap of old bleach and damp concrete. I stood barefoot on the cracked blue tile of the YWCA pool deck in Northampton, Massachusetts, my toes curling over the edge where the grout had turned gray and spongy. My swimsuit, navy Lycra purchased online after three false starts and one panicked return, clung too tightly under the arms. I was forty years, two months, and seventeen days old.

“First time in the water?” asked Lena, who ran the adult beginner class. She wore goggles pushed up on her forehead like a headband, her dark hair pulled into a low bun streaked with silver at the temples. Her voice wasn’t loud, but it carried—calm, unhurried, the kind that didn’t ask for permission to settle into your ear. She held a laminated card with my name printed in neat block letters: *Eleanor Vance*. I’d signed up under my full name, not “Ellie,” as if formality might lend gravity to the absurdity of what I was attempting.

I nodded. My throat felt tight, not from nerves exactly, but from the sheer weight of unspent decades—the childhood summers spent watching cousins cannonball off the dock while I sat cross-legged on the sun-warmed wood, knees drawn to my chest, pretending I preferred the shade. The high school gym pool where I’d changed in a stall, heart hammering, then walked straight past the shallow end to the locker room, claiming a migraine. The wedding in Nantucket where I’d declined the harbor cruise, citing “sea legs,” though I’d never set foot on a boat larger than a rowboat—and even that, once, with my knuckles white on the oarlocks.

Lena didn’t say *It’s never too late*. She didn’t need to. She just handed me a foam noodle the color of bruised plums and said, “Hold it like it’s your cousin’s wrist—you don’t want to drop it, but you don’t have to squeeze the life out of it either.”

We started in the zero-depth entry, water barely kissing our shins. She showed me how to blow bubbles—not frantic puffs, but slow, steady exhalations through pursed lips, like cooling soup. I did it wrong three times: snorting, gasping, then laughing, a brittle sound that startled a woman doing aqua aerobics nearby. “Good,” Lena said, nodding. “Now do it again. Laughing counts as breathing out. That’s half the battle.”

By week four, I could float on my back—if someone held my shoulders. Not gracefully. My neck arched too far, chin jutting, spine rigid as a broomstick. “You’re holding your breath like it’s evidence,” Lena observed one Tuesday, her fingers light on my collarbone. “Try humming. Just a note. Any note.” So I hummed—flat, wavering, the opening phrase of “Danny Boy,” which my father used to sing off-key while folding laundry. And something loosened. My ribs dropped. My hips rose. For seven seconds, I stayed afloat, staring up at the stained acoustic tiles, listening to the echo of my own thin, trembling voice bouncing off the wet walls.

Then came the day of the deep end. Not for swimming—just for standing. The ladder descended into water that dropped from waist- to chest- to shoulder-deep within three rungs. I gripped the cold metal, knuckles bleaching white, while Lena stood waist-deep beside me, arms crossed, watching the surface ripple. “Your feet won’t leave the floor,” she said. “But your brain might tell you they will. That’s okay. That’s just your brain being polite.”

I stepped down. Water rose over my sternum, then my clavicles. My breath hitched. A memory surfaced, unbidden: age six, at my aunt’s pool in Amherst, slipping off the step, mouth open, swallowing chlorinated panic before my mother’s hand closed around my wrist. I hadn’t told Lena that. Didn’t need to. She saw the tremor in my hands, the way my eyes darted to the lifeguard chair, then away.

“Breathe in,” she said. “Now breathe out—longer than you think you can.” I did. And when I opened my eyes, she was still there, not touching me, just present, her gaze steady as tide-pool water.

Weeks passed. I learned to kick without flailing, to glide with my face in, to lift my head and breathe without jerking upright like a startled heron. One rainy Thursday in early October, I swam—really swam—across the width of the pool. Twenty-five yards. No stops. No noodle. Just me, my arms slicing, my legs churning, my breath finding its rhythm: *pull-breathe-kick, pull-breathe-kick*, like a metronome set to human tempo. When I touched the far wall, I didn’t cheer. I turned, floated on my back for a full minute, watching the fluorescent lights blur through the water’s surface, feeling the gentle, insistent push of the current against my ribs.
