After class, I sat on the bench, towel wrapped tight, watching the next group file in—women and men with salt-and-pepper hair, hesitant smiles, damp sneakers squeaking on the tile. A man in his sixties adjusted his goggles, muttering to no one in particular, “Forty-three years since I last dipped a toe in anything deeper than a bathtub.” Lena caught my eye and gave the smallest nod—not congratulatory, not pitying—just acknowledgment, like passing a neighbor on a fogged-up street.

Later, walking home past the old brick library, I stopped at the corner of Main and Pleasant and watched a maple leaf spin down from a branch, landing softly on the wet sidewalk. It wasn’t a miracle. It wasn’t transformation. It was just water, and breath, and the quiet, stubborn fact of my body moving through space it had long refused to inhabit. My left shoulder ached faintly, a dull, familiar throb from years of carrying tension like a second coat. I kept walking. My shoes were damp. My hair smelled like chlorine and autumn air. I didn’t think about forty. I thought about the next stroke. And the one after that.

title: short story|two sisters clearing out their mother's flat
text:
The dust motes hung suspended in the weak afternoon light slanting through the kitchen window—thick, golden, indifferent. Elara’s knuckles were raw from scrubbing the enamel sink, her nails rimmed with grey grime no amount of soap could lift. Beside her, Maya sat on the floor, back against the cold radiator, methodically folding a stack of faded floral tea towels. Her movements were slow, precise, almost ritualistic. She hadn’t spoken in seventeen minutes.

Elara rinsed the sponge, watching the grey water swirl down the drain. “Found the chipped one,” she said, her voice rougher than intended. She held up the small, cobalt-blue teacup—the one with the hairline crack near the handle, the one Mum always used for her first cuppa after waking, the one she’d refused to replace, calling it ‘characterful’. Maya didn’t look up. Just folded another towel, the corner aligned perfectly with the edge of the pile.

They’d started at dawn. The flat felt less like a home and more like an archive slowly collapsing under its own weight. Every drawer opened a sigh of stale air and forgotten things: a single pearl earring nestled in a tissue, a packet of lavender sachets gone brittle and scentless, a bundle of rubber-banded letters addressed in their father’s tight, looping hand—postmarked 1978, never opened. They’d moved through the rooms like archaeologists in a quiet panic, cataloguing grief in cardboard boxes labelled *Donations*, *Keep*, *Unsure*, and, most ominously, *Mum’s Things (Ask)*—a category neither dared define.

The living room was worse. It held the ghosts most insistently. The armchair still bore the faint, permanent indentation of Mum’s small frame. The bookshelf sagged under decades of paperbacks, their spines cracked and faded, many still bookmarked with bus tickets or dried rose petals. Elara had pulled out *Pride and Prejudice* this morning—Mum’s copy, dog-eared, annotated in pencil. On page 213, beside Mr. Darcy’s letter, she’d written, *‘Truth is rarely pure and never simple. (Oscar Wilde, but true.)’* Elara had stared at that for a long time, the ink slightly blurred, as if written in haste or tears. She hadn’t put it back. It sat now, face-down, on the coffee table beside Maya’s untouched mug of cold tea.

Maya finally spoke, her voice low, barely audible over the hum of the fridge. “Remember the biscuit tin?”

Elara paused, sponge hovering mid-rinse. “The blue one? With the daisies?”

“The very one.” Maya lifted her gaze. Her eyes were red-rimmed, but dry. “She kept the good biscuits in there. The ones with the silver foil. And the… other things.”

A flicker—something unspoken—passed between them. Not just biscuits. The small, wrapped bars of dark chocolate Mum would slip into their lunchboxes when they were teenagers, the ones she’d call ‘fortification’. The little box of mints she’d keep in her cardigan pocket, offering one with a conspiratorial wink. And the pills. The little orange bottle, tucked beneath layers of tissue, labelled *‘For Nerves – Dr. Evans’*, its contents long gone, the bottle itself empty and light as ash. They’d found it yesterday, behind the loose floorboard under the bed—Mum’s private, unspoken architecture of endurance.

Elara turned off the tap. The silence rushed back in, heavier now. She wiped her hands on her jeans, leaving smudges. “I found the photo album. The red one. Under the spare duvet.”

Maya nodded, folding the last towel with exaggerated care. “The one with the beach trip?”

“The one where you’re seven and have sand in your hair and you’re crying because the seagull stole your ice cream.” Elara managed a thin smile. “And Mum’s holding you, laughing, her hair full of salt, looking utterly ridiculous and completely… there.”

Maya’s breath hitched, just once. She didn’t cry. She just looked down at her hands, stained faintly yellow from the old tea towels. “She hated that photo. Said she looked like a drowned rat.”

“She also said it was the best photo ever taken, because it showed us all exactly as we were.” Elara stepped away from the sink, her knees stiff. She walked to the small, cluttered side table by the sofa—the one Mum called her ‘command centre’. Stacked there were three years’ worth of unopened utility bills, a half-finished crossword puzzle (clue 7 across: *‘A type of lily, often white and fragrant’*—Mum had pencilled in ‘lily’, then crossed it out, wrote ‘iris’, then ‘tulip’, finally settling on ‘*calla*’), and a small, smooth river stone painted with a single, wobbly blue heart. Elara picked it up. Cold, dense, impossibly heavy. She remembered painting it with Maya, aged eight and ten, sitting on the bank of the River Lea, dipping cheap brushes into acrylics, their fingers sticky with blue paint and river mud. Mum had watched, sketching them in her notebook, humming tunelessly.

“Why did she keep this?” Maya whispered, not looking at the stone, but at the blank TV screen reflecting the dim room.

Elara turned the stone in her palm. The blue heart was chipped at one corner. “Because it was ours. Because it was real. Because sometimes, the only thing that holds the shape of love is something small and flawed and entirely, stubbornly handmade.”

Maya finally stood. She walked past Elara, not touching her, and went to the bookshelf. She didn’t reach for *Pride and Prejudice*. Instead, she pulled out a slim, cloth-bound volume titled *Common Wildflowers of Britain*. She opened it to a page marked with a pressed violet, its purple almost black with age. Beneath it, in Mum’s neat script: *‘Viola odorata. Sweet Violet. Symbol: modesty, faithfulness, humility. Also: a mild sedative. For calm.’*

Maya traced the dried flower with a fingertip. “She never took the pills for calm. She took them to get through the day. To make the noise stop.”

Elara didn’t contradict her. She just watched her sister’s profile—the sharp line of her jaw, the vulnerable curve of her throat. The silence wasn’t empty anymore. It was thick with the unsaid: the years of hushed arguments about appointments missed, the way Mum’s hand would tremble slightly when pouring tea, the exhaustion that lived in the hollows beneath her eyes long before the diagnosis, the quiet, constant labour of being the one who held everything together while quietly falling apart.

Maya closed the book. She placed it gently on top of the stack of tea towels. Then she walked to the kitchen doorway and looked out—not at the view, but at the space where the sink, the counter, the worn linoleum met. “We need to decide about the sink,” she said, her voice suddenly practical, grounded. “It’s stained. But it’s original. Mum loved it. Said it sang when the water ran.”

Elara looked at the sink, its chipped enamel, the stubborn stain near the plug hole that looked like a bruise. She thought of Mum standing here, humming, wiping steam from the window, the blue teacup steaming in her hand. She thought of the river stone, the violet, the chipped cup, the silent, singing sink.

“Let’s leave it,” Elara said softly. “Just… clean it. Properly. One last time.”

Maya nodded. She didn’t smile. But she picked up the sponge Elara had left on the counter, dipped it in the warm, soapy water, and began to scrub the stain near the plug hole, her movements steady, her focus absolute, as if erasing the stain was the only thing in the world that mattered, and also, somehow, the only thing that might begin to hold.

title: historical novel|a cartographer's apprentice in eighteenth-century Lisbon
text:
In the heart of Lisbon, where the Tagus River met the city's ancient stones, there lived a young man named Tomás. He was an apprentice to Master António, a renowned cartographer whose maps were as much works of art as they were tools of navigation. The year was 1750, and the city still bore the scars of the great earthquake that had shaken it just five years before. Yet, amidst the ruins, there was a sense of rebirth, a fervent desire to rebuild and chart a new course.

Tomás, with his keen eye and steady hand, was a natural at the delicate art of mapmaking. He spent long hours in the workshop, hunched over large sheets of vellum, carefully etching lines and contours with fine quills. The air was thick with the scent of ink and the soft rustle of parchment. Outside, the sounds of hammering and construction filled the streets, a symphony of renewal.

Master António was a man of few words but many secrets. His eyes, sharp and discerning, seemed to hold the wisdom of countless voyages. He had sailed the world, mapping distant shores and uncharted territories. Now, he imparted his knowledge to Tomás, teaching him not only the technical skills of cartography but also the art of seeing the world in all its complexity.

One day, as the sun cast a golden glow through the workshop's high windows, Master António placed a particularly intricate map on the table. It depicted the coast of Brazil, a land rich in resources and opportunity. "This is your next project, Tomás," he said, his voice low and measured. "You will add the details of the new sugar plantations and the ports. But remember, a map is more than lines and names. It tells a story, and you must be its storyteller."

Tomás nodded, his heart racing with excitement. He had always been fascinated by the idea of far-off lands, and the chance to bring them to life on paper was a dream come true. For weeks, he pored over the map, adding each plantation, each port, each river and mountain range with painstaking precision. As he worked, he imagined the bustling docks, the ships laden with sugar, and the people who toiled in the fields.

But Tomás' world was not confined to the workshop. He often wandered the narrow, winding streets of Lisbon, observing the lives of those around him. The city was a tapestry of cultures and traditions, with sailors from every corner of the globe mingling with locals in the taverns and markets. In the evenings, he would sit in the small square near the workshop, listening to the tales of seafarers and merchants, their stories as varied as the stars in the sky.

One such evening, as the twilight deepened, Tomás found himself in conversation with a weathered old sailor named João. The man's face was a map of its own, etched with lines of hardship and adventure. João spoke of the dangers of the sea, of storms and pirates, and of the mysterious islands that some claimed lay beyond the known world. "There are places, lad, that no map has ever shown," he said, his eyes gleaming. "Places where the waters sing and the winds whisper secrets."

Tomás listened, entranced. The idea of undiscovered lands, of mysteries waiting to be revealed, stirred something deep within him. He realized then that the true magic of cartography lay not just in the accuracy of the lines and the precision of the measurements, but in the unknown, in the spaces between the known and the imagined.

As the months passed, Tomás' skills grew, and so did his reputation. Merchants and explorers began to seek him out, commissioning maps for their voyages. Each map he created was a masterpiece, a blend of science and art, a window into the world. Yet, despite his success, Tomás never forgot the lessons of Master António, or the stories of the sailors like João.

One day, as he stood by the shore, watching the sunset paint the sky in hues of orange and pink, Tomás felt a profound sense of purpose. He knew that his work was not just about marking the known, but about exploring the unknown. And in that moment, he vowed to continue his journey, to chart not only the physical world but also the dreams and aspirations of those who dared to venture beyond the horizon.

The years that followed were filled with both triumph and challenge. Lisbon continued to rebuild, and Tomás' maps became an integral part of the city's revival. But he never stopped dreaming, never stopped searching for the hidden corners of the world. And in the end, it was not just the maps he left behind, but the stories they told, stories of courage, of discovery, and of the boundless spirit of exploration.

title: memoir|a childhood split between two countries and two languages
text:
The Grammar of Leaving  

I learned to count in two ways: *uno, dos, tres*, then *one, two, three*—not as a game, but as a reflex, like blinking. The numbers didn’t live side by side; they occupied separate rooms in my head, each with its own light and temperature. Spanish was the language of my grandmother’s hands—knuckles swollen from decades of kneading dough, fingers pressing *empanada* edges with a rhythm older than my father’s passport. English was the language of the school nurse’s office in New Jersey, where I’d sit cross-legged on a vinyl chair, tracing the grain of the floor tile while she asked, “Does it hurt *here*?” and I’d nod, not because the ache was sharp, but because *here* felt safer than naming the bruise on my thigh—the one I’d gotten falling off the rusted swing set behind our apartment building, not the one from the cane my uncle used when I mixed up the subjunctive in a letter home.  

We moved every eighteen months, back and forth across the Atlantic—not for adventure, not for diplomacy, but because my parents’ marriage had dissolved into something quieter and more persistent than divorce: a shared custody agreement written in visas and visa runs. One country was always provisional. Even the air smelled different: in Seville, dust carried the scent of dried orange blossom and hot stone; in Newark, it tasted of wet concrete and exhaust that clung to the tongue like a film. I never learned to exhale fully in either place.  

Language wasn’t just vocabulary. It was syntax as geography. In Spanish, time bent inward: *Había una vez*—there *had been* once—already implying distance, memory, the softening of edges. In English, verbs anchored me to the present: *I am here. This is happening.* But which *here*? The kitchen where my abuela stirred *sopa de ajo*, garlic sizzling in olive oil until the whole room shimmered? Or the fluorescent-lit cafeteria where I sat alone, pushing tater tots around a plastic tray, listening to the cadence of other children’s laughter—so fast, so untranslatable in its pitch and pause?  

I remember standing at the airport gate in Madrid, seven years old, holding my mother’s hand so tightly my knuckles whitened. She wore her good coat, the wool one with the brass buttons, and her voice was low, steady: *“No llores. Ya volverás.”* Don’t cry. You’ll come back. But I knew—knew with the certainty of a child who has memorized departure times—that “back” was a word without coordinates. It meant nothing solid. It meant the same suitcase, the same laminated boarding pass, the same weight of a backpack too heavy for my shoulders, stuffed with notebooks in both languages, none of them ever quite finished.  

School was a series of small betrayals. In Seville, I was *el niño americano*, slow to conjugate, my accent thick with American vowels, my jokes landing with a thud. In New Jersey, I was *the Spanish kid*, mispronouncing “schedule” as “shed-yool,” writing *“I have 10 years”* instead of *“I am 10”*, my grammar marked in red ink like blood. Teachers would lean in, kindly: *“Just pick one. Which feels more real?”* As if reality were a preference. As if I could choose between the taste of my grandmother’s *mantecados*—crumbly, anise-scented, dissolving on the tongue—and the synthetic sweetness of Fruit Roll-Ups, sticky and bright, unspooling from their plastic wrapper.  

There was no grand epiphany, no moment when the two worlds fused. Only accumulation: the way I began to dream in fragments—my father’s voice saying *“mira”* while my teacher’s face floated above me, mouth moving silently; the way I’d catch myself switching mid-sentence, not out of confusion, but because the right word simply *wasn’t there* in the language I’d started with—like reaching for a spoon and finding only a fork, perfectly functional, yet wrong for the task.  

I still carry the residue. Not nostalgia—that’s too clean, too curated—but a low hum of dislocation. When I hear rapid-fire Spanish, my body tenses before my mind catches up. When I read English poetry aloud, I sometimes insert a rolled *r*, a ghost of Andalusian speech I haven’t spoken regularly in twenty years. My passport expires every ten years, and each renewal feels less like documentation and more like a reminder: this is temporary. Even now, standing in my own kitchen, boiling water for pasta, I’ll reach for the salt and pause—*sal*, or *salt*?—and the hesitation isn’t linguistic. It’s gravitational. A fraction of a second where neither country holds me.  

I don’t miss one place more than the other. What I miss is the certainty of belonging to a single grammar—to a syntax that doesn’t require translation, a tense that doesn’t ask you to hold past, present, and future in the same breath. I miss the illusion of wholeness.  

But illusions are fragile things. They shatter easily—in the gap between a question asked in English and the answer formed, too late, in Spanish; in the silence after someone says *“Where are you from?”* and I feel the familiar, weary calculation begin: *Which version do they need? Which story will fit the shape of their curiosity?*  

I don’t know how to end this. There is no resolution, no synthesis. Just the ongoing work of holding two grammars in the same throat, two geographies in the same chest, and learning—not to reconcile them—but to let them coexist, unsoftened, unsmoothed, like stones worn by different rivers. The weight remains. The ache, too. But it is mine. Not borrowed. Not translated. Just mine.

title: narrative poem|a ferry crossing in a storm
text:
The *Marianne* groaned—not like a ship, but like a man with cracked ribs dragging himself up a cliff. Rain didn’t fall that afternoon; it hurled itself sideways off the North Sea, thick as wet gravel, stinging the face raw. I stood at the starboard rail in my oilskin, collar pulled high, watching the grey smear of Tynemouth recede behind us, while ahead, the mouth of the Tyne yawned black and churning, its usual brown silt churned into something viscous and livid, like spoiled milk mixed with engine oil.

Captain Alistair Finch—bald as a boiled egg, with knuckles swollen from decades gripping cold brass—stood braced in the wheelhouse doorway, chewing a sliver of dried kelp he kept tucked behind his lower lip. “She’s got her teeth in us now,” he said, not looking at me, voice flat as a dock plank. His breath fogged the glass beside him. “That’s not wind, lad. That’s the river *spitting*.”

Inside the passenger cabin, damp wool and damp fear hung thick. Mrs. Elsie Thorne sat bolt upright on the cracked vinyl seat, clutching a wicker basket containing two sleeping geese—*Barnaby* and *Peggy*, she’d told me earlier, her voice tight with pride. Their necks were swaddled in blue flannel, their beaks tucked under wings like folded hands. Beside her, young Liam Byrne—twelve, freckled, wearing his father’s too-large navy cap—gripped the armrests, knuckles white, eyes fixed on the porthole where water sheeted down like liquid lead. “Is the ferry *supposed* to tilt like that?” he whispered, not turning.

“It’s supposed to stay upright,” said Mr. Aris Thorne, Elsie’s husband, standing near the galley hatch, arms crossed over his chest. He wore a tweed waistcoat buttoned wrong, one silver cufflink missing. “But it’s also supposed to have a working radar, and that screen’s been blinking ‘ERROR’ since we left the slip.” He nodded toward the darkened console behind the ticket booth, where a single red LED pulsed weakly, like a dying heartbeat.

Then the *Marianne* shuddered—not a roll, but a violent, sickening *lurch* to port. The overhead light flickered, died, then flared back with a buzz, casting long, leaping shadows. Barnaby the goose startled awake, let out a sharp, guttural honk, and flapped wildly, knocking over Elsie’s thermos. Dark tea spilled across the floorboards, steaming faintly in the cold air. “Steady, steady,” Elsie murmured, patting the basket, though her own hand trembled.

Outside, the world had narrowed to noise: the shriek of wind through the rigging, the hollow *thump-thump-thump* of waves hammering the hull’s port side, the constant, wet slap of spray against the windows. Rain lashed the glass in frantic, horizontal streaks. Through a brief clearing in the storm’s fury, I saw it—the *Cullercoats Light*, usually a steady amber eye on the headland, now just a smudge of yellow swallowed whole by grey. Then the light vanished entirely, and the darkness pressed in, deeper, older.

A woman screamed—not loud, but thin and ragged, like tearing cloth. It came from the far end of the cabin, where a young nurse named Anya Petrova sat hunched over a child wrapped in a tartan blanket. The boy, maybe five, had a feverish flush beneath his pallor and kept whispering, “The water’s breathing. Can you hear it breathe?” Anya held him close, humming a fragment of a Ukrainian lullaby, her thumb stroking his temple, her own eyes wide and unblinking, fixed on the ceiling where a rivet had begun to weep rust-coloured water.

The *Marianne* dropped—a sudden, stomach-lurching descent—as if the sea had opened its mouth and let her fall. For three seconds, silence. Absolute, suffocating silence, broken only by the drip-drip-drip from the rivet and the low, animal whimper of the geese. Then the engines roared, not with power, but with a strained, protesting whine, like metal grinding on bone. The ship heaved back up, listing hard to starboard this time, throwing Liam Byrne sideways onto the floor. He didn’t cry out. Just lay there, hat askew, staring at the ceiling, breathing fast and shallow.

Captain Finch appeared in the doorway, water streaming from his eyebrows, his oilskin dark with salt. He didn’t shout. Didn’t gesture. Just met each of our eyes—Elsie’s calm dread, Aris’s simmering anger, Anya’s quiet intensity, Liam’s stunned stillness—and finally mine. “We’re not sinking,” he said, voice low, gravelly, utterly certain. “Not today. But the pilot boat’s gone dark. And the tide’s running *against* us now, full ebb, pulling us sideways into the Black Middens.” He paused, wiped saltwater from his cheek with the back of his hand. “So we hold course. We hold *her*. And we wait for the eye.”

No one moved. No one spoke. Even Barnaby subsided, tucking his head back under his wing, a soft, rhythmic *huh-huh-huh* vibrating the basket. The storm raged on, a living thing outside the thin skin of steel and glass. Rain drummed. Waves slammed. The lights flickered again, dimmed, steadied. Outside the port window, a wave rose—not a crest, but a wall of black water, thick with foam like curdled cream, towering higher than the wheelhouse, blotting out the sky, the light, the very idea of land. It hung there, suspended for a breath, immense and terrible, green-black at its heart, lit from within by a flash of distant, indifferent lightning. Then it fell—not on us, but *past*, a thunderous, shuddering crash that vibrated the deck plates, sending a fresh cascade of spray over the rails, glittering like shattered glass in the fractured light.

Liam slowly sat up. He picked up his cap, brushed salt crystals from the brim, and placed it carefully back on his head. He looked at the wave’s retreating back, then at Captain Finch, who gave the smallest nod—no smile, just acknowledgment. Elsie Thorne reached into her basket and gently stroked Peggy’s downy head. Anya shifted the boy in her arms, pressing her cheek to his hot forehead, her humming resuming, softer now, steadier. The *Marianne* groaned again, deep in her iron bones, and pushed forward, inch by stubborn inch, into the grey throat of the storm, carrying us all—geese, children, nurses, captains, the salt-stung and the quietly terrified—across the water’s wild, breathing heart.

title: personal essay|the last video rental shop in town
text:
There’s something undeniably nostalgic about the last video rental shop in town. It’s tucked away on a quiet street, sandwiched between a laundromat and a small, family-owned grocery store. The sign above the door, "Videoland," is faded, with the letters peeling at the edges. But it’s still there, stubbornly holding on, like a relic from another era.

I remember the first time I walked into Videoland. I was probably around 10 or 11, and my dad had just gotten his driver’s license back after a long hiatus. We were both excited, so we decided to make a night of it—pizza, a movie, and maybe some ice cream. The place was dimly lit, with rows upon rows of VHS tapes and DVDs. The smell of popcorn and dust filled the air, and there was a constant hum from the old fluorescent lights. It felt like stepping into a different world, one where time moved a little slower.

The owner, Mr. Thompson, was a tall, lanky man with a graying beard and a kind smile. He always wore plaid shirts and jeans, and he had this way of making you feel welcome, even if you were just a kid. He knew every movie on the shelves, and he could recommend something for anyone. I remember asking him for a horror movie once, and he gave me a look that said, "You sure about that, kid?" but he handed over a copy of "Poltergeist" anyway. I didn’t sleep for a week, but I couldn’t stop thinking about it.

Over the years, Videoland became a second home for me. I’d spend hours browsing the shelves, reading the backs of the boxes, and sometimes just chatting with Mr. Thompson. He had a dog, a scruffy terrier named Max, who would sit by the counter and wag his tail at anyone who came in. There was a worn-out couch in the corner where people could watch trailers, and I’d often find myself sitting there, lost in the flickering images on the small TV screen.

But as the years went by, things started to change. Streaming services began to take over, and fewer and fewer people came to the store. The shelves, once packed with movies, started to thin out. Mr. Thompson tried to keep up, adding a few new releases here and there, but it was a losing battle. Still, he kept the place open, out of a sense of duty, I think, or maybe just because he loved it too much to let it go.

One summer, when I was in college, I came back to visit. I walked into Videoland, and it was almost empty. The lights were a bit dimmer, and the smell of dust was stronger. Mr. Thompson was behind the counter, looking a little older, a little more tired. We talked for a while, and he told me about how hard it was to keep the place going. But he also talked about the community, the regulars who still came in, the kids who would ask for recommendations, and the occasional tourist who stumbled in, surprised to find a video rental shop still in business.

He showed me a box of old VHS tapes that he was trying to sell, and I bought a few, just because. I don’t even have a VCR anymore, but there was something comforting about having them, like a piece of history, a reminder of a simpler time.

As I left that day, I looked back at the store, and I felt a pang of sadness. It’s not just a video rental shop; it’s a place where memories are made, where stories are shared, and where people connect. In a world that’s moving so fast, it’s a place that stands still, a sanctuary of sorts.

I haven’t been back to Videoland in a while, but I think about it often. I wonder if it’s still there, if Mr. Thompson is still behind the counter, if Max is still wagging his tail. Maybe one day, I’ll go back, and I’ll rent a movie, just for old times’ sake. And maybe, just maybe, I’ll find that the magic is still there, waiting for me, like an old friend.

title: short story|a night bus driver and a passenger who never gets off
text:
The bus groaned like a tired animal shifting in its sleep, its headlights cutting twin tunnels through the city’s damp breath—mist clinging to streetlamps, blurring their halos into soft, bleeding stars. Elias kept his hands steady at ten and two, knuckles pale under the dim green glow of the dashboard clock: 2:47 a.m. The route was familiar as muscle memory—the slow dip down Cedar Hill, the sharp left onto Holloway where the pavement cracked like old porcelain, the long stretch past shuttered bodegas and laundromats humming with refrigerated silence. He’d driven this loop for seventeen years, every night except when he buried his mother, and even then he’d taken the next shift, numb and hollow, gripping the wheel as if it were the only thing keeping him from dissolving into the rain-slicked asphalt.

She boarded at the corner of Ninth and Elm, always at 3:12 a.m., never earlier, never later. Tonight, she wore a coat the colour of dried ink, its collar turned up against the chill that seeped through the bus’s ill-fitting windows. Her hair was pinned back with a single tortoiseshell clip, one strand escaping near her temple, trembling faintly each time the bus hit a pothole. She paid with exact change—three quarters and a nickel—her fingers cool and dry, nails clipped short, no polish. No bag, no phone, no book. Just a small, folded square of cloth she held in her lap, its edges worn soft.

Elias had memorized the rhythm of her boarding: the sigh as the doors hissed open, the slight hesitation on the first step, the way her left foot always landed half an inch before the right, as though testing the metal step for give. She walked past the empty seats near the front and settled into the same spot—row seven, window side—where the vinyl seat was cracked just above the seam, revealing a sliver of yellow foam beneath. She sat upright, spine straight but not stiff, gaze fixed somewhere beyond the rain-streaked glass, her reflection faint and wavering in the dark pane.

He’d tried, once, to make conversation. A week after she’d started riding—always the same stop, same time, same silence—he’d asked, voice low, “Cold night.” She’d turned her head just enough to meet his eyes in the rearview mirror. Her irises were the colour of weak tea, flecked with gold. She didn’t speak. Didn’t blink. Just watched him until he looked away, throat tight, and the bus lurched forward into the next block.

After that, he stopped trying. He watched her instead—not with suspicion, but with the quiet attention one gives to a recurring weather pattern, a particular shadow cast by a lamppost at dusk. She never slept. Never yawned. Never adjusted her coat or checked her watch. At each stop, the doors opened, passengers shuffled on and off, breath fogging the air, jackets zipped, scarves tightened. She remained still. Once, a young man in a hoodie dropped his earbuds and bent to retrieve them; she didn’t flinch, didn’t glance down, her gaze unwavering on the wet pavement sliding past.

Tonight, the city felt thinner. The streetlights flickered more often, their light stuttering like a failing pulse. Rain fell in silver needles, stitching the darkness together. Elias noticed the way the mist coiled around fire escapes, how the neon sign of the all-night diner—*Maggie’s*, its ‘g’ burnt out—pulsed erratically, casting a sickly pink wash across the sidewalk. He caught her reflection again: her eyes weren’t looking out. They were looking *in*, at something behind the glass that wasn’t there—or wasn’t there yet.

At 4:03 a.m., the bus rounded the final curve before the depot, where the route officially ended. The depot gates stood open, floodlights bleaching the concrete grey-white. Elias slowed, brakes sighing, the engine dropping to a low, exhausted hum. He pulled into bay three, the designated spot. Doors wheezed open. No one got on. No one got off. The other passengers—two nurses, a delivery driver with a thermos, a student clutching a notebook—rose, gathered coats, stepped down onto the dry, warm concrete. Their footsteps echoed, then faded into the depot’s fluorescent hush.

Elias waited. Counted to thirty. Checked the rearview.

She was still there.

He turned off the engine. The silence rushed in, thick and sudden, broken only by the drip-drip-drip of condensation from the roof vent. He unclipped his seatbelt, stood, and walked slowly down the aisle, his boots whispering on the worn rubber floor. He stopped beside her seat. She didn’t turn. Didn’t breathe any differently. Her hands rested on her knees, palms down, fingers relaxed but precise, like a pianist waiting for the first note.

“Ma’am,” he said, voice softer than he intended. “We’re at the end.”

She tilted her head, just slightly, and for the first time, her eyes met his—not in the mirror, but directly. There was no fear in them. No confusion. Only a deep, quiet recognition, as if she’d been expecting this moment for longer than he’d been driving the route.

“The depot,” he repeated, gesturing vaguely behind him. “It’s closed now. I have to lock up.”

She looked past him, toward the open doors, then back. Her lips parted, but no sound came. Instead, she lifted her left hand—slow, deliberate—and pointed, not at the door, but at the window beside her. Elias followed her gaze. Outside, the rain had stopped. The mist was lifting, thinning into veils. And there, reflected in the glass—not in the street, not in the depot lights—was a different street. Narrower. Cobblestones slick with rain. Gas lamps burning low. A wrought-iron bench, empty. A cat darting between shadows. A street sign, blurred but legible: *Cedar Hill, 1958*.

He blinked. Looked again. The reflection was gone. Just wet glass, the depot’s harsh lights, the puddle outside catching the glow.

When he turned back, the seat was empty.

He stood there, breath held, listening to the hollow click of cooling metal. Then he walked to the front, locked the doors, and climbed back into the driver’s seat. His hands found the wheel. The ignition turned over with a familiar cough. He pulled out of the bay, turned right onto Holloway, and began the route again. At 3:12 a.m., he slowed at Ninth and Elm. The doors hissed open. A woman in a coat the colour of dried ink stepped aboard, paid with three quarters and a nickel, and walked to row seven. She sat. Folded her hands. Looked out the window.

Elias kept driving. The city breathed around him—wet, indifferent, endlessly folding itself into new shapes. The bus rolled on, its headlights pushing forward, carving temporary paths through the dark.

title: free verse poem sequence|a year of weather in one valley
text:
Valley Almanac: A Year in the Fold  

I. January  
The cold doesn’t arrive—it settles. Not like snow, but like sediment in still water: fine, dense, unannounced. The creek contracts to a black thread under ice that doesn’t gleam but *sucks* light, matte and breathless. I walk the east ridge at dawn, boots crunching not on snow but on rime—frost grown inward, crystalline filigree clinging to dried bracken, to the bark of hawthorn, to the knuckles of my gloves. It’s not beautiful. It’s *occupied*. The air tastes of iron and damp wool. Ravens lift from the pines, their wings stiff, reluctant—no soaring, only vertical labor against the weight of the sky. When the wind comes, it doesn’t whistle. It *grinds*, low and continuous, like stone on stone deep underground. We don’t speak much then. Words feel like sparks too small to catch.  

II. March  
Thaw is not relief. It’s a slow, sullen unraveling. The snowpack doesn’t melt; it *deflates*, collapsing inward with soft, wet sighs. Meltwater doesn’t run—it *leaks*, seeping sideways through frozen ground, pooling in hollows where last autumn’s oak leaves float, sodden and dark as bruises. The mud here has its own grammar: slick, treacherous, smelling of decayed roots and something older—wet limestone, maybe, or the mineral tang of groundwater pushing up through fissures. One afternoon, I find a vole’s nest half-buried in the muck, woven tight from dried grass and mouse fur, collapsed but intact, empty. No sign of struggle. Just absence, precise and quiet.  

III. May  
The valley holds its breath before the green arrives—not with fanfare, but with a kind of *insistence*. First, the willows along the creek blush, not yellow, but a bruised, luminous chartreuse, almost fluorescent against the grey water. Then the ferns uncurl—not delicately, but with a faint, papery *shush*, unfurling in tight, damp fists. Rain comes in horizontal sheets, not falling but *sliding* off the hillsides, turning the air thick and green-scented, heavy with pollen that coats the tongue and sticks to the inside of the throat. One evening, standing in the orchard, I watch a hawk hang motionless above the ridge—not riding thermals, but *pinned* there by the sheer density of the air, wings rigid, tail fanned, utterly still except for the minute tremor in its primaries. It wasn’t hunting. It was waiting for the air to thin.  

IV. July  
Heat doesn’t bake here. It *presses*. A physical weight, humid and low, settling into the hollows like warm oil. The creek shrinks to a series of disconnected pools, each one a mirror holding only the exact, unblinking blue of the sky directly overhead—no clouds, no birds, just that relentless, vacant blue reflected back at itself. Dragonflies dart, not in arcs, but in sharp, angular zips, their wings humming a frequency just below hearing. At noon, the air shimmers—not like heat haze, but like the surface of hot asphalt, distorting distance until the far ridge blurs into a single, breathing line. I sit on the porch steps, sweat tracing cold paths down my ribs, listening to the cicadas’ drone, which isn’t sound so much as a vibration felt in the molars, in the fillings, in the hollow behind the ear. There is no breeze. Only the slow, sticky passage of time.  

V. September  
The light changes first—not golden, not soft, but *flatter*, less volumetric. Shadows lose their depth, becoming mere stains on the ground. The maples don’t blaze; they *fade*, leaching color downward from the tips of their leaves, leaving the undersides a dusty, exhausted yellow. The air cools at dusk, yes, but it’s a different cold—not clean, but *damp*, carrying the scent of fallen apples rotting in the tall grass, of mushrooms pushing through leaf litter with a faint, sweet-sour musk. One morning, I find the first frost—not white, but a delicate, almost invisible silver film on the spiderwebs strung between fence posts, catching the weak sun like shattered glass. By ten o’clock, it’s gone, leaving only dampness and the faint, metallic taste of ozone.  

VI. November  
Wind returns—not the grinding January wind, but a restless, searching thing. It lifts dead leaves not in spirals, but in frantic, skittering bursts, scraping them across dry earth like fingernails. The creek, swollen by rain, runs fast and brown, churning debris—broken branches, clods of soil, the waterlogged husk of a squirrel’s nest. The trees stand stripped, revealing architecture: the stark, interlocking bones of branches, the deep fissures in bark, the nests built high and hidden all summer, now exposed and vulnerable—empty, or sometimes, occupied by a single, watchful jay, its feathers puffed against the chill. I see a fox cross the lower field at twilight, moving low and quick, its brush held tight against its body, not running, but *concentrating* its presence into a single, urgent line across the grey. It doesn’t look back. It doesn’t need to.  

VII. December  
The first real snow falls not at night, but mid-afternoon—a slow, silent descent of large, wet flakes that don’t accumulate, but *muffle*. They land on the already-damp ground, on the bare branches, on the roofs, and simply… absorb. The world doesn’t go quiet. It goes *dull*. Sound loses its edges, its resonance. Voices carry strangely, flat and close, as if the air itself has thickened. The light is the colour of old paper—warm, but exhausted. That night, walking home, I pause beneath the single streetlamp at the bend in the road. Its sodium-yellow glow illuminates only a small, perfect circle of falling snow—countless flakes swirling in that amber pool, then vanishing into the darkness beyond the light’s reach. I watch them fall, not towards the ground, but *into* the dark. There is no landing. There is only the falling, and the dark receiving it.  

The year doesn’t end. It folds. The valley closes in on itself, not in sleep, but in a kind of patient, granular waiting—waiting for the next pressure change, the next shift in the deep, slow currents beneath the rock, the next subtle, unnameable signal carried on the wind that isn’t quite wind yet. I stand at the window, watching the dark shape of the ridge dissolve into the gathering night. No conclusions. No promises. Just the weight of the air, the damp cold on the glass, and the slow, inevitable turn of the earth, pulling the valley deeper into the fold.

title: literary novel|a sound archivist who finds a confession hidden on an old tape
text:
In the dimly lit, cluttered office of the Sound Archive at the University of Edinburgh, Eleanor MacLeod was surrounded by a labyrinth of shelves, each crammed with spools of tape, vinyl records, and an assortment of outdated audio equipment. The air smelled faintly of dust and old paper, a scent that had become as familiar to her as the sound of her own heartbeat. It was here, amidst the echoes of the past, that she spent most of her days, cataloging, preserving, and sometimes, discovering.

Eleanor, with her chestnut hair tied back in a loose bun and glasses perched on the bridge of her nose, was meticulously organizing a new collection of tapes donated by the estate of a recently deceased local historian, Dr. Alexander Graham. She had known Dr. Graham, a kind and eccentric man, from her early days at the university. His passing had left a void in the academic community, and his collection was a testament to his lifelong passion for oral history.

As she carefully unwrapped a box marked "Miscellaneous - 1970s," Eleanor's fingers brushed against a small, unmarked reel. It was different from the others, its surface slightly worn and the label long faded. Intrigued, she placed it on the playback machine, a vintage Revox B77, and pressed play.

The tape hissed and crackled before a voice emerged, deep and gravelly, yet unmistakably Scottish. The accent was thick, and the tone was heavy with sorrow. Eleanor leaned in, her curiosity piqued.

"Hello, my name is Malcolm Campbell. I am recording this on the 14th of October, 1975. If you are listening to this, then I am no longer here. I need to confess something, something I have kept hidden for far too long."

Eleanor's heart raced. Confessions were rare, and the gravity in Malcolm's voice suggested this was no ordinary admission. She reached for a notepad and pen, ready to transcribe what she was about to hear.

"I was young, only twenty-three, when it happened. It was a summer evening, and the sun was setting over the hills of the Highlands. I was driving home from a friend's wedding, a bit tipsy, but not drunk. As I rounded a bend, I saw a figure on the road. I swerved, but it was too late. I hit him, and he flew off the bonnet, landing in a ditch. I stopped, got out, and found him lying there, motionless. He was dead. I panicked. I didn't know what to do. So, I did the worst thing possible. I left him there and drove away."

Malcolm's voice broke, and there was a long pause. Eleanor could almost feel the weight of his guilt through the speakers.

"I never told anyone. Not the police, not my family, not even my wife. I buried the memory deep inside, but it never left me. Every night, I see his face, and every day, I carry this burden. I don't expect forgiveness, but I hope that by telling this, someone, somewhere, might find some peace. His name was John McAllister. He was a good man, and I took his life."

The tape clicked to a stop, and the room fell silent. Eleanor sat frozen, the pen still poised over the notepad. The confession had been raw and honest, and it left her with a mix of emotions: shock, sadness, and a strange sense of duty. She knew she had to do something with this information, but what?

She rewound the tape and listened again, making sure she hadn't missed any details. Then, she carefully wrapped the reel and placed it in a separate, secure box. This was more than just an archive; it was a piece of someone's soul, a cry for absolution.

Eleanor decided to visit Dr. Graham's widow, Margaret, who lived in a quaint cottage on the outskirts of Edinburgh. Margaret, a gentle woman with silver hair and warm eyes, welcomed her with a cup of tea and a smile.

"Eleanor, it's lovely to see you. What brings you here today?"

Eleanor hesitated, unsure how to begin. "Margaret, I found something in Dr. Graham's collection. A tape, a confession. It's... it's quite personal, and I thought you should be the first to know."

Margaret's expression changed, a mixture of curiosity and concern. "A confession? Oh, dear. Please, tell me more."

Eleanor recounted the story, and as she spoke, Margaret's eyes filled with tears. When she finished, Margaret reached for her hand, squeezing it gently.

"Thank you, Eleanor. Alex would have wanted this to be heard. We must do the right thing, for Malcolm and for John."

Together, they decided to contact the local authorities, providing them with the tape and any additional information they could gather. It was a small step towards closure, but it felt like the right one.

As Eleanor left Margaret's cottage, the sky was painted with the soft hues of twilight. She walked slowly, her mind replaying the words of Malcolm Campbell. In the quiet of the evening, she realized that sometimes, the most important stories are the ones that are whispered, the ones that hide in the shadows, waiting to be found.

title: legend|a drowned village whose church bell still rings at low tide
text:
The bell rings. Not *every* low tide—only when the wind’s coming off the estuary, damp and smelling of rotting kelp and old mud—and only if the water’s receding fast enough to suck air through the fissure in the church tower’s north wall. You’d think it’d be a hollow, watery clang. It isn’t. It’s clear. Sharp. Like struck brass, not drowned bronze. My gran heard it once, in ’53, standing knee-deep in the salt marsh with her laundry basket full of goose feathers she was plucking for a mattress. She dropped the basket. Feathers went everywhere—white ghosts in the grey light. She said the bell didn’t *sound* like it was underwater. Sounded like it was *waiting*.

The village was called Tidewell. Not “Tide Well” like a spring—though there *was* one, a brackish trickle behind the smithy that tasted of iron and boiled turnips—but *Tidewell*, one word, carved crookedly into the lintel of the old post office (now just a mossy slab half-buried near the causeway marker). People forget how small it was. Not even a proper green—just a patch of wiry grass where the children played hopscotch on stones painted with lard and soot. Three pubs, but only two had names: *The Salty Gull* (closed by ’29, roof caved in during the ’31 gale) and *The Drowned Man* (still open, technically, though the landlord, old Mr. Pellow, serves warm cider and tells the same three stories, none of which mention the drowning). The third pub? Just *The One*. No sign. Just a door with a rusted latch and a smell of damp wool and pickled onions. It vanished first, in ’47, swallowed sideways by the marsh, like the land exhaled and forgot to inhale again.

They say it wasn’t the sea that took Tidewell. Not really. It was the *silence* before the sea came. A dry, crackling hush that settled over the marshes for seventeen days in late August ’48. No birdsong. No wind in the reeds. Even the frogs stopped croaking. Then the rain started—not gentle, but *vertical*, as if the sky had tipped sideways. It rained for thirty-eight hours straight. The river swelled, yes, but the real trouble was the *ground*. It didn’t soak it up. It *rejected* it. The clay beneath Tidewell turned slick, then greasy, then finally… *soft*. Like cold porridge left too long. Houses didn’t fall. They *sank*. Slowly. First the cellar steps vanished. Then the front doors became windows looking out at muddy water. The schoolhouse tilted—its blackboard slid sideways, chalk letters smearing into grey rivers down the plaster. Mrs. Hargreaves’ prize-winning marigolds floated away in a single, bright orange raft.

The church—St. Elmo’s—held out longest. Built on the only bit of solid rock in five miles, a lump of grey granite the size of a cottage, jutting up like a stubborn tooth. The bell tower stood proud, even as the nave filled to the rafters with tea-coloured water. They tried to save it. Men from Larkham came in rowboats, hauling ropes, shouting prayers into the wind. But the rock *moved*. Not much. Just an inch. A groan deep in the earth, felt in your molars. Then another inch. The tower cracked—not across, but *up*, a hairline fracture snaking from foundation to belfry. That’s when they knew. Not to fight. To *witness*.

They rang the bell. All day. Not the alarm peal—the slow, heavy toll for the dead—but the *call to worship*. Full, ringing, defiant. Even as water lapped the altar steps. Even as the vicar, Reverend Pike (a man who wore his spectacles on a string and kept bees in the vestry), stood waist-deep in the chancel, holding the baptismal font aloft like a sacred cup. He didn’t drown. Walked out, dry-shod, across the sucking mud at dawn on the 12th. Left his boots behind. They’re still there, buried, I reckon. Right foot slightly larger than the left. Size eight and a half. Brown leather, scuffed heel.

The bell didn’t ring after that. Not until ’62. A boy named Danny Cray, twelve years old, chasing a lost football across the newly exposed mudflats at extreme low tide. Heard it. Ran home screaming about “ghost bells.” His mother slapped him for lying. But he was right. And it’s rung, fitfully, ever since. Not on schedule. Not for the weather. For the *tide’s mood*. When it’s retreating fast, pulling hard, leaving ribbons of wet sand that gleam like fish scales—that’s when you might hear it. A single, pure note. Then silence. Then maybe, if you’re very still and the wind drops just so, a second note. Lower. Sadder.

I’ve stood there. Many times. On the causeway marker—three stones stacked, tied with faded blue twine (don’t ask me why blue; no one remembers). Boots sinking, cold mud sucking at my ankles. Watch the water retreat, inch by reluctant inch. Smell the marsh gas, sharp and sweet, like rotten apples left in a cupboard. Hear the curlews cry, high and lonely. And wait. Not *for* the bell. Just… listening. Because the strangest thing? When it rings, it doesn’t sound *from* the water. It sounds *through* it. Like the bell isn’t submerged. Like the water is just… a veil. Thin. Temporary. And sometimes, standing there, boots full of icy sludge, I swear I catch the faintest scent—not of salt or decay—but of beeswax polish. And the ghost of warm bread baking.  

That’s the part they never put in the guidebooks. Or the council’s “Heritage Trail” pamphlet (which calls it “The Submerged Settlement of Tidewell – A Cautionary Tale of Coastal Erosion”). They don’t mention the beeswax. Or the bread. Or how, if you press your ear to the cold, wet stone of the causeway marker at exactly the moment the note fades… you can feel, just for a second, the faint, steady *thrum* of a thousand wings. Busy. Untroubled. Alive.  

The bell rings. It always has. It always will.  

It’s not mourning.  

It’s remembering how to ring.

title: short story|two sisters clearing out their mother's flat
text:
The dust motes hung suspended in the weak afternoon light slanting through the kitchen window—thick, golden, indifferent. Elara’s knuckles were raw from scrubbing decades of grease from the oven door. She’d peeled back the first layer of grime only to reveal another, darker, older, like the skin of some forgotten thing. Beside her, Maya sat on the floor, back against the cold radiator, methodically folding a stack of faded floral tea towels. Her movements were precise, unhurried, but her eyes kept drifting—not to the towels, but to the chipped enamel mug on the counter. *World’s Best Mum*, it read in cheerful, slightly crooked script. Their mother had used it every morning for twenty-seven years, even after the diagnosis, even when her hands trembled so badly she’d need Elara to steady the kettle.

Elara wiped her brow with the back of her wrist and left a smudge of grey. “Found the biscuit tin,” she said, her voice rougher than usual. “Still full. Digestives. Stale as sin.”

Maya didn’t look up. “She never threw anything away. Not even the receipt for the toaster she bought in ’98.” A pause. Then, quieter: “I think she kept it because it was the first thing she bought after Dad left. Like proof she could still choose.”

Elara turned off the tap, water dripping rhythmically into the sink. *Plink. Plink. Plink.* The sound filled the silence between them—the kind that wasn’t empty, but thick with unspoken things: the hospital vigils they’d taken turns keeping, the hushed arguments in corridors about dosages and dignity, the way their mother’s voice had thinned to parchment in the final weeks, yet still insisted on correcting Elara’s grammar during a visit, just as she always had.

They’d started at the bedroom—*her* room, not theirs. The one with the rose-scented sachets tucked into every drawer, the one where the wallpaper curled at the ceiling like tired eyelids. They’d packed the clothes quickly: donations, mostly. But the jewellery box—that small, velvet-lined square—had stopped them both cold. Inside, nestled beside a single pearl earring (the mate lost years ago, no one remembered how), lay two tiny silver bells on a thin chain. Elara picked one up. It was warm from the box, impossibly light. She remembered them—the bells had been sewn onto the cuffs of their matching winter coats when they were six and eight. They’d run down the street after school, jingling like tiny, impatient fairies, their mother watching from the gate, laughing, her scarf whipping in the wind. Elara hadn’t thought of that sound in fifteen years. Now, holding the bell, she heard it again—clear, bright, utterly out of place in this quiet, sun-dusted flat.

Maya finally looked up. Her gaze landed on Elara’s hand, then flickered to her face. She didn’t reach for the bell. Didn’t ask to hold it. Just said, “She kept the coat, you know. In the back of the wardrobe. With the bells still on.”

Elara swallowed. “I didn’t know.”

“You weren’t looking for coats.” Maya’s voice held no accusation, only a quiet, weary fact. “You were looking for the will. Or the tax returns. Or the reason why the heating bill was £300 last winter.” She folded another towel, the fabric whispering. “I found it yesterday. Under the spare duvet. Folded in tissue paper. Like something sacred.”

Elara leaned against the counter, the cool Formica pressing into her spine. “What did you do?”

“Nothing. I put it back.” Maya’s fingers stilled on the towel’s edge. “It’s not mine to keep. Or yours. It’s just… a coat. With bells.”

A gust rattled the loose pane in the window, sending a fresh swirl of dust into the light. Elara watched it dance, thinking of how their mother had hated draughts. She’d tape the gaps with brown paper and duct tape, muttering about “wasting heat and good sense.” Elara had rolled her eyes then. Now, she wondered if the tape was still there, hidden behind the frame.

They moved to the living room next, the air heavier there, saturated with memory. The armchair where their mother had read aloud to them—*The Hobbit*, *Anne of Green Gables*, her voice rising and falling like waves. The bookshelf, crammed with well-thumbed paperbacks and encyclopaedias, their spines cracked and softened by handling. Maya pulled out a volume of poetry—*Sylvia Plath*. Their mother’s favourite, though she’d never spoken of it openly, only slipped it into Elara’s bag before university, saying, “For when things get sharp.”

Elara opened it. A pressed violet fell out, brittle and purple, its stem a thread of black. On the flyleaf, in their mother’s neat, looping hand: *For Elara, who sees the cracks in the light. Love, M.*

Elara’s breath hitched. She hadn’t known her mother knew she saw cracks. Hadn’t known she’d noticed.

Maya glanced over, saw the violet, the inscription. She didn’t comment. Just reached past Elara and took the book from her hands, her fingers brushing Elara’s wrist—light, fleeting, warm. She turned to the shelf, slid the book back into place, then carefully removed the next one: *Birds of Britain and Ireland*. Their father’s. He’d loved birds. Used to take them on Sunday walks, binoculars slung around his neck, pointing out robins and wrens with quiet, intense focus. After he left, the binoculars vanished. Elara had assumed he’d taken them. But Maya, kneeling now, pulled open the narrow drawer beneath the bookshelf—a drawer neither of them had ever opened—and there they were. Tucked inside a faded blue cloth, lenses fogged with age, straps stiffened with time. And tucked into the strap, a single, smooth river stone, grey and worn, exactly the size of a child’s fist.

Maya lifted it. Turned it in her palm. “He gave me this,” she said, her voice barely above the hum of the fridge in the next room. “The day he walked out. Said, ‘Hold onto something real, Maya. Even if it’s just a rock.’” She looked at Elara, really looked, her eyes clear and dry and impossibly old. “I never told you.”

Elara stared at the stone, then at her sister’s face—the same stubborn chin, the same slight tilt to the left eyebrow their mother had. The dust motes swirled. The radiator clicked softly, settling. Somewhere, a neighbour’s radio played a muffled, melancholy jazz tune.

Elara didn’t say *I’m sorry*. She didn’t say *Why didn’t you tell me?* She just stepped forward, slowly, and placed her hand over Maya’s, covering the stone, their palms meeting, fingers interlacing—not tightly, not desperately, but with the quiet, weathered certainty of roots finding purchase in familiar soil. They stood like that, breathing the same air thick with dust and memory and the faint, lingering scent of roses, while the afternoon light bled from gold to amber, and the flat, for the first time in weeks, didn’t feel like a tomb. It felt, simply, like a space waiting—not for erasure, but for breath. For the slow, necessary work of letting go, one fragile, jingling, stone-cold thing at a time.

title: personal essay|why I keep a notebook of overheard sentences
text:
In the labyrinthine corridors of my daily existence, I carry a small, unassuming notebook. It is not a journal in the traditional sense; rather, it serves as a repository for the ephemeral fragments of human speech that drift through the air like dandelion seeds. These are not the words of friends or family, nor even those of acquaintances, but the stray utterances of strangers—snippets overheard on buses, in cafes, at street corners. Each sentence, each phrase, is a window into another life, a fleeting glimpse into a narrative that will forever remain untold to me. This practice, which might seem peculiar to some, has become an integral part of my experience, a way of engaging with the world that is both intimate and detached.

The notebook itself is nothing special: a simple, leather-bound volume, its pages yellowed with age and filled with a scrawl that often seems as chaotic as the thoughts it captures. Yet, within its covers, there is a kind of order, a rhythm that mirrors the ebb and flow of human conversation. The sentences I collect are not always profound, nor are they always coherent. They are, however, always authentic, raw and unfiltered, the unscripted dialogue of lives unfolding in real time.

I began this habit almost by accident. One afternoon, while waiting for a train, I overheard a woman say, "The only thing worse than being alone is being with someone who makes you feel alone." The poignancy of her words struck me, and I found myself reaching for a scrap of paper, jotting down the sentence before it could slip away. In that moment, I realized that these fragments, these stray thoughts, were not just random noise but a form of poetry, a testament to the complexity of the human condition.

Since then, I have become an avid collector, a silent archivist of the spoken word. I listen for the unexpected, the offhand remark that reveals a deeper truth, the casual observation that hints at a larger story. There is something deeply satisfying about capturing these moments, about preserving them in a way that acknowledges their significance, even if that significance is only apparent to me.

One of my favorite entries comes from a young man in a coffee shop, who, speaking into his phone, said, "I don't know, man. Sometimes I feel like I'm just a character in someone else's story." The irony of his statement, given my own role as an observer, was not lost on me. It made me wonder how many of us go through our days feeling like bit players in a drama we do not fully understand. How many of us, in our most private moments, question the very nature of our existence?

These snippets, these fragments, are not just a collection of words; they are a mosaic of human experience. Each one is a piece of a larger puzzle, a fragment of a narrative that, when pieced together, reveals something about the human condition. They are, in a sense, a form of literature, a genre that exists outside the bounds of conventional storytelling. They are the stories that are never written, the novels that are never published, the plays that are never performed.

But why, you might ask, do I keep this notebook? What purpose does it serve, beyond the simple act of collecting? The answer, I think, is that it is a way of connecting with the world, of finding meaning in the mundane. In a society that often values efficiency and productivity above all else, there is something subversive about taking the time to listen, to pay attention to the small, seemingly insignificant moments that make up our lives. It is a reminder that every person, no matter how ordinary, has a story worth hearing, a voice worth listening to.

There is also, I admit, a certain voyeuristic pleasure in this practice. I am, in a sense, a peeping Tom, a listener at keyholes, a reader of diaries. But there is, I hope, a more noble motive as well. By collecting these fragments, I am, in a small way, honoring the lives of others, acknowledging the beauty and the pain, the joy and the sorrow, that we all share. It is a way of saying, "I see you. I hear you. Your story matters."

Yet, as much as I value this notebook, I am also acutely aware of its limitations. These sentences, these fragments, are just that: fragments. They are incomplete, out of context, and, in many ways, they raise more questions than they answer. They are, in a sense, a form of literary ambiguity, a reminder that the world is complex and that the stories we tell ourselves are often just that: stories, partial and imperfect.

In the end, perhaps the true value of this notebook lies not in the sentences themselves but in the act of listening, in the act of paying attention. In a world that often feels fragmented and disconnected, there is something profoundly human about the desire to connect, to find meaning in the chaos, to hear the voices of others and, in doing so, to better understand our own. The notebook, in this sense, is not just a collection of words; it is a reflection of my own search for connection, for understanding, for a sense of place in a world that can sometimes feel overwhelming and alien.

And so, I continue to listen, to write, to collect. The notebook grows thicker, the pages more worn, but the impulse remains the same. It is a way of holding onto the world, of grasping at the fleeting moments that make up our lives. It is, in the end, a way of being present, of being here, now, in the midst of it all.

title: legend|a drowned village whose church bell still rings at low tide
text:
The salt air still carries it—faint, coppery, and impossibly clear—on the breath of the ebb. Not every tide, mind you. Only when the water pulls back past the old sea wall at Penhallow Cove, past the barnacle-crusted granite teeth of the drowned causeway, and the mudflats exhale that thick, iodine-sweet rot of kelp and buried peat. Then, just as the first gulls tilt low over the grey water, the bell rings. Once. Not a chime, not a peal, but a single, resonant *thong*—deep in the throat of the earth, as if something heavy had shifted underwater.

Old Man Tregenna swears he heard it the night his father drowned. “1953,” he told me last October, leaning on his gate in St. Ives, his knuckles raw from scrubbing mussels off the rocks. “Dad went out for the lobster pots at slack water. Came back with his boots full of seaweed and his mouth full of sand, but no breath left. And just before the undertaker’s van turned onto the lane? *Thong.* Like the bell was clearing its throat.” He spat into the gutter. “Folks said it was the wind in the old church tower, half-submerged. But wind don’t sound like brass.”

Penhallow wasn’t drowned by storm or siege, but by quiet, bureaucratic drowning. In 1927, the Cornwall Water Board deemed the valley too prone to flooding, too expensive to drain, too far from the new rail line. They offered £12 per acre for the land, £30 for a cottage—enough to buy a room above a fishmonger’s in Hayle, if you were lucky. The villagers signed. Most. Not Elara Pender, who kept the schoolhouse and taught arithmetic by candlelight even after the roof began sagging under the weight of rain. She stayed until ’31, teaching three children—the twins, Ben and Lora Trevithick, and young Silas Gwavas—by the light of the one window still unclouded with salt-mist. Her logbook, found wedged inside a waterlogged chest in the ruins of the rectory in ’89, records: *“Lora cried today. Said she heard the bell ring when the tide was low. Told her it was the wind in the west tower. But the wind does not sound like Father’s voice.”*

The church itself, St. Erth’s, stood on the highest knoll, its slate roof visible even at high tide until ’48, when the last gable collapsed inward during a nor’easter. Now only the tower remains—a jagged tooth of Cornish granite, half-swallowed by the cove’s silt. Divers have tried. In ’62, a team from Plymouth University lowered a camera. The footage shows green water, shifting light, and the blurred outline of the tower’s lower arches. Then, for three seconds, the lens catches it: the bell, suspended not by rope, but by thick, blackened iron chains bolted directly into the stone vault. Its clapper hangs motionless. Yet the diver, listening through hydrophones, reported static—and beneath it, a vibration. A hum, low as a cello’s C-string.

Last spring, I met Lora Trevithick—now Lora Penhaligon—at the St. Ives Literary Festival. She wore a cardigan stitched with tiny silver fish. “They say it’s resonance,” she murmured, stirring honey into her tea. “Tidal pressure shifts the silt, the water compresses the air pockets in the tower’s foundations, and the bell vibrates. Science.” She paused, watching a seagull tear at a dropped pasty. “But Ben heard it the morning he buried his wife. Low tide. No wind. Just that sound—clean, cold, and full of waiting. He stood there on the shingle, tears freezing on his cheeks, and whispered, ‘Mam, is that you?’” She didn’t smile. “We never asked why the bell rang *then*. We just listened.”

I went down to the cove at dawn last Tuesday. The tide was receding fast, pulling the water back like a slow, reluctant sigh. The mudflats glistened, ribbed with channels where lugworms pulsed like buried veins. I stood where the old village green would have been—now just a slight rise in the marsh grass, marked by a single, lichen-bleached gravestone: *Here lies Thomas Kellow, 1872–1928. He loved the sea, though it took his house.* A pair of oystercatchers skittered across the wet sand, their red beaks sharp against the grey.

Then it came. Not loud. Not sudden. It rose—not from the water, but *through* it, vibrating up the soles of my boots, humming in my molars. *Thong.* The sound held for perhaps two heartbeats, rich and round and ancient, then faded into the lap of waves. A heron lifted from the reeds, wings cracking the silence.

Later, walking back along the cliff path, I passed the new holiday cottages—white-washed, with slate roofs and names like *Seabreeze* and *Driftwood Lodge*. One had a brass plaque beside the door: *Built 2019. Former site of Penhallow Schoolhouse.* I stopped. On the damp stone, half-hidden by ivy, someone had scratched, with what looked like a nail or a key, three letters: *E.P.* Elara Pender. Or perhaps *Erth’s Parish.* Or maybe just *Echo Point.*

A woman in wellington boots and a waxed jacket came up behind me, carrying a bucket of mussels. “Heard it?” she asked, not unkindly.  
I nodded.  
She tipped her head toward the cove. “My gran used to say the bell doesn’t ring *for* anyone. It rings *because* the water leaves. Because the stone remembers being dry. Because some things refuse to be forgotten—even when they’re buried under ten feet of salt and time.” She patted the wall, where the scratch gleamed faintly. “Listen close next time. You’ll hear the echo *before* the ring. Like the village holding its breath.”  

The wind shifted. From the cove, the smell of wet stone and deep water rose, clean and cold and unmistakable. And somewhere, beneath the surface, the metal waited—not for rescue, not for explanation—but for the tide to pull away, just enough, so it could speak again.

title: short story|a piano tuner who visits the same blind client for thirty years
text:
The first time I tuned Mrs. Lark’s Steinway, it was 1994. Late October. A damp chill clinging to the brickwork of her brownstone on 82nd Street—same building where she’d lived since ’58, same third-floor apartment with the warped oak floorboards that groaned *exactly* like a tired bassoon when you stepped near the radiator. She opened the door barefoot, socks pulled up to her shins—navy blue, one with a tiny hole at the big toe—and held out a hand not to shake, but to *feel* the weight of my tuning fork. “C-sharp,” she said. Not a question. Her fingers traced the metal tine, then pressed lightly against my wrist, checking pulse. “You’re nervous. That’s fine. The piano isn’t.”

She’d lost her sight at thirty-seven—retinitis pigmentosa, slow and thorough as tide receding. By ’94, she hadn’t seen a sky in seventeen years. But she knew light by its heat on her left cheek in the late afternoon, knew rain by the way the brass door knocker hummed dully before it fell, knew *me*, eventually, by the slight rasp in my left knee when I crouched to adjust the damper pedal—a sound I didn’t know I made until she named it: “Like gravel shifting in a tin can.”

I brought my own stool. Not fancy. Folding aluminum, painted over three times in mismatched shades of green. The first year, I used a borrowed one—wobbly, with a broken rung. She heard the wobble. “That stool’s lying,” she said. So I bought the green one. Still have it. Still fold it with the same stiff hinge that squeaks *shhhk* every time.

Her piano wasn’t just an instrument. It was a geography. The middle C key had a faint ridge where her thumb rested for decades—polished smooth as river stone, but the ridge remained, like a seam in old leather. The sustain pedal felt gritty underfoot—not dirt, but the accumulated dust of thirty years’ worth of lifted heels and settled sighs. I cleaned it once, carefully, with a soft cloth and distilled water. She noticed the next visit. “It sings differently now,” she said, frowning. “Too bright. Like sunlight on new glass.” So I stopped cleaning the pedal. Let the grit stay. Became part of the resonance.

We never talked much about music theory. Never discussed Beethoven’s deafness or Chopin’s coughing fits. She’d ask, sometimes, if the A-string on the bass clef was “holding its breath too long.” Or if the high E was “still flirting with the ceiling.” Once, during a blizzard in ’03, the power went out mid-tuning. I lit the kerosene lamp on her mantel—its flame tilted sideways in the draft from the ill-fitting window frame. She sat beside me, silent for twenty minutes, then whispered, “That flame’s humming in F-sharp minor. I think it’s sad.” I checked. It was. Almost exactly.

Her hands were always warm. Always dry. She’d rest them flat on the closed lid while I worked—palms down, fingers splayed—feeling the vibrations travel up through the wood, the cast iron, the strings themselves. “The low D is dreaming,” she’d murmur. “The G above middle C is impatient.” I learned to listen *with* my bones, not just my ears. To feel the tension shift in the wrest pins, the subtle give in the felt hammers, the way humidity made the soundboard swell like a held breath.

She never played for me. Not once. Said the piano was for listening, not performance. “Playing is for the eyes,” she told me once, stirring tea with a spoon that clinked twice against the cup’s rim—*ping, ping*. “Listening is for the whole body. You learn to hear the silence *between* the notes. That’s where the truth lives.”

In ’17, her son moved her to assisted living uptown. Small room. No piano. Just a digital keyboard with plastic keys and a headphone jack. I visited anyway. Brought my green stool. Tuned the little thing—even though it couldn’t *be* tuned, not really. Just adjusted the volume, the reverb, the timbre. She sat with headphones on, eyes closed, nodding slowly. When I finished, she took them off, touched my forearm, and said, “The silence between the notes is thinner here. Like tissue paper. But it’s still there.”

She died last spring. April 12th. A Tuesday. I got the call from the hospice nurse—her voice soft, apologetic, like she’d interrupted something sacred. I drove straight to the brownstone. The new tenants were young—artists, probably—left the front door unlocked. I climbed the stairs. The third-floor hallway smelled of lemon oil and burnt toast. Her apartment was empty except for the Steinway. Covered in a faded floral sheet, like a ghost draped in grandma’s curtains.

I lifted the sheet. Dust motes swirled in the slant of afternoon light. Ran my palm over the lid. Cold. Dry. The ridge on middle C was still there.

I didn’t open it. Didn’t sit. Didn’t tune.

Just stood. Listened.

The radiator ticked. A car backfired three blocks away—*crack!*—and the bass strings vibrated, faint, sympathetic. A single, quiet hum.

Then silence.

Not empty. Not dead.

Just waiting.

I folded my green stool. The hinge squeaked *shhhk*.

Went home.

Didn’t touch my tuning fork for two weeks.

Still haven’t.

title: memoir|a father's ledger found after his death
text:
...as I turned the page, a dried flower fell out, its petals so fragile they crumbled at the slightest touch. It was a forget-me-not, and it seemed to have been there for decades. I couldn’t help but wonder if it had any significance, or if it was just another of my father’s small, forgotten gestures. The ledger itself was an old, leather-bound book, its pages yellowed with age and filled with his meticulous handwriting. Each entry was dated, and as I read, I felt like I was stepping back in time, walking through the corridors of his life.

The entries were not just financial; they were a blend of the mundane and the profound. There were notes about payments made, debts collected, and even the occasional recipe scribbled in the margins. But what struck me most were the personal reflections. On one page, he wrote about the day my mother accepted his proposal, her eyes shining with tears of joy. He described the ring, a simple gold band, and how he had saved for months to buy it. The love he felt for her was palpable, and it brought a lump to my throat.

As I continued to flip through the pages, I found a section dedicated to our family’s milestones. Birthdays, graduations, and even the first day I rode a bike without training wheels—all meticulously recorded. There was an entry from when I was six, and I had lost my first tooth. "Ella was so proud," he wrote, "she showed it to everyone, even the mailman. She put it under her pillow, and I slipped a dollar in there, hoping she would find it in the morning." I remembered that moment vividly, the excitement of waking up to find the money, and the belief in the magic of the tooth fairy. Now, seeing it through his eyes, I realized how much joy it brought him to see me happy.

But not all the entries were happy. There were times of struggle and hardship, too. One entry, dated during a particularly difficult year, spoke of a loan he had taken out to keep the family afloat. The stress and worry were evident in his words, and he wrote, "I don’t know how we will make it, but I must keep trying. For them, I must keep trying." It was a stark reminder of the sacrifices he made, often without us knowing. I felt a pang of guilt, realizing how little I knew about the burdens he carried.

There were also moments of deep reflection. On the night my grandmother passed away, he wrote, "She was the rock of our family, and now she is gone. I feel a void, a deep emptiness. How do I tell the children? How do I explain that the world is a little less bright now?" His grief was raw and unfiltered, and it was the first time I saw him as more than just a father, but as a man who felt pain and loss deeply.

One of the most poignant entries was from the day I left for college. "Ella packed her bags and said goodbye. She hugged me tight, and for a moment, I could see the little girl she once was. Now, she is a young woman, ready to take on the world. I am proud, but I will miss her. The house feels empty without her laughter." I could almost hear his voice, the mixture of pride and sorrow, and it made me wish I could go back and give him one more hug, tell him how much I appreciated everything he did.

As I delved deeper into the ledger, I began to see patterns in his life. There were recurring themes of resilience, love, and a deep sense of responsibility. He wrote about the importance of hard work, the value of education, and the need to always be kind. These were lessons he lived by, and they shaped the man he was. I realized that this ledger was not just a record of transactions, but a chronicle of his values, his dreams, and his love for us.
