I spent hours poring over the pages, each entry revealing a new facet of my father. I laughed at some of the stories, cried at others, and felt a profound connection to the man who had raised me. In many ways, the ledger was a gift, a way for him to speak to me even after he was gone. It was a testament to his life, and it gave me a deeper understanding of the person he was.

As the afternoon light faded, I closed the ledger, feeling a mix of emotions. Sadness, of course, for the loss of him, but also gratitude for the legacy he left behind. I placed the book back in its box, the forget-me-not still lying beside it. I knew that I would return to these pages again, to remember, to learn, and to find solace in the memories. And in that moment, I felt closer to my father than I ever had before.

title: memoir|a childhood split between two countries and two languages
text:
The first thing I remember is the smell of rain on hot pavement in Lisbon—sharp, metallic, like licking a battery—and then, instantly, the damp wool of my grandmother’s cardigan, thick with the scent of mothballs and dried lavender. She’d lift me onto the kitchen counter while she peeled potatoes, her knuckles swollen, her voice a low hum in Portuguese that felt like warm honey poured slowly into a jar. I’d watch the peels curl away from the knife, translucent and trembling, and try to mimic the syllables she murmured: *batata, água, avó*. But my tongue was clumsy, too English, too soft at the edges, and she’d laugh—not unkindly—pressing a kiss to my temple that left a faint salt-taste behind.

Then, the suitcase. Always the same one: navy canvas, one wheel wobbling slightly, the zipper stubborn near the handle. My father would kneel beside it in our Lisbon apartment, lining up my shoes—brown lace-ups for school, sandals for summer—and folding my clothes with military precision. He spoke English only when necessary, his accent clipped, as if each word were a stone he had to carry across a river. In London, he became someone else: shoulders looser, jokes quicker, voice rising at the end of sentences like a question he’d never quite answer. At Heathrow, the air changed—colder, drier, smelling of disinfectant and burnt coffee—and my throat would tighten, not from sadness, but from the sudden, physical effort of switching languages. Portuguese lived low in my belly; English sat high, behind my teeth, sharp and ready.

School in London was a geography of silence. I’d sit at the back, tracing the grain of the wooden desk with my fingernail, listening to the other children’s laughter—their vowels round and open, their consonants crisp as snapped twigs. When the teacher called my name, I’d flinch, then answer in English so careful it sounded rehearsed, like reciting lines from a play I hadn’t read. At break, I’d stand near the fence, watching the others kick a football, their shouts bouncing off the brick walls. Sometimes, a boy named Leo would toss me the ball without looking, and I’d catch it, fumble it, drop it—my hands still learning the weight of things in this new gravity. He’d grin and say, “You’re all right, yeah?” and I’d nod, the words stuck somewhere between my ribs.

In Lisbon, I was different. There, I ran barefoot through the courtyard behind my grandparents’ building, chasing lizards that darted like green sparks across sun-baked tiles. My cousin Marta and I would climb the fig tree in the alley, its bark rough under our palms, its leaves broad and waxy, catching the afternoon light like stained glass. We’d whisper secrets in Portuguese, giggling over words that had no English equivalent—*saudade*, which wasn’t just missing someone, but feeling the hollow where they’d been, like a tooth pulled and the gum still remembering its shape; *desenrascanço*, the art of improvising your way out of trouble with whatever’s at hand. We’d eat *pastéis de nata* still warm, the custard oozing slightly, cinnamon dusting our fingers, and talk about ghosts in the basement and whether the old man who swept the street could really see angels.

But even there, language slipped. When I tried to tell my grandfather about my science project—the one with the vinegar and baking soda volcano—he listened patiently, nodding, but his eyes flickered, just once, toward the radio playing fado in the next room. Later, he handed me a small wooden box painted with blue and white tiles, empty inside, and said, *“Para guardar as palavras que não cabem em nenhuma língua.”* For the words that don’t fit in any language. I didn’t understand then. Now I do. There were words I couldn’t place—like the ache behind my eyes when the plane descended into Heathrow and I saw the grey sprawl below, or the quiet pride in my mother’s voice when she corrected my Portuguese pronunciation, her own accent thick with decades of London fog and tube trains.

I learned to hold both tongues like stones in my mouth—one smooth and cool, the other jagged and warm—and to shift them without swallowing. At twelve, I translated for my grandmother during a doctor’s visit in London, her Portuguese flowing like a river, my English precise and measured, the doctor nodding, unaware that the sentence I delivered was not quite what she’d said, but what she needed him to hear. And later, in Lisbon, I helped my father fill out a form at the post office, his English faltering, my Portuguese firm, the clerk smiling at me like I was something rare and delicate.

The train from Santa Apolónia to Cascais still smells the same—dust, sea salt, and the faint sweetness of orange blossoms clinging to the air. I ride it sometimes, alone, watching the coastline blur past: cliffs, coves, fishing boats bobbing like toys. My fingers trace the condensation on the window, drawing shapes that vanish almost as soon as they appear. A woman across the aisle speaks to her child in rapid, musical Portuguese. I catch a phrase—*“Olha lá!”*—and my chest tightens, not with longing, exactly, but with recognition, deep and wordless, like the echo of a bell heard underwater. The child turns, meets my gaze, and grins, showing two missing front teeth. I smile back. No translation needed. Just the light on the water, the rhythm of the wheels, the quiet, constant hum of two languages breathing side by side, neither one ever fully silent, neither one ever quite whole.

title: personal essay|why I keep a notebook of overheard sentences
text:
It began in the spring of 2019, on a rain-slicked bench outside the old Barnes & Noble on 82nd and Broadway—just before they shuttered the Upper West Side store for good. I was waiting for my sister, Maya, who was late, as usual, and nursing a lukewarm oat-milk latte when a woman sat beside me, unzipping a canvas tote stamped with faded letters: *Museum of Modern Art, 1997*. She pulled out a paperback copy of *The House on Mango Street*, its spine cracked at page 43, and murmured—not to me, not to anyone—“I used to read this aloud to my son when his voice was still soft as lint.” Her voice didn’t rise above the city’s low hum—the hiss of bus brakes, the clatter of a dropped MetroCard—but the phrase lodged in me like a splinter: *soft as lint*. I dug a pen from my coat pocket and wrote it down in the margin of my Moleskine, next to a half-sketch of a pigeon with one wing slightly larger than the other.

That notebook—black, cloth-bound, with a frayed elastic band holding it shut—is now six years old and contains 217 pages of overheard speech, transcribed in ballpoint, fountain pen, pencil, and once, during a power outage in Brooklyn, in charcoal stubbed from a burnt-out candle. I don’t record everything. Only what lands with weight: syntax that bends unexpectedly, metaphors that arrive unannounced, grief or joy so precise it feels like eavesdropping on someone’s bones.

Last October, I sat in the back booth of Sami’s Diner in Astoria—red vinyl, chrome trim, the kind of place where the coffee is served in thick white mugs marked with tiny blue stars. A man in a navy work jacket, name tag reading *LEO*, wiped the counter while talking to the cook, Rosa, whose hair was pinned up with two chopsticks. “My daughter,” he said, wiping the same spot for thirty seconds, “she asked me yesterday if ghosts get tired. I told her yes—especially the ones who stayed behind to fix things.” He paused, dipped a rag into soapy water, wrung it out slow. “She looked at me and said, ‘Then why don’t you rest, Papa?’” I wrote it down fast, my hand shaking a little—not from cold, but from the sudden, vertiginous sense that I’d just witnessed something sacred, unscripted, and utterly unrepeatable.

Sometimes the sentences come wrapped in contradiction. Like the day I stood in line at the post office on St. Mark’s Place, behind a teenager in a glitter-stitched beanie arguing with her grandmother over FaceTime. The grandmother’s voice crackled through tinny speakers: “You think love is fireworks? No. Love is the sound of your husband snoring *in the right key*.” The girl laughed, sharp and startled, then repeated it to her friend: “In the right key!”—as if testing the phrase for resonance. I copied it verbatim, then underlined *right key*, because it was absurd and true, musical and domestic, all at once.

I’ve written down a toddler in Prospect Park saying, “The sky is chewing clouds,” and a retired librarian in Beacon, NY, telling her grandson, “When I forget your name, I’ll call you *the boy who brought me dandelions*—that’s how I’ll know you’re still you.” I’ve recorded fragments from subway platforms (“My therapist says I’m allowed to want less”), hospital cafeterias (“The morphine doesn’t take the pain away—it just gives it a different address”), and a laundromat in Bushwick where a man folded shirts while explaining to his daughter, “Your mother didn’t leave us. She left the version of herself that believed she had to hold everything together.”

People ask if it feels intrusive. Sometimes, yes—like the afternoon I sat too long near the fountain in Bryant Park, listening to two women dissect a decades-old betrayal, their voices low and liquid, punctuated by the splash of falling water. One said, “I forgave him, but I never gave back the silence I kept while doing it.” I wrote it, then closed the notebook and walked away, heart pounding—not from guilt, exactly, but from the sheer, staggering intimacy of hearing language do its quiet, devastating work.

My notebook isn’t a collection of curiosities. It’s a ledger of survival tactics—how we stitch meaning from breath and syntax, how we name the unnamed, how we reach across chasms with three words strung together like prayer beads. Last week, I opened it to page 162, where I’d written, in ink that had bled slightly from humidity: *“He didn’t say goodbye—he said, ‘I’ll keep the light on for you,’ and I believed him, even though I knew the bulb was burnt out.”* I stared at it for a long time, remembering the speaker: a woman named Priya, sitting alone at the Greyhound terminal in Port Authority, her backpack zipped tight, her eyes fixed on the departure board. She hadn’t been speaking to me. She’d been speaking into the air, into the architecture of waiting, into the thin, trembling membrane between hope and surrender.

I still carry the notebook everywhere—even to the dentist’s office, where I once jotted down the hygienist’s offhand remark: “Teeth remember every bite you ever took, even the ones you pretended not to.” It’s heavy now. The spine is warped. Pages stick together in summer humidity, peel apart in winter dryness. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve replaced the elastic band. But I haven’t stopped. Not after Maya died last March—though for three weeks I couldn’t open it, couldn’t bear the thought of adding anything to a world that suddenly felt unbearably loud and unbearably silent all at once. Then, one rainy Tuesday, I found myself in that same Barnes & Noble location—now a Duane Reade—and heard a child say to her father, “Daddy, your shadow is holding my hand.” I bought a new pen. I opened the notebook. I wrote it down.

title: literary essay|silence and omission in short fiction
text:
Silence and omission in short fiction are like the quiet, unassuming shadows that follow a person on a sunny day. You don't always notice them, but they’re there, shaping the contours of the light, adding depth and dimension to the scene. In the hands of a skilled writer, silence and omission can be more powerful than any word or sentence. They create an invisible architecture, a subtext that whispers to the reader, urging them to fill in the gaps with their own imagination, their own fears, and their own desires.

Take, for instance, Ernest Hemingway's "Hills Like White Elephants." The story is a masterclass in what isn’t said. Two characters, a man and a woman, sit in a train station, discussing something that is never explicitly named. The tension between them is palpable, but it’s not the words that convey this; it’s the silences, the pauses, the things left unsaid. The conversation dances around the topic of abortion, but the word itself is never mentioned. Instead, Hemingway uses the landscape, the drinks, the gestures, to hint at the deeper, more painful truths. The white elephants, those large, unwieldy symbols, loom in the background, silent but ever-present, much like the unspoken decision that hangs over the couple.

But why do writers choose to use silence and omission? Sometimes, it’s because the truth is too painful, too raw, to be spoken aloud. Other times, it’s because the unsaid creates a kind of mystery, a puzzle that the reader must solve. It’s like when you’re in a room with someone, and you both know something, but neither of you wants to be the one to say it. The air becomes thick with unspoken words, and the tension builds until it’s almost unbearable. That’s the power of silence in fiction—it can make the reader lean in, straining to hear the unspoken, to understand the unexplained.

In Alice Munro’s "The Bear Came Over the Mountain," the omissions are as deliberate and meaningful as the words. The story follows an elderly couple, Fiona and Grant, as Fiona begins to slip into dementia. The narrative is filled with gaps, moments where the past and present blur, and the reader is left to piece together the fragments. Munro doesn’t spell out every detail of their relationship, nor does she provide a clear timeline of events. Instead, she lets the silences speak, allowing the reader to infer the complexity of their history, the layers of love and betrayal, the unspoken regrets and longings. The bear, a symbol of the past, comes over the mountain, and its presence is felt, even if it’s never fully seen.

Sometimes, the omissions are more subtle, more personal. In Raymond Carver’s "Cathedral," the narrator, a man who is skeptical and closed off, has his world opened up by a blind man. The story is about connection, about seeing and being seen, but it’s also about the things that go unsaid. The narrator’s wife, who is friends with the blind man, has been writing letters to him, sharing her life, her thoughts, her feelings. The narrator, jealous and resentful, resents this intimacy, but he never voices his discomfort. It’s only through the act of drawing a cathedral with the blind man that he begins to understand the power of connection, the importance of communication, even in its most silent forms.

Silence and omission can also be used to create a sense of ambiguity, a feeling that the story is open-ended, that there are multiple interpretations. In Flannery O’Connor’s "A Good Man Is Hard to Find," the ending is brutal and shocking, but it’s the silences leading up to it that make it so powerful. The grandmother, a talkative, self-righteous woman, is confronted with the Misfit, a criminal who seems to see through her facade. The dialogue between them is sparse, filled with pauses and non-sequiturs, and it’s in these silences that the true horror of the situation is revealed. The Misfit’s final act, the killing of the grandmother, is almost a relief, a release from the tension that has been building throughout the story. But the questions remain: was the grandmother truly evil, or was she just human, flawed and selfish, like all of us?

I once read a short story—can’t remember the title, or even the author, but I remember the feeling it left me with. It was about a couple, and the entire story was a series of phone calls, each one shorter than the last. The first call was full of promises, of plans, of shared dreams. But as the calls went on, the words became fewer, the pauses longer. By the end, there were no words at all, just the sound of breathing, the click of the phone being hung up. It was a story about the slow, painful disintegration of a relationship, and it was told entirely through the silences, the things that weren’t said.

In the end, perhaps the most profound use of silence and omission in short fiction is to remind us of our own limitations, our own inability to fully express or understand the complexities of human experience. We can try to capture the essence of a moment, a feeling, a thought, but there will always be something that slips through the cracks, something that remains unspoken, unexplored. And maybe that’s the beauty of it. Maybe the real magic of short fiction lies in the spaces between the words, in the silences that we fill with our own hopes, fears, and dreams.

title: personal essay|living next to a railway line for twenty years
text:
The train hits the crossing bells just as I’m stirring the porridge—*clong, clong, clong*, low and insistent, vibrating the spoon handle against my palm. Steam rises in slow curls from the pot; outside, the air is still thick with the damp hush of early autumn, the kind that settles like dust on the tongue. I don’t look up. My wrist moves, steady, circular. The rhythm is older than memory: stir, wait, stir again—just as the first freight car groans into view beyond the fence, its rust-streaked flank sliding past the maple whose roots have buckled our back step. Twenty years. Not counted in birthdays or anniversaries, but in the thousand subtle ways the rails have rewired my nervous system, my grammar, my sense of time.

It wasn’t loud at first—not the way you’d expect. When we moved in, the line felt like a distant relative: acknowledged, occasionally visited, never quite *present*. We’d hear the whistle—long, mournful, almost apologetic—and glance out the kitchen window, curious, then return to unpacking boxes. But presence isn’t about volume. It’s about frequency. It’s about the way the ground hums under bare feet on the porch slab at 3:17 a.m., when the overnight grain hauler shudders past, its couplings clicking like knuckles cracking in the dark. It’s about how your daughter, at four, stopped saying “train” and started saying *“thrum”*—a word she invented, soft and guttural, to describe the vibration that made her sippy cup tremble on the high chair tray.

We learned to parse the language. The sharp, staccato *beep-beep-beep* of the commuter shuttle meant school drop-off was safe. The deep, throaty moan of the eastbound coal train meant the windows needed closing before the fine grey dust settled on the sill, on the bookshelf, on the sleeping cat’s fur. The sudden, metallic shriek of brakes—always from the south end, where the grade steepens—meant someone had misjudged the timing, or the signal failed, or the world simply hiccuped. We never knew. We only knew the sound, and the way it tightened something behind our ribs until the last car cleared the curve.

There were seasons measured not by solstices but by rail. Spring brought the Amtrak Cascades, gleaming white and blue, carrying tourists who pressed their faces to the glass as if viewing a diorama of small-town life. We’d wave, half-embarrassed, half-amused, and they’d wave back, fleeting and bright as fireflies. Summer meant the freight trains ran heavier, slower, sweat-slicked and sun-baked, dragging heatwaves in their wake. You could smell them before you heard them—the hot iron, the diesel tang, the faint, sweet rot of old timber ties baking in the sun. Autumn was the quietest, the rails seeming to exhale after months of strain. Then winter: ice-glazed rails singing a thin, high whine as wheels passed, snow muffling everything except the rhythmic *shush-shush-shush* of the plow car clearing the siding, its yellow light cutting twin tunnels through the blizzard.

We adapted in small, stubborn ways. The bedroom curtains weren’t just for privacy—they were layered: blackout lining, then thick cotton, then a final drape of quilted fabric salvaged from my grandmother’s attic. Not for sound, exactly, but for *weight*. For the illusion of containment. We bought a second-hand record player not for nostalgia, but because vinyl crackle filled the silences between trains better than any digital loop ever could—warm, imperfect, alive. When our son learned to ride a bike, he didn’t practice on the street; he pedaled up and down the gravel shoulder of the service road, learning balance and momentum alongside the rhythm of passing steel. He learned to gauge speed by ear: the rising pitch meant it was coming fast; the falling pitch meant it was already gone, leaving only the echo and the settling dust.

There were losses, of course. A neighbour moved out after three years, citing “chronic fatigue.” Another installed triple-glazed windows and a white-noise machine that hummed louder than the trains themselves. We stayed. Not out of stubbornness, but because the noise had ceased to be an intrusion and become a texture—like the creak of floorboards, the sigh of the furnace, the wind in the eaves. It was the bassline to our domestic symphony. Without it, the silence felt thin, untrustworthy, like holding your breath underwater.

I remember the night the power went out during the ice storm. No lights. No furnace. Just the wind screaming in the pines and the occasional, hollow *thump* of a branch hitting the roof. We lit candles, wrapped ourselves in blankets, and sat on the living room rug. And then, cutting through the chaos, came the unmistakable rumble—not of a train, but of the maintenance crew’s diesel generator, powering the switch heaters down at the junction. A steady, comforting *vrrrrr-oom*, steady as a heartbeat. My daughter, then seven, leaned her head against my knee and whispered, “That’s the train’s heartbeat.” She wasn’t wrong. In that moment, the line wasn’t outside us. It was *in* us—the pulse beneath the pavement, the thrum in the walls, the low, constant hum in the bones.

Now, standing here at the stove, porridge thickening, the train recedes into the distance, its sound dissolving into the rustle of leaves and the distant bark of a dog. My hand is still. The spoon rests against the pot’s rim. I watch the steam rise, then vanish. Twenty years haven’t made me deaf to the rails. They’ve taught me to listen differently—to hear not just the noise, but the pause within it, the space between the cars, the breath before the whistle, the quiet that isn’t empty, but full: of waiting, of memory, of the slow, relentless, beautiful insistence of something larger than us, moving steadily forward, carrying its own weight, its own history, its own quiet, unbroken song.

title: short story|a night bus driver and a passenger who never gets off
text:
The bus groaned like a tired animal shifting in its sleep, its headlights cutting twin tunnels through the city’s damp breath. Rain slicked the asphalt into black mirrors that fractured the sodium-orange glow of streetlamps, and the windshield wipers slapped a slow, arrhythmic pulse—left, pause, right, pause—as if counting seconds no one else could hear. Elias kept his hands at ten and two, knuckles pale under the thin skin, fingers resting lightly on the worn leather of the wheel. He knew every bump in the route: the shudder over the cracked slab near Seventh and Maple, the low hum as the chassis settled onto the bridge’s steel grating, the way the rearview mirror trembled just so when passing the shuttered laundromat with its flickering neon sign that hadn’t lit in three years.

He’d driven this loop for seventeen winters. Not the same bus—not quite—but the same bones: the same rust bloom along the doorframe, the same dent above the emergency exit where someone once slammed a suitcase in haste, the same faint, sweet-sour tang of old coffee and vinyl upholstery that never quite washed out. His uniform was a second skin, the collar frayed at the nape, the epaulettes softened by time and sweat. He didn’t listen to the radio anymore. The static between stations had begun to sound like voices whispering names he almost recognized.

Then there was her.

She boarded at 11:47 p.m., always, at the corner stop beneath the broken streetlamp whose bulb sputtered violet before dying altogether last October. She wore a coat the colour of dried river clay—unbuttoned, hanging open—and carried no bag, no umbrella, though the rain fell steadily, blurring the world beyond the glass into watercolour smudges. Her hair was dark and pulled back tightly, revealing the sharp line of her jaw, the hollow beneath her cheekbone. She never looked at him directly, only at the window, her reflection superimposed over the passing streetlights, her eyes fixed on something just beyond the glass, something moving faster than the bus.

She sat in the third row, left side, two seats from the aisle. Always the same seat. Never moved. Never adjusted her posture. Her hands rested folded in her lap, palms down, fingers long and still. Once, Elias glanced in the rearview and saw her watching a pigeon hop across the wet pavement outside, its feathers plastered dark against its body, its head cocked, listening to something only it could hear. When the bus pulled away, she didn’t blink. Just turned her face back to the window, as if the bird had been a punctuation mark in a sentence she’d already finished reading.

He started noticing things. The way her breath fogged a small, perfect circle on the glass, then faded without smearing. How she never took out a phone, never read, never even shifted her weight. How the other passengers—students with earbuds, night-shift nurses rubbing their temples, a man in a stained apron carrying a paper sack smelling faintly of grease—would glance at her, then look away quickly, as if catching sight of something they weren’t meant to witness. They’d sit elsewhere, even when the bus was half-empty. One woman stood holding the pole near the front, swaying slightly with the motion, rather than sit beside her.

Elias checked the manifest each night. No name. No transfer slip. No fare collected—not because she evaded it, but because the machine beside the door never beeped when she passed. It stayed silent, inert, as if she were walking through air. He tried once, during a lull at the depot, to log her in manually on the tablet. The screen froze, then displayed a single error code: *ERR 73—INVALID ENTITY*. He tapped it. Swiped. Held the power button. The tablet rebooted, clean, blank, as if nothing had happened.

One Tuesday, the rain turned to sleet. Ice glittered on the bus windows like shattered sugar. At 2:13 a.m., the bus slowed for the usual stop at the old library—its windows boarded, its steps choked with dead leaves—but she didn’t rise. Elias waited, foot hovering over the brake, the engine idling low. Thirty seconds. A minute. He exhaled, eased forward. The doors hissed shut without his command.

Later, near dawn, he pulled into the terminal lot. Empty buses lined up like sleeping cattle. He turned off the engine. The silence rushed in, thick and sudden. He watched her in the mirror. Still seated. Still staring out. He stepped down, walked slowly up the aisle, his shoes soft on the rubber matting. Stopped two rows behind her. Didn’t speak. Just stood, listening to the slow drip of meltwater from the roof lining into the floor drain.

She didn’t turn. Didn’t flinch. But the reflection in the window shifted—just slightly—as if her gaze had tilted, not toward him, but toward the space where his shoulder met the air.

He went back to the driver’s seat. Started the engine. Pulled out again, onto the empty streets, the city exhaling steam from manholes, the sky lightening to the colour of weak tea. The route reset. The clock rolled over. She remained.

He drove past the same laundromat, the same cracked slab, the same bridge. The wipers slapped. The heater wheezed warm, dry air. Her coat hung open. Her hands stayed folded. Her breath made its small, perfect circle, then vanished.

At 5:08 a.m., the first delivery van rumbled past, yellow lights blinking. A jogger appeared, headphones on, breath pluming. The world began to stir. Elias kept his hands at ten and two. The bus rounded the final curve before the terminal, tires humming on wet asphalt. He glanced in the mirror.

She was gone.

Not vanished. Not dissolved. Simply… absent. The seat was empty. The coat wasn’t draped over the backrest. No impression in the vinyl. No trace of dampness on the fabric where she’d sat. He braked gently, pulled into the bay, killed the engine.

Stepped out. Walked to the seat. Touched the armrest. Cold. Dry. Checked the floor. Nothing. No dropped hairpin, no scrap of paper, no scent—not even the faintest echo of rain or wool or skin.

He stood there, breathing in the stale, warm air of the bus, listening to the distant clang of a dumpster lid, the murmur of the city waking. Then he returned to the driver’s seat, adjusted the mirror, turned the key. The engine caught. Headlights flared. He eased forward, into the grey morning, hands steady at ten and two, waiting for the next stop, the next passenger, the next breath held just beyond the glass.

title: personal essay|learning to swim at forty
text:
At forty, I found myself standing at the edge of a pool, toes curled over the concrete lip, staring into water that shimmered like liquid glass. The chlorine scent was sharp and clean, a stark contrast to the musty air of the indoor facility. Around me, children splashed and shrieked, their laughter echoing off the high ceilings. I felt out of place, an adult among the young, my body heavy with the weight of years and unspoken fears.

I had never learned to swim. As a child, I had always been too afraid, too self-conscious. My parents, busy with work, never insisted, and as I grew older, the opportunity slipped away. Now, in my forties, I found myself drawn to the water, perhaps out of a desire to reclaim something lost, or maybe just to prove to myself that it was not too late.

The decision to take swimming lessons came after a summer spent watching others glide effortlessly through the ocean, their bodies slicing through the waves with a grace I envied. I signed up for a beginner class, telling no one, ashamed of my age and my inability. The first day, I arrived early, my heart pounding as I changed into a swimsuit that felt foreign on my skin. I sat on a bench, watching the other students—mostly adults, but all younger than I—chatting and stretching, seemingly at ease.

Our instructor, a woman named Sarah, was in her thirties, with a lean, athletic build and a calm, reassuring demeanor. She began the class by asking us to sit on the edge of the pool and dip our feet in. The water was cool, almost cold, and I shivered as it lapped against my calves. We were then instructed to lie back and float, supported by a kickboard. I hesitated, my mind filled with images of sinking, of gasping for breath, of the humiliation of failure.

Sarah noticed my reluctance and came over, her voice gentle. "It's okay," she said. "Just take your time. There's no rush."

I took a deep breath and lay back, feeling the water cradle my body. For a moment, I was buoyant, weightless, and a sense of peace washed over me. But then, panic set in. I flailed, my arms thrashing, and Sarah quickly steadied me. "Breathe," she reminded me. "Focus on your breathing."

Over the next few weeks, I struggled. Each lesson was a battle between my fear and my determination. I learned to blow bubbles, to kick, to move my arms in a rudimentary front crawl. But every time I tried to put it all together, I would freeze, my body tense and unyielding. Sarah was patient, breaking down each movement, encouraging me to relax, to trust the water. Yet, despite her efforts, I could not shake the feeling of being out of control, of being at the mercy of an element I did not understand.

One evening, after a particularly frustrating session, I stayed behind, watching the other students leave. The pool was empty, the lights dimmed, and the silence enveloped me. I stood at the edge, my reflection rippling in the water. I thought about giving up, about the futility of trying to learn something so late in life. But there was also a part of me that refused to surrender, that yearned to overcome this obstacle, to find some measure of mastery, however small.

I stepped into the water, wading until it reached my waist. The coolness embraced me, and I took a deep breath, letting it out slowly. I began to move, tentatively at first, then with more confidence. My arms and legs worked in unison, and for a brief, glorious moment, I felt as if I were gliding, as if the water and I were one. It was fleeting, and soon I was sputtering, gasping for air, but in that instant, I had tasted something new, something powerful.

Learning to swim at forty is not a journey of triumph. It is a series of small, incremental steps, each one fraught with doubt and uncertainty. It is a reminder that growth is often painful, that progress is slow, and that mastery is elusive. But it is also a testament to the human spirit, to the capacity for change, even when it seems impossible.

As I continue to practice, I am learning to embrace the discomfort, to accept that perfection is not the goal. I am learning to be kinder to myself, to celebrate the small victories, and to find joy in the process. The water, once a source of fear, has become a place of solace, a space where I can confront my limitations and, perhaps, transcend them.

In the end, I may never be a graceful swimmer, but I will keep trying. Because, at forty, I have come to realize that the act of trying, the willingness to face one's fears, is its own form of victory.

title: elegy in free verse|a closed coal mine and the men who worked it
text:
Elegy for the Black Diamond Shaft  

It’s quiet now. Not peaceful—*quiet*. Like the kind of silence that settles after someone’s stopped breathing but before you’ve quite accepted it. You stand at the gate, rust eating the chain-link like slow cancer, and the wind carries nothing but dust and the dry rattle of a plastic bag snagged on the old weighbridge post. *That* post. The one with the chipped yellow paint and the faint, greasy thumbprint still visible near the base—somebody’s, not mine, but I know it’s real because I saw Joe Miller wipe his forehead there in ’87 and leave it, and I remember how the grease mixed with coal-dust made it look like a smudge of burnt sugar.  

The headframe’s gone. Just concrete stubs jutting from the earth, capped with cracked asphalt and stubborn dandelions. They tore it down in ’93. Said it was “hazardous.” Funny word. Hazardous *now*, after thirty years of men going down in cages that smelled of hot iron and sweat and the sweet, sour tang of damp timber. Back then, hazard was just Tuesday.  

I walked the haul road last week—not all the way, just to the old change-house door. Still hangs crooked on one hinge. Inside: floorboards warped, light coming through the roof where the corrugated sheeting blew off in the ’72 gale. On the wall, chalked in shaky block letters: *Gus 12-4-68*. And below it, smaller: *Lunch pail left*. No date. No signature. Just that. I stood there, holding my breath, listening to the mice scuttle behind the collapsed locker bank. Felt stupid. Felt like trespassing on a grave nobody tends.  

They called it Black Diamond. Sounded fancy. Sounded like something you’d find in a jeweler’s case, not a hole two miles deep where the rock breathed back at you—hot, wet, thick with methane you could *taste*, metallic and old, like licking a battery wrapped in wet wool.  

Tommy Varga worked the third shift for twenty-one years. Never missed a day. Died of black lung at fifty-eight, coughing up clots the colour of motor oil. His wife kept his lunch pail. Tin, dented, lined with wax paper stained brown at the edges. She showed it to me once, opened it slow, like unwrapping something sacred. Inside: a bent spoon, a chipped thermos cup with “World’s Best Dad” half-scraped off, and a single, fossilized wedge of bologna, still curled at the corners. She didn’t say anything. Just closed it. Snapped the latch. *Click.*  

Some days, the air in the pit was so thick you had to chew it. Other days, cold enough your breath froze on the cage rails. I remember Frank Doherty—big man, hands like cured hams—coming up at shift end, peeling off his gloves, and blowing into his palms. Steam rising. Then he’d pull a small, folded square of newspaper from his pocket, unfold it carefully, and eat three cold, hard-boiled eggs, one at a time, without salt, without bread, just the eggs, the shell fragments caught in his stubble. He never explained why. Just did it. Every. Single. Day.  

The union hall’s a hair salon now. “Curls & Coal Dust” they call it—no, wait, that’s not right. *“Curls & Coiffure.”* But the sign’s crooked, same as the old hall sign used to be. And the woman who cuts hair there? Her dad was a trapper. Used to check the ventilation shafts. Told me once he’d hear the rats before he saw them—*skitter-scratch, skitter-scratch*—like tiny pickaxes on the brick. Said they sounded hopeful.  

We buried Charlie Rourke in ‘81. Fell into a void behind the longwall. Took three days to bring him up. They wrapped him in canvas, not a coffin—too narrow for the cage, they said. His boots were still on. Left foot only. Right boot came off somewhere in the fall. We found it wedged in a rib support, sole worn smooth, laces tied tight. Nobody untied them. Just carried the boot home in a coffee can. His widow kept it on the mantel for seventeen years. Then one morning, she put it in the stove. Lit a match. Didn’t watch it burn. Went out to feed the chickens.  

There’s no monument. No plaque. Just this: a faded sticker on the back window of a pickup parked by the access road—*“Black Diamond Miners Local 147 — 1942–1991”*—peeling at the corners, half-obscured by mud and rain streaks.  

I keep thinking about the lamps. Not the electric ones—the carbide. How you’d strike the flint, that sharp *tink*, and hold the wick close until the blue-white flame caught, steady and fierce, burning acetylene, bright enough to see the veins in your own hand, bright enough to cast your shadow huge and trembling on the rib wall. That light didn’t just show you the coal. It showed you *yourself*, down there—small, breathing, temporary.  

The ground here still sighs sometimes. A low groan, deep, felt more than heard. Old-timers say it’s the seams settling. Or the ghosts shifting. Or just the earth remembering the weight of all those men, going down, going down, going down—  
and the terrible, beautiful fact that they *did*.  

Not for glory. Not for history.  
For the pay envelope. For the kid’s braces. For the furnace oil. For the quiet pride in a straight-backed walk, even when the spine ached like hellfire.  

The gate’s locked.  
The dust keeps falling.  
I spit on the gravel.  
It doesn’t stain.

title: folk tale|the miller's third son and the talking millstone
text:
The millstone spoke again—not with a voice like wind through reeds or water over gravel, but with the low, resonant hum of stone settling after centuries of turning, layered with the dry rasp of grinding grain. “You’re the third,” it said, and the words vibrated up through the soles of Finn’s bare feet, making his molars ache. He hadn’t meant to touch it. Had only knelt to wipe flour-dust from the axle pin, his fingers brushing the cold, grooved rim where the ancient iron band met the granite face. Now the whole wheel seemed to hold its breath—no creak of timber, no sigh of the river beyond the millrace, not even the flutter of the sparrow that had nested in the rafters all spring.

Finn drew back, but his hand remained hovering, palm-out, as if stilled by an unseen thread. “Third son,” he echoed, voice thin as sifted bran. “Aye. My brothers took the silver cup and the map to the salt mines. I got the mill—and this.” He gestured helplessly at the great stone, its surface etched with spirals worn smooth by time and wheat, its center a dark, hollow eye.

“Not *this*,” the millstone corrected, and a tremor ran through its mass—not violent, but deep, like a sigh drawn from bedrock. “This is *me*. And you are the first in seventy-three years who has touched me without fear… or greed. Your brothers flinched when the dust puffed off my rim. Called me ‘cold’ and ‘hungry’. They never heard me breathe.”

Finn swallowed. His throat tasted of river-mist and old flour. “What do you breathe?”

“Memory,” the stone said. “And weight. And waiting.”

Then, without warning, the millstone *turned*—not on its axle, not with the river’s pull, but inward, like a slow, deliberate blink. A section of its outer rim—a slab no bigger than a loom shuttle—swung aside with a sound like a mountain shifting its shoulder. Behind it lay not darkness, but a soft, amber light, warm as honeyed mead, and the scent of sun-baked barley and crushed mint. A doorway. Not carved, not built—*revealed*.

“Step in,” the stone murmured. “But know this: the mill does not grind grain alone. It grinds *time*. And what lies within is not a place, but a moment—held, unspooled, waiting for the right hand to turn the handle.”

Finn hesitated. His father’s warnings echoed: *Stones don’t speak, boy. If they do, they lie. Or hunger.* But the stone’s voice held no malice—only a weariness older than the oak beams holding up the roof, a patience deeper than the river’s current. And Finn, who’d spent his life listening to the mill’s rhythms—the groan of the hopper, the whisper of chaff, the steady, soporific *shush-shush-shush* of stone on stone—knew this was no trick. This was the mill’s truest voice, finally unmasked.

He stepped through.

The air changed. Thicker. Warmer. The scent of barley sharpened, mixed now with woodsmoke and damp wool. He stood not in a cavern, but in a sun-drenched barn loft—dust motes dancing in golden shafts slanting through high windows. Below, through a gap in the floorboards, he saw not the mill’s waterwheel, but a wide, slow river, its banks lined with willows heavy with catkins. A woman sat on a low stool, her back to him, weaving straw into a delicate basket. Her hair, the colour of ripe wheat, fell over one shoulder. She hummed—a tune Finn knew, though he’d never heard it sung: the lullaby his mother used to croon, the one that always ended with a sigh and a tear she’d quickly brush away.

His breath caught. *Mother.*

But she was younger than he remembered—her hands strong and sure, not knotted with rheumatism; her shoulders straight, not bowed by the weight of three sons and a failing mill. He took a step forward, the old floorboard groaning softly beneath his boot.

She didn’t turn. Didn’t pause her weaving. But her humming faltered, just for a heartbeat, then resumed—softer now, almost questioning.

“Who’s there?” she asked, her voice clear as a bell rung in spring air.

Finn opened his mouth, but no sound came. His throat closed tight, not with fear, but with the sheer, staggering *presence* of her—alive, vibrant, *here*, in a moment he’d only known as a faded story told in hushed tones by the hearth. He’d been six when she died—fever, swift and cruel, burning through the village like dry grass. He remembered the smell of bitter herbs, the cold weight of her hand in his, the terrible silence after the last rattle in her chest.

“You’re not lost,” she said, still not looking up, her fingers deftly tucking a strand of straw. “The millstone only opens for those who carry its weight in their bones. You carry mine.”

“How do you know me?” Finn whispered, the words raw.

She smiled, a small, knowing thing that crinkled the corners of her eyes. “I wove your first cradle basket. I ground the flour for your first loaf. I listened to your first cry echo off these very stones.” She finally turned, and Finn’s heart hammered against his ribs. Her eyes were the same—deep brown, flecked with gold—but they held a quiet, luminous certainty he’d never seen in the woman who’d faded in that sickroom. “The millstone remembers every grain it’s ground, every sigh it’s absorbed, every tear shed on its rim. It remembers *me*. And it remembers *you*, Finn. Not the boy who wept, but the man who stands here now, barefoot and breathing, asking the stone to speak.”

She rose, setting the half-finished basket aside. “It doesn’t offer answers, Finn. It offers *witness*. It holds the weight so you don’t have to break beneath it alone.” She walked to the edge of the loft, gazing down at the river. “Your brothers sought riches. You sought… what? To keep the mill turning? To prove you weren’t the least?”

“I sought,” Finn said, the truth rising like dough, “to hear her voice again.”

She turned back, her gaze gentle. “Then listen. Not to me. To the stone. Its voice isn’t in the words. It’s in the *grind*. In the slow, patient turning. In the way it takes the hard, the broken, the bitter—and makes it nourishing. That is its magic. Not speaking. *Sustaining*.”

As she spoke, the amber light began to soften, the scent of mint fading, the warmth receding like tide from shore. The barn loft blurred at the edges, the dust motes slowing, then stilling.

“The moment is held,” she said, her form growing translucent, woven straw dissolving into light. “Not to trap you. To remind you. You are not the third son left with nothing. You are the one who stayed. Who listened. Who *touches*.”

The light flared, warm and blinding.

Finn blinked.

He stood once more in the mill, knees gritty with flour, hand still hovering over the cold, silent rim of the millstone. The river chuckled outside. A sparrow chirped in the rafters. Dawn light, pale and tentative, slanted through the high window, catching motes of dust dancing in the air—just as they had in the loft.

The millstone was still. Utterly, profoundly still.

But Finn didn’t step back. He lowered his hand, not in fear, but in quiet reverence, and placed his palm flat against the cool, grooved granite. He felt no vibration, no hum—only the deep, solid, ancient calm of stone.

Yet beneath his palm, something else thrummed. Faint. Steady. Like the first, slow pulse of a heart waking after long sleep.

He closed his eyes.

And for the first time since his mother’s death, Finn didn’t hear absence.

He heard the millstone breathe.

title: memoir|a father's ledger found after his death
text:
In the quiet of an afternoon, under a sky heavy with clouds that promised rain, I found it tucked away in the back of his old desk, a relic from another era. The ledger, bound in cracked leather, its pages yellowed and brittle, was a testament to time, a silent witness to the years my father had spent meticulously documenting every detail of our lives. It wasn’t just a book; it was a map, a diary, a confessional, and a ledger all at once.

The first entries were dated from the early 1970s, when he and my mother were newly married, their dreams as vast and uncharted as the future. Each page was a grid, filled with neat, precise handwriting, the kind that spoke of a man who took pride in order and control. He recorded everything: the cost of groceries, the dates of doctor’s appointments, the milestones of their early marriage. There were notes about the car repairs, the mortgage payments, and the occasional splurge on a night out. But interspersed among these mundane details were fragments of their conversations, snippets of laughter, and the occasional poem or quote, as if he couldn’t help but capture the beauty of their life together.

As I turned the pages, the years marched on. The entries grew more frequent, more detailed, and the handwriting became slightly less rigid, as if the act of writing had become a comfort, a ritual. My birth was marked with a simple, “Son born. 8 lbs. 2 oz. Perfect.” But the margins around that entry were filled with sketches of tiny hands and feet, and a few lines of a lullaby. The years that followed were a tapestry of childhood memories, each one carefully recorded. There were notes about my first steps, my first words, the day I lost my first tooth. He wrote about the books we read together, the games we played, and the long walks we took, his observations so vivid that I could almost feel the warmth of those summer evenings.

But the ledger also held darker moments, times when the weight of the world seemed to press down on him. There were entries about financial struggles, arguments with my mother, and the slow, painful realization that some dreams would remain unfulfilled. In the margins, he wrote of his fears, his doubts, and his hopes for the future. These entries, written in a smaller, more hurried script, were like whispers, secrets shared only with the pages.

As I delved deeper into the ledger, I saw the transformation of a young, ambitious man into a father, a provider, and, eventually, a grandfather. The later entries, from the last few years of his life, were sparse, the handwriting shaky. He wrote less about money and more about the people he loved. There were notes about my children, his grandchildren, and the joy they brought into his life. He wrote about the small moments, the ones that often go unnoticed: the way the sunlight filtered through the leaves, the sound of birds singing in the morning, the taste of a perfectly ripe peach. These entries, though fewer, were filled with a profound sense of gratitude and contentment.

On the last page, there was a final entry, written just days before he passed. It was a simple note, a reminder to himself, and perhaps to us, to find joy in the everyday. “Life is short,” he wrote. “Love deeply, laugh often, and never forget the small things.”

I closed the ledger, feeling a mix of sorrow and gratitude. It was a bittersweet discovery, this ledger, a window into a life that was both ordinary and extraordinary. It was a reminder of the man my father was, and the legacy he left behind. As I placed the ledger back in the drawer, I knew that I would return to it, again and again, to find solace in the familiar handwriting, to relive the memories, and to remember the lessons he had taught me, not through grand gestures, but through the quiet, steady love that filled the pages of his ledger.

title: nature essay|a winter of watching one heron on the same canal
text:
The Heron at the Lock

It began in November, not with fanfare but with a subtraction: the mallards vanished, then the coots, then the last pair of moorhens, their frantic peeping silenced by the first real frost. The canal—narrow, brick-lined, choked with silt and the drowned skeletons of reeds—had been my habitual detour for years, a damp corridor between the city’s edge and the ragged woods beyond. But that winter, something held me there. Not the heron itself, at first, but the *absence* it occupied so precisely.

He stood on the east bank, just upstream of the old lock gate, where the water slowed and pooled, black and still as cold oil. Not a great blue, not a grey—just *a heron*. A single, unadorned *Ardea cinerea*, its plumage the colour of wet slate and dust, its neck folded into a loose, deliberate kink. No drama in his posture, no theatrical stillness. He simply *was* there, like a stone placed by an indifferent hand.

I began watching him not out of reverence, but because he was the only fixed point in a landscape that felt increasingly provisional. Frost didn’t linger long on the canal’s surface; it formed a brittle skin at dawn, then surrendered to the sluggish current by mid-morning, leaving only a greasy sheen and the smell of wet brick and decaying weed. The air tasted metallic, sharp with the tang of frozen mud and distant diesel. My own breath plumed, then dissolved—a brief, futile signature against the grey.

He didn’t acknowledge me. Not with a glance, not with a shift of weight. His eyes, pale yellow and deeply set, scanned the water’s surface with a patience that felt less like waiting and more like *recognition*: this is the water, this is the light, this is the depth where the small things move. I learned his rhythms. At dawn, he’d be standing, head low, one leg drawn up, the other planted deep in the muck. By noon, he might wade three slow steps, each movement a studied transfer of mass, a hinge of knee and ankle clicking almost audibly over the water’s hush. He never flew unless startled—then a violent, ungainly lurch, wings beating hard and low, a sound like wet canvas tearing—and always returned within the hour, settling back onto the same patch of bank, as if the interruption had been a minor correction in a longer calculation.

I brought binoculars, then stopped using them. They flattened him, made him a specimen under glass. Better to watch with the naked eye, to see the way the weak sun caught the faint, almost invisible barring on his secondary feathers, or how the wind, when it rose, ruffled the downy plumes at his nape—not like a flourish, but like dust disturbed on a shelf. His stillness wasn’t emptiness. It was dense. It held the weight of the water he watched, the chill of the air, the slow decay of the submerged alder roots beside him. He seemed less a creature *in* the winter than a concentration *of* it—its austerity, its patience, its quiet, relentless metabolism.

One afternoon, thick snow fell—not the feathery kind, but heavy, wet flakes that clung to his back, melting instantly into dark, irregular patches. He didn’t shake. Didn’t flinch. Just stood, a grey smudge against the white bank, steam rising faintly from his shoulders. I thought of warmth, of blood moving beneath that damp feathering, of the fierce, compact furnace of his small body sustaining itself against the drain of cold. It wasn’t heroism. It was simple, unremarkable biology. Yet watching him endure the snow’s slow, insistent weight felt like witnessing a kind of quiet, stubborn grammar: *this is how life persists, not by defiance, but by absorption.*

There were days I didn’t go. Rain turned the towpath into a slick of black mud. Sleet stung the face. Once, a week passed, and I found him gone. Not vanished—just absent from his station. My pulse quickened, absurdly. Had he fallen? Been taken? Then, two days later, there he was again, standing exactly where he’d been, as if the absence had been a punctuation mark, not a break in the sentence. I felt foolish, then ashamed of my foolishness. His continuity wasn’t for me. It was incidental. He hadn’t waited. He hadn’t returned for my benefit. He’d simply resumed his place in the water’s slow, necessary rhythm.

The thaw came late, a reluctant seep rather than a surge. Ice cracked with soft, subterranean sighs. The water level rose, inch by muddy inch, pushing the heron further up the bank. One morning, he was gone. Not the abrupt departure of before, but a gradual withdrawal. First, he stood further back, on drier ground. Then, he was seen near the weir, where the current ran stronger. Then, not at all. I walked the towpath for days, scanning the banks, the reedbeds, the open water. Nothing. The canal filled with the tentative, grubby green of new shoots. A pair of coots returned, paddling furiously, their chicks like damp, black pebbles bobbing behind them.

I still walk the canal. The water flows. The bricks are damp. The reeds are taller now, greener, louder with insects. Sometimes, I catch myself scanning the east bank, just upstream of the lock gate. Habit, not hope. There’s no lesson in his absence, no tidy epiphany about transience or resilience. He wasn’t a symbol. He was a heron, doing what herons do: occupying space, metabolising cold, watching water, surviving until he didn’t. His presence was a fact, not a parable. His departure, another fact. The canal remains, neither sadder nor wiser, just holding the memory of his stillness in the silt, in the angle of the light on the water, in the particular way the brickwork weathers where he once stood.

I don’t miss him. But I notice, sometimes, how the light falls on that stretch of bank at dawn—the flat, silver-grey light—and how utterly empty it looks. Not peaceful. Not desolate. Just empty. As if the space he occupied hadn’t been filled, hadn’t been erased, but simply… left. And that, perhaps, is the most accurate thing I know about winter, or about watching, or about the quiet, unceremonious passing of one living thing through the indifferent, enduring world.

title: memoir|working nights in a hospital kitchen at nineteen
text:
The fluorescent lights in the basement kitchen of St. Brigid’s Hospital in South Bend, Indiana, didn’t hum—they groaned. A low, persistent thrum that vibrated up through the rubber soles of my worn Keds and settled behind my molars. It was 2:17 a.m. on a Thursday in November 1998, and I was nineteen, stirring a vat of oatmeal that had long since surrendered its porridge integrity and become a lukewarm, viscous slurry flecked with burnt sugar crystals from the bottom of the steam table. My hair was pinned under a paper cap I’d folded crookedly, one bobby pin already missing; a smear of butter—cold, greasy—streaked my left temple.

I’d started three weeks earlier, hired off a bulletin board near the LaSalle Street bus depot after my shift at the Red Lobster got cut to six hours. Sister Agnes, the food service director, had interviewed me in her office smelling of Lysol and stale peppermints, her habit rustling like dry leaves as she asked if I could lift thirty pounds. I lied and said yes. She handed me a clipboard with a laminated schedule: *0000–0800. Kitchen Support. Report to Mr. Ruiz.*  

His name was Hector Ruiz—not “Mr. Ruiz,” not even “Hector.” Just *Ruiz*, spoken with the clipped finality of someone who’d spent twenty-three years feeding the dying, the drugged, the disoriented, and never once been thanked for it. He stood five-foot-four in steel-toed boots, his forearms corded with old burns and the kind of muscle that doesn’t flex—it just *is*. His apron was stained black at the cuffs, the fabric stiff with decades of splashed broth and dried gravy. Every night at 1:45 a.m., he’d appear at the double doors, push them open with his hip, and say, without looking up from his thermos, “Oatmeal. Not glue. Not soup. Oatmeal.”  

That night, I’d over-scraped the caramelized sugar from the griddle while making French toast for the early-shift nurses’ lounge. Ruiz caught me licking the spatula. He didn’t yell. He just set his thermos down—*clack*—and pointed at the industrial dishwasher. “Rinse. Then re-rinse. Then rinse again. That sugar sticks like grief.” He paused, wiped his nose with the back of his wrist. “You ever see a man cry over cold oatmeal? Not cry *because* of it. Cry *into* it. Like it’s the only thing warm left.”  

I hadn’t. But I saw it two nights later, when Mr. Delaney—Room 412, stage IV pancreatic—was brought down in a wheelchair by a night nurse named Keisha, who’d wrapped an extra blanket around his shoulders and tucked it tight under his chin. He sat at the small Formica table near the walk-in, shivering, his hands trembling so badly he couldn’t hold the spoon. Ruiz didn’t bring him a new bowl. He brought a clean spoon, wiped the handle with a hot towel, and knelt beside the chair. “Let’s get this right,” he said, his voice lower than usual, almost tender. He guided Mr. Delaney’s hand, his own fingers wrapping gently over the knuckles, and lifted the spoon together—slow, deliberate—to the man’s mouth. Mr. Delaney swallowed. Closed his eyes. A single tear tracked through the stubble on his cheek, catching the sickly yellow light. Ruiz didn’t wipe it away. He just held the spoon steady until the man nodded, faintly, and let go.  

The prep list was always handwritten on a grease-smeared legal pad taped to the stainless-steel counter: *32 turkey sandwiches (no mustard, per Dr. Vance), 17 bowls chicken rice (low sodium, no parsley), 6 jello cups (peach, soft diet, *not* cherry—cherry stains the teeth, makes them look bruised).* I learned the difference between “soft diet” and “pureed”—how applesauce needed to pass through a chinois twice, how mashed potatoes required whole milk, not skim, or they’d congeal into grey lumps by dawn. I learned that Mrs. Cho in 307 liked her tea brewed exactly four minutes, then poured over ice *before* adding honey, never after—“or the honey sinks, and the first sip is bitter, and the last is sweet, and life shouldn’t be like that.” She told me that every night, sitting upright in her wheelchair, wrapped in a quilt stitched with tiny blue cranes.  

At 5:58 a.m., Ruiz would shut off the steam tables. The lights dimmed slightly—the building’s circadian rhythm kicking in, the overheads shifting to a paler, less insistent white. We’d mop. Not sweep. *Mop.* Twice. Front to back, overlapping strokes, no puddles. He’d hand me the mop bucket, full of hot water and Pine-Sol so sharp it made my sinuses ache. “Water’s hot,” he’d say. “Not because it cleans better. Because it reminds you you’re still warm.”  

One morning, after a blizzard had buried the city and the backup generator whined all night like a trapped dog, I found Ruiz sitting on an overturned milk crate behind the walk-in, smoking a cigarette he wasn’t supposed to smoke, the tip glowing orange in the dimness. Steam rose from his coffee cup. He didn’t offer me one. Didn’t ask if I was tired. Just watched the condensation crawl down the freezer door and said, “My wife used to work here. In radiology. Before the MS took her hands. She’d come down sometimes, just to watch me plate the tuna salad. Said it was the only thing in the hospital that looked like food instead of medicine.” He tapped ash into the toe of his boot. “She died last Tuesday. Didn’t tell anyone. Didn’t need to.”  

I nodded. Didn’t speak. The groan of the lights filled the silence. Outside, the first ambulance siren rose, thin and urgent, then faded toward the ER entrance. Ruiz crushed the cigarette under his heel, stood, and walked back to the line. “Oatmeal,” he said, as if nothing had passed between us. “Not glue. Not soup. Oatmeal.”  

I stirred. The spoon scraped the bottom of the vat, a sound like bone on metal. A drop of sweat fell from my hairline and vanished into the grey swirl. Somewhere upstairs, a monitor beeped—steady, insistent, utterly indifferent. I kept stirring.

title: fable|a crow who collects lost keys
text:
...and so, the crow perched high above the bustling town square, its keen eyes scanning the sea of people below. In its beak, a gleaming silver key dangled, catching the light of the midday sun. The townsfolk hurried about their daily business, unaware that a silent guardian watched over them from the rooftops, keeping a careful inventory of all that was lost and forgotten.

For years, the crow had made it its mission to collect these misplaced keys. It began one rainy afternoon when the bird stumbled upon a small, ornate key half-buried in the mud. Curiosity piqued, the crow picked it up with its beak and carried it to its nest. As days passed, the crow found more and more keys, each with its own story, each a small piece of someone’s life left behind. The collection grew, and soon, the crow's nest was a glittering trove of metal and memories.

The crow’s reputation spread, and the townspeople began to whisper of a mysterious key-keeper who roamed the skies. Some said it was a spirit, others a guardian angel, but only a few knew the truth. The children were the first to catch on, often leaving out small offerings of bread and seeds, hoping to catch a glimpse of the elusive crow. Over time, even the adults came to believe that if you lost something precious, the crow might just return it to you, as long as your heart was pure and your intentions good.

One day, a young girl named Elara approached the town square, her face etched with worry. She had lost the key to her grandmother’s antique music box, a family heirloom passed down through generations. The box played a melody that had comforted her since childhood, and without the key, it remained silent. Elara had searched everywhere, retracing her steps, but the key seemed to have vanished into thin air.

As she sat on a bench, tears welling in her eyes, the crow noticed her distress. It had seen this look before, a mixture of frustration and sorrow, and it knew it had to help. With a swift, graceful dive, the crow swooped down and landed beside her, the silver key still clutched in its beak. Elara gasped, her eyes widening in surprise and hope.

“Is that… my key?” she asked, her voice trembling with emotion.

The crow cocked its head, its eyes sparkling with intelligence. It hopped closer, gently placing the key at Elara’s feet. The girl reached out hesitantly, her fingers closing around the cool metal. As she lifted the key, a sense of relief washed over her, and a smile spread across her face. She looked up, meeting the crow’s gaze, and whispered, “Thank you.”

From that day forward, Elara became the crow’s closest friend. She would visit the town square every afternoon, bringing treats and sharing stories. The crow, in turn, would bring her keys it had found, and together, they would try to reunite them with their rightful owners. The bond between the two grew stronger, and the town began to see the crow not just as a collector of keys, but as a symbol of hope and kindness.

But not everyone in the town shared this sentiment. A grumpy old man named Mr. Grindle, who owned a locksmith shop, saw the crow as a threat to his business. He resented the bird for finding and returning keys, which meant fewer customers for him. One day, he decided to take matters into his own hands. Armed with a net, he set out to capture the crow and put an end to its meddling.

Elara, sensing something was amiss, followed Mr. Grindle at a distance. She watched as he climbed onto the roof of a nearby building, carefully positioning the net. Just as the crow landed, Mr. Grindle lunged, but the bird, quick and agile, dodged out of the way. It cawed loudly, a sound that echoed through the square, drawing the attention of the townspeople.

Elara rushed to the crow’s side, shouting, “Stop! You can’t do this!” The crowd gathered, murmuring in disapproval. Mr. Grindle, red-faced and flustered, tried to justify his actions, but the townspeople would hear none of it. They rallied around the crow, forming a protective circle, and Mr. Grindle, seeing the support for the bird, slunk away, defeated.

In the aftermath, the town came together, realizing the value of the crow’s work. They built a small shelter for the bird, where it could rest and keep its collection safe. The crow, grateful for the kindness, continued its mission, now with the full support of the community. And Elara, with the crow by her side, learned that sometimes, the smallest acts of kindness could make the biggest difference in the world.

title: memoir|working nights in a hospital kitchen at nineteen
text:
The fluorescent lights hummed—not a steady tone, but a wavering, insectile whine that settled behind the molars and vibrated in the hollows beneath the eyes. I was nineteen, and the hospital kitchen smelled of bleach, boiled cabbage, and something deeper, older: the faint, metallic tang of blood that had seeped into grout and never quite left, no matter how many times the night crew scrubbed. My uniform—a stiff, starched white jacket with epaulets fraying at the shoulders—had already yellowed at the cuffs from repeated washings and the steam of industrial ovens. I’d stolen it from a locker labeled *R. Delaney*, though she’d quit three weeks prior, her name still taped crookedly to the metal door like a forgotten epitaph.

My shift began at 10:30 p.m., when the last cafeteria tray clattered into the dish pit and the day staff vanished into the humid August night, leaving behind coffee rings on Formica and a silence so thick it felt like walking into cold water. The night kitchen wasn’t for patients—it was for the keepers: nurses pulling double shifts, residents with caffeine in their veins and exhaustion in their knuckles, orderlies who moved through corridors like shadows with stretchers and linen carts. We fed the machinery that kept the hospital breathing while the rest of the city slept.

I learned the rhythm before the recipes. The clatter of stainless steel pans hitting the prep table at exactly 11:07 p.m., always, because Marta—the night supervisor, sixty-two, with forearms corded like rope and a silver hairpin shaped like a stork—refused to be late for anything, least of all the first batch of oatmeal. She’d stand over the giant steam kettle, stirring counterclockwise with a wooden paddle worn smooth by decades, her mouth a thin line, eyes scanning the room like a general surveying trenches. “Oatmeal isn’t porridge,” she’d say, not unkindly, but with finality, “it’s armor. It holds.” And so we made it thick, lumpy with raisins plumped in hot water, served in dented aluminum bowls stamped with the hospital’s faded logo—a caduceus half-erased by years of dishwashing.

At 2:14 a.m., the call came over the intercom—crackling, urgent—“Code Blue, 4 West, repeat, Code Blue”—and the kitchen didn’t pause. But Marta paused her stirring. Just for two seconds. Then she nodded once, turned off the burner, and reached for the thermos of strong black coffee she kept behind the flour bin, its surface warm from constant refills. She poured two cups, handed one to me, and we stood side by side at the pass-through window, watching the hallway lights flicker as runners in scrubs blurred past, gurneys squealing on linoleum. No words. Just the steam rising between us, thin and transient.

I peeled potatoes in the pre-dawn hours, my fingers raw and pruned, knuckles split where the cold water and sodium hydroxide from the dishwasher rinse cycle had gnawed at the skin. The peeler was dull, deliberately so—Marta said a sharp blade made you careless, and carelessness got people hurt, even here, even with potatoes. I’d watch the shavings curl and fall into the slop bucket, translucent and fragile, like discarded membranes. Sometimes, a nurse would slip in, hair escaping her bun, eyes red-rimmed, and lean against the counter while I sliced apples for the breakfast trays. She wouldn’t speak, just exhale, long and slow, as if releasing something heavy she’d been holding since midnight. Once, she rested her forehead against the cool tile wall, and I handed her a slice of apple without looking up. She ate it standing there, juice running down her wrist, and when she left, she left behind a single glove, pale blue, still faintly warm.

The dish pit was worse than the prep. Steam rose in thick, wet veils; the water scalded at 180 degrees, and the detergent left a film on the skin that no amount of soap could lift. I’d load trays—stained with egg yolk, smeared with jam, crusted with congealed gravy—and feed them into the machine’s maw. Its roar was deafening, a mechanical beast swallowing evidence of hunger, of life, of small comforts taken in haste. Occasionally, a tray would jam. You’d have to reach in, past the curtain of heat, past the hissing jets, and pry it free with tongs. Your arm would emerge dripping, skin pink, smelling of grease and chlorine.

At 5:45 a.m., just before the day shift arrived, we baked muffins—blueberry, bran, occasionally chocolate chip, though Marta called those “distractions” and only allowed them on days when the ICU had discharged three patients before dawn. The oven light glowed amber, casting long, trembling shadows across the floor. I’d pull the racks out, feel the radiant heat bloom on my face, and watch the muffins rise, golden and uneven, tops cracking like miniature landscapes. They cooled on wire racks, steam lifting in quiet spirals, and we’d wrap them in wax paper, tie them with twine, label them with masking tape and a Sharpie: *For 3 East, Night Nurses, Please*. No names. Just function.

When my shift ended at 6:30 a.m., the sky was the color of weak tea—pale, hesitant, washed out. I’d step outside, blinking, squinting at the world as if emerging from underwater. The air smelled of dew and exhaust, of damp pavement and distant coffee shops beginning to grind beans. My hands trembled slightly—not from fatigue, exactly, but from the sudden absence of motion, the abrupt silence after hours of clanging, steaming, stirring. I’d walk home past shuttered bodegas and sleeping laundromats, my shoes squeaking on wet concrete, the weight of the night still lodged in my ribs, dense and quiet, like something swallowed and not yet digested. The city was waking, but I was still inside the hum, still hearing the whistle of the pressure cooker, still feeling the ghost of Marta’s hand on my shoulder when I dropped a tray, still tasting the salt of my own sweat mixed with the faint, persistent iron of the place where the living and the almost-gone shared the same air, the same steam, the same stubborn, necessary warmth.

title: free verse poem sequence|a year of weather in one valley
text:
Valley Almanac: A Year in the Fold  

I. January  
The valley doesn’t freeze—it *settles*. Not like water locking into glass, but like dust settling after a long tremor. Frost doesn’t bloom on the barn roof; it *crawls*, a slow, silver fungus along the eaves, brittle at the edges, damp and grey at the heart. The creek doesn’t ice over solid. It breathes—thin, black water threading through fractured plates of ice that groan at dawn, not with violence, but with the weary sigh of something holding its shape just a little longer than it wants to. My boots sink past the crust into snow that’s neither powder nor slush, but a granular, sugar-fine grit packed by wind from the north ridge. It doesn’t sparkle. It absorbs light, swallowing the weak sun whole. I watch a crow land on the frozen manure pile behind the shed—not for food, but because the surface is smooth, cold, and utterly indifferent. It tilts its head. No caw. Just the dry rattle of wings adjusting. Later, I find a single deer track pressed deep into the snow near the alder thicket—no exit. Just the print, sharp as a knife-cut, then nothing. The animal didn’t leave. It stood. Then stopped standing.  

II. April  
The thaw isn’t gentle. It’s a sullen, seeping surrender. Snowmelt doesn’t run; it *leaks*—brown, viscous, smelling of wet clay and buried roots. The ground exhales a sour, fungal breath. Ditches fill not with clear water, but with a suspension: silt, shredded bark, the translucent, gelatinous husks of last autumn’s earthworms. One morning, the creek rises three feet overnight, not roaring, but *bulging*, its surface thick with foam the colour of weak tea and old dishwater. It carries a fallen birch branch, stripped bare, rotating slowly, endlessly, caught in an eddy just below the stone bridge. I stand there for twenty minutes. The branch doesn’t free itself. It doesn’t need to. It’s exactly where the current put it.  

III. June  
Heat arrives not as a wave, but as a pressure change—a sudden, dense stillness that presses down on the valley floor until even the cicadas seem to hesitate mid-chirp. The air tastes metallic, charged, tasting of ozone and the iron tang of the old mine tailings up on the west slope. Wild roses bloom, yes—but their scent is thin, almost medicinal, cut through by the sharper, greener smell of crushed ferns underfoot. One afternoon, a storm gathers not in the sky, but *in the trees*: the pines go utterly silent. Not quiet, but *vacant*. Then, the first drop hits the dry oak leaf beside me—not a plink, but a soft, hollow *thud*, like a pebble dropped into a tin can. Rain follows, not in sheets, but in heavy, spaced drops, each one leaving a dark, expanding bruise on the dust. By dusk, the air is cool again, but the dampness lingers—not refreshing, just *present*, a weight on the skin.  

IV. August  
Drought isn’t absence. It’s a slow, insistent *presence*. The creek shrinks to a thread of tarnished silver, then to a chain of stagnant, green-black pools separated by stretches of cracked, grey mud that fissures like ancient pottery. Cattails at the marsh edge curl inward, their brown tips brittle, snapping off at a touch. The grass on the south-facing slopes isn’t golden; it’s the colour of old bone, bleached and porous. One evening, walking the lower pasture, I see a hawk hover, motionless, ten feet above the ground. Not hunting. Just *holding*. Its wings don’t beat. They barely tremble. It hangs there, suspended in the thick, hot air, until the light shifts and it simply… dissolves into the haze. No descent. No flight. Just gone.  

V. October  
Frost returns, but differently—sharper, hungrier. It doesn’t creep; it *etches*. One night, it draws intricate, branching patterns on the inside of my bedroom window, not like lace, but like the fine, branching cracks in a dried riverbed. Outside, the maples don’t blaze. They *fade*: crimson leaching into rust, then ochre, then a dull, papery brown that clings stubbornly, refusing to fall. Wind doesn’t shake them loose; it *peels* them, layer by brittle layer, revealing the grey, knotted wood beneath. The first hard frost kills the last of the asters—not with a wilt, but with a sudden, chalky pallor, as if the colour has been vacuumed out of them overnight. Their stems remain upright, hollow, rattling faintly in the breeze like tiny, dry bones.  

VI. December  
Snow falls again, but this time it’s different. Not the granular January stuff, but fat, wet flakes that cling, then melt on contact, then refreeze into a treacherous, transparent glaze on every surface—the fence rails, the tractor tires, the low branches of the hawthorn. It’s not beautiful. It’s treacherous. It makes the world feel unmoored, slippery, unreliable. At dusk, the valley fills with fog—not the soft, rolling kind, but a dense, pearlescent bank that rises from the creek bed and swallows the lower fields whole, leaving only the tops of the oaks visible, like islands in a slow, silent sea. I walk to the edge of the fog line. The air is warm, damp, smelling of decay and cold stone. On the other side, the world is gone. Not hidden. *Absent*. I stand there, listening. There is no silence. Only the low, continuous *hush* of moisture condensing on a million unseen surfaces. It doesn’t sound like peace. It sounds like waiting. Or forgetting.  

The year doesn’t end. It folds. The valley holds its breath, then releases it—not as a sigh, but as a slow, deep exhalation of cold air down the east ravine. The cycle isn’t a circle. It’s a fold in cloth—creased, layered, holding the memory of pressure, the ghost of shape. Nothing resolves. Nothing concludes. The creek will thaw, the frost will etch, the fog will rise. But the valley remembers the weight of the drought, the silence before the rain, the exact, hollow *thud* of the first drop. It holds these things not as lessons, but as sediment—fine, persistent, unremarkable. Like the dust in the corners of the barn, like the slow, inevitable seep of water into the foundation stones. Like the way the crow tilted its head, and did not speak.
