title: myth retelling|the smith who forged the first bell
text:
In the heart of the ancient city of Eryndor, where the mountains met the sky and the rivers whispered secrets to the stones, there lived a blacksmith named Thaddeus. His forge was nestled in a narrow alley, its walls blackened by soot and the air thick with the scent of molten metal. Thaddeus was known throughout the land for his skill, but he had never faced a challenge quite like the one that came to him on a cold, misty morning.

A tall, gaunt figure wrapped in a dark cloak approached the forge. The man’s face was hidden in shadows, but his voice was clear and commanding. “Thaddeus,” he said, “I have heard of your legendary skill. I need you to forge something extraordinary—a bell, the first of its kind, to summon the spirits and guide the lost.”

Thaddeus, intrigued and slightly wary, asked, “Who are you, and why do you seek such a creation?”

The man stepped closer, revealing eyes that glowed with an otherworldly light. “I am called Malakai, and I am a guardian of the old ways. This bell will be a beacon, a bridge between the worlds. It must be perfect, for it will hold the power to call forth the spirits and protect the living.”

Thaddeus, though skeptical, was drawn to the challenge. He agreed, and Malakai left him with a single, enigmatic instruction: “The bell must be forged from the metal of the stars and the tears of the earth. Only then will it possess the power to bridge the realms.”

For days, Thaddeus pondered the riddle. He scoured the mountains for rare metals, and he delved into the depths of the earth, searching for the elusive materials. One night, as he stood atop a hill, gazing at the stars, a shooting star streaked across the sky, leaving a trail of fire. Thaddeus followed the path, and in the morning, he found a small, glowing fragment of celestial metal. 

Next, he sought the tears of the earth. In the deepest part of the forest, near a sacred spring, he discovered a stone that wept with a liquid that shimmered like moonlight. Thaddeus carefully collected the tears, feeling the weight of the task before him.

With the materials in hand, Thaddeus returned to his forge. The fire roared as he melted the celestial metal, and the tears of the earth were added, causing the molten metal to glow with an ethereal light. For hours, he hammered and shaped, pouring his soul into the work. The bell began to take form, and as it did, the air around the forge grew charged with an inexplicable energy.

Finally, after many sleepless nights, the bell was complete. It was a thing of beauty, its surface etched with intricate designs and symbols, and it emitted a soft, resonant hum. Thaddeus, exhausted but filled with a sense of accomplishment, rang the bell for the first time. The sound was unlike anything he had ever heard—deep, rich, and full of power. It seemed to resonate not just through the air, but through the very fabric of reality.

Malakai returned, his eyes widening in awe. “You have done it, Thaddeus. You have created something truly extraordinary.” He took the bell and held it aloft, and as he did, the air shimmered, and the spirits of the realm appeared, drawn by the sound. They swirled around the bell, their forms ethereal and beautiful, and Thaddeus felt a deep connection to the world beyond.

From that day forward, the bell was a symbol of hope and guidance, used to protect the people of Eryndor and to keep the balance between the living and the spirits. Thaddeus, though he continued to forge, knew that he had created something that would be remembered for generations to come. And in the quiet moments, when the bell’s gentle hum filled the air, he felt a profound sense of peace, knowing that he had bridged the worlds.

title: elegy in free verse|a closed coal mine and the men who worked it
text:
Elegy for the Black Diamond Shaft  

It’s quiet now. Not peaceful—*quiet*. Like the kind of silence that settles after someone stops breathing but before you’ve quite registered it. The headframe’s still there, rust bleeding down its steel ribs like old blood under thin skin. They didn’t tear it down. Too expensive, they said. Or maybe just too tired.  

I walked past yesterday—boots crunching on the slag heap, that brittle black gravel that never breaks down, never softens. Still smells faintly of sulfur and damp coal dust, even after thirty years. You’d think rain would wash it out. It doesn’t. It just sinks deeper.  

Dad worked here. Shift 2, from ’58 to ’83. Came home smelling like wet stone and sweat and something metallic—not iron, not copper—something *older*, like licking a battery wrapped in damp burlap. His hands were maps: knuckles swollen at the joints, nails permanently rimmed with grey, cuticles split and crusted. He’d soak them in lye soap and hot water every Sunday night, humming off-key, steam rising in little ghosts off the basin. I remember watching one hang there, trembling, then vanishing.  

The mine wasn’t deep—only 480 feet—but narrow. Tight as a coffin lid. They called it “the rabbit hole.” Men went in sideways sometimes, knees bent, helmet lamps cutting cones into the dark. No room to stand straight in the lower drifts. Just crawl, scrape, push.  

Old Man Hargrove told me once—he lost two fingers in the skip hoist in ’67—said the worst part wasn’t the noise or the heat or even the dust. It was the *weight*. Not the roof pressing down, but the weight of all that earth *above*, pressing *in*, like the whole county was holding its breath over your back. “You could feel it in your molars,” he said, tapping his own, yellow and cracked. “Like they’d hum, low, when the shift bell rang.”  

There were jokes, of course. Terrible ones. About the canaries—they kept three in cages near the ventilation shaft until ’72, when the last one keeled over mid-tweet and nobody laughed. After that, they used electronic sniffers. Cold blue lights blinking in the dark. Felt like being watched by something that didn’t care if you lived or not.  

I found a lunch pail last month in the tool shed behind the old company store—rust-eaten, dented on one side, the latch still stiff. Inside, folded tight in oilcloth: a grease-stained paper bag with the ghost of a peanut butter smear, a bent spoon, and a single, dried-up clove of garlic wrapped in wax paper. Must’ve been Tommy Varga’s. He always ate garlic—said it kept the “black lung” at bay. (It didn’t. He died in ’91, coughing up slurry that looked like wet ash.)  

They shut it down in November ’84. Not with fanfare. Not even a ceremony. Just a notice taped to the locker room door: *Operations suspended indefinitely.* Someone crossed out “indefinitely” and wrote “forever” in ballpoint, then smudged it with a thumb.  

Afterwards, the men stood around the parking lot like they’d forgotten how to walk home. Some lit cigarettes. One man—I think it was Eli Ritter—just sat on the fender of his pickup, staring at his boots, picking at a loose thread on his glove until the thread came free and he let it fall. Didn’t look at anyone. Didn’t speak. Just watched it drift down, caught in the wind off the ridge.  

The town tried. We got a “Heritage Park” sign last year. Granite slab, bronze plaque: *In Memory of the Miners of Black Diamond Shaft, 1912–1984.* Clean lettering. No mention of the strike in ’47, when they locked the gates for six weeks and the company doctor wouldn’t treat Billy Crowe’s crushed foot because “he wasn’t on payroll.” No mention of the methane pocket that killed seven in ’53—the official report blamed “unforeseen geological variance.” (We all knew what that meant: the surveyor was drunk. His name was on the payroll, too.)  

The school kids do projects. Draw pictures of helmets and pickaxes. One girl painted a mine entrance glowing gold inside, like heaven had a coal seam. I didn’t correct her.  

Sometimes, late at night, if the wind’s right—northwest, cold and dry—I swear I hear it. Not voices. Not machinery. Just a low, rhythmic *thump-thump-thump*, like a heart buried deep, still beating against the rock. Maybe it’s the old pump house settling. Maybe it’s just my ears ringing from years of silence.  

But I go down to the fence line anyway. Stand where the gate used to swing open at 6:15 a.m., steam rising from men’s shoulders, coffee steaming in tin mugs, breath pluming white as prayer.  

The grass grows thick now over the rail spur. Daisies push up through cracks in the concrete pad. A robin’s nest is wedged in the crook of the headframe’s upper brace—feathers and twigs, soft and stubborn.  

I don’t know what to say to the men who are gone. Not prayers. Not speeches. Just this:  

Your hands knew the shape of darkness better than most people know their own names.  
You carried the weight so the rest of us could walk upright.  
And when the lights went out—yours, and then the mine’s—you didn’t vanish.  
You’re in the rust. In the daisies. In the way the wind pauses, just once, before it crosses the ridge.  

That’s enough.  
For now.  
That’s enough.

title: prose poem|a kitchen at four in the morning
text:
The refrigerator hums, a low, persistent thrumming in the hollow of the house—like a sleeping animal’s breath, steady and slightly damp. Its light spills across the linoleum, yellowed at the seams, revealing dust motes suspended mid-air, trembling in the chill. The air smells of yesterday’s garlic, faint but insistent, layered over the metallic tang of the sink drain and the ghost of burnt toast from three mornings ago. A single coffee mug sits on the counter, handle facing east, its interior glazed with a dried crescent of brown, cracked like old riverbed clay. Inside it, a spoon rests sideways, bent slightly at the neck, as if it tired mid-stir.

The faucet drips. Not rhythmically—not quite—but in irregular intervals: *plink*… pause… *plink-plink*… longer pause… then nothing for nearly a minute, as if holding its breath. When it comes again, it startles a moth that has been clinging to the window screen, wings powdered silver-gray, trembling not from cold but from some ancient, unnameable vigil. Outside, the streetlamp casts a sodium-orange halo on the wet pavement, and beyond that, only blackness—not empty, but thick, dense, breathing in slow tides.

A wooden spoon lies abandoned in the ceramic bowl beside the stove. It’s stained near the bowl’s edge with turmeric, a faded sunburst of ochre. The bowl itself holds the remnants of dough—pale, slack, half-risen, its surface dimpled and soft as a child’s cheek. A film of flour dusts the countertop around it, fine as ground bone, catching the fridge-light like scattered ash. Near the toaster, a crumb trail leads in a hesitant arc toward the cabinet where the sugar lives. Not straight. Not purposeful. Just a quiet, granular migration, interrupted by the heel of a loaf left out overnight—its crust hardened into something brittle and honey-colored, its crumb still tender beneath, yielding with a soft sigh when pressed.

The clock above the stove reads 4:03. Its plastic digits glow faintly green, bleeding just a little at the edges, as though the light is seeping out of time itself. The second hand stutters—jumps forward, hesitates, jumps again—like a heart skipping under thin skin. No one is watching it. No one needs to. It ticks anyway, because ticking is what clocks do when no one listens.

A teakettle sits cold on the burner. Its spout is tilted slightly, as if listening. Its lid is askew, revealing the dull, water-stained interior. A single drop of condensation clings to the underside of the lid, swelling, trembling, gathering weight until—without sound—it falls onto the cold metal ring below, vanishing before it hits.

The floorboards near the pantry creak—not from pressure, but from settling. A slow exhalation of pine and glue and decades. In the pantry, a jar of mustard glows dully in the dark, its label peeling at the corners, the yellow inside thick and unmoving, like congealed sunlight. Next to it, a half-empty bag of rice sags at the seam, grains spilling in a tiny, precise mound onto the shelf—each one distinct in the low light, each one identical, each one waiting.

A dishrag hangs over the tap, twisted once, damp and heavy, its blue dye faded to the color of storm clouds before rain. One corner drags in the shallow puddle beneath the faucet, slowly darkening, absorbing the drip, drop by slow drop, as if drinking time itself.

The oven light is off. Its glass door reflects only the fridge’s glow and the vague, warped shape of the room behind—the counter, the chair pulled out just so, the back of a sweater draped over its rung, sleeves dangling like tired arms. On the chair seat, a single hair—dark, long, caught in the weave of the fabric—curled at the tip, holding its shape even now, even here, even at this hour.

Somewhere upstairs, a pipe groans. Not loudly. Not urgently. Just a deep, subterranean murmur, like stone shifting in its sleep. Then silence returns, deeper than before, as if the house has drawn the air inward, holding it.

The microwave clock blinks 12:00. It has blinked that way since the power flickered two nights ago. No one has pressed the buttons to reset it. It does not matter. Time here is not measured in hours but in states: the coolness of the tile under bare feet, the slight tackiness of the counter where syrup dried, the way steam rises from a forgotten pot left too long on the stove—now cold, now just a ring of white residue on the bottom, perfect and concentric.

A fly bumps softly against the windowpane—once, twice—then lands, legs splayed, antennae twitching, tasting the glass, tasting the dark beyond. Its wings are iridescent in the weak light, shifting from violet to black depending on the angle, like oil on water.

The kettle remains cold. The dough does not rise further. The drip continues. The moth settles again. The hair stays curled. The fridge hums. The house breathes. The light stays on—not bright, not warm, just present, like memory, like residue, like the afterimage of heat on skin long after the stove has gone cold. And the air, thick with absence, holds its breath—not waiting, not hoping—just holding, just being, just this: the quiet, the chill, the slow accumulation of small things, all luminous in their ordinariness, all suspended, all real, all here, at four in the morning, in the kitchen, where nothing happens and everything remains.

title: personal essay|the last video rental shop in town
text:
In the quietude of our small town, nestled between a bustling bakery and an old-fashioned barber shop, stands the last video rental store. Its façade is unassuming, a relic from another era, with a neon sign that flickers intermittently like a dying star. The windows are plastered with faded posters of films long forgotten, their edges curling with age. This place, Video Visions, has become something of a sanctuary for me, a space where the past and present coexist in a delicate, almost sacred balance.

The first time I walked into Video Visions, it was out of sheer curiosity. The world outside had moved on, embracing streaming services and instant downloads, but here, time seemed to have paused. The air inside was thick with the scent of old carpet and the faint, musty aroma of celluloid. Shelves lined the walls, each one crammed with DVDs, VHS tapes, and even a few dusty Betamax cassettes. The titles were a mix of classics, cult favorites, and obscure foreign films, a testament to the eclectic tastes of its patrons.

Behind the counter, Mr. Thompson, the owner, sat hunched over a ledger, his spectacles perched precariously on the bridge of his nose. He looked up as the bell above the door jangled, his eyes narrowing slightly before a warm smile spread across his face. "Welcome," he said, his voice a gentle rumble. "Looking for anything in particular?"

I shook my head, unsure of what to say. I had come in without a specific film in mind, driven more by a sense of nostalgia than any real desire to rent a movie. But as I wandered the aisles, running my fingers along the spines of the cases, I felt a strange comfort. Each title was a portal to a different world, a different time. There was something tactile and reassuring about holding a physical copy, the weight of it in my hands, the artwork on the cover, the promise of a story waiting to be told.

Over the weeks, I found myself returning to Video Visions, not just to rent movies, but to lose myself in the quiet, almost meditative atmosphere. Mr. Thompson and I developed a kind of unspoken understanding. He would nod in greeting, and I would browse, occasionally pausing to ask for a recommendation. He knew his collection intimately, and his suggestions were always spot-on, as if he could read the moods and desires that I couldn't quite articulate.

One afternoon, as I was leaving, I noticed a stack of letters on the counter. They were handwritten, addressed to Mr. Thompson from people all over the country. Some were thank-you notes, others were heartfelt messages of support. It was then that I realized how much this place meant to others, too. In a world that was constantly moving forward, Video Visions was a reminder of the value of slowing down, of savoring the experience of discovery and connection.

But the reality of the situation was never far from my mind. The store was struggling. The once-bustling streets were now often empty, and the few customers who did come in were mostly regulars, like me, drawn by the same inexplicable pull. I could see the worry etched in Mr. Thompson's face, the lines deepening with each passing day. Yet, he never spoke of closing, never gave any indication that he was ready to let go of this place that had been his life for so long.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows through the window, I found myself sitting in the small, dimly lit back room of the store. Mr. Thompson had invited me in, and we sat in companionable silence, sipping tea and watching an old black-and-white film projected onto a makeshift screen. The images flickered, the characters' voices crackled, and for a moment, it felt as though nothing else existed. We were suspended in a timeless bubble, insulated from the relentless march of progress.

As the credits rolled, Mr. Thompson turned to me, his eyes reflecting the soft glow of the projector. "You know, I've been thinking a lot about the future of this place," he said, his voice tinged with a hint of sadness. "It's hard to imagine a world without these shelves, without the stories they hold."

I nodded, feeling a lump form in my throat. I wanted to offer words of reassurance, to tell him that the store would endure, that there would always be a place for it. But the truth was, I didn't know. The world was changing, and sometimes, no matter how much we want to hold on, we have to let go.

In the end, Video Visions became more than just a video rental store. It was a refuge, a place where the past and present intertwined, where the stories of others became a part of my own. As I left that night, the neon sign flickering behind me, I knew that whatever happened, the memories and the connections I had made here would stay with me, a bittersweet reminder of a time when the world was a little slower, a little simpler, and a little more magical.

title: fable|a crow who collects lost keys
text:
The crows of Blackwood Lane were known for their particular brand of thievery—not shiny coins or wedding rings, but keys. Not all crows, mind you. Just one: a female with left wing feathers slightly ruffled, as if perpetually caught in a crosswind, and eyes the colour of wet slate. Her name, whispered first by Mrs. Elara Finch—retired librarian, keeper of neighbourhood lore—was Cora. “Not *Corvus*, no,” she’d say, tapping her temple with a bent forefinger, “*Cora*. Like the old apothecary’s daughter who vanished from the millpond in ’37. The crow remembers what people forget.”

Blackwood Lane itself was a narrow, cobblestone street in the north quadrant of Ashwick, a town where rain fell in polite, persistent drizzles and chimneys leaned just enough to suggest quiet resignation. Its houses wore peeling paint in shades of faded mustard, seafoam green, and tired lavender. Every morning at precisely 7:18 a.m., Cora would alight on the wrought-iron fence outside number 12—the blue house with the crooked bay window—and cock her head, listening. She didn’t listen for birdsong. She listened for the metallic *clink* of a dropped key, the muffled *thunk* of a keychain hitting pavement, the frustrated sigh that usually followed.

It began, Mrs. Finch claimed, after the Great Key Shortage of ’22—the winter the municipal locksmith, Mr. Silas Croft, retired without training an apprentice and the local hardware store burned down, taking its spare-key inventory with it. People grew careless. Keys slipped from coat pockets worn thin at the seams; they tumbled from shopping bags heavy with sourdough and tins of Earl Grey; they were mislaid on park benches slick with dew, beside the duck pond where children fed stale breadcrumbs to indifferent mallards.

Cora’s collection wasn’t hoarded in some hidden oak hollow. It lived, meticulously arranged, inside the hollow base of the ancient copper beech tree at the lane’s eastern bend—known locally as the Whispering Beech. Its trunk bore a fissure, wide enough for a human fist, lined with smooth, dark moss. Inside, resting on a bed of dried foxglove leaves, lay the keys. Not jumbled. Not tangled. Each hung from a slender loop of braided willow bark, suspended like tiny, silent pendulums. A Yale key with a chipped blue plastic fob (belonging to young Leo Chen, who’d dropped it chasing his runaway scooter on Maple Street); a heavy, tarnished brass key stamped “MILLS & SONS, 1914” (from Mr. Armitage’s workshop, lost during his stroke recovery walk); a delicate silver key shaped like a swan, its bow engraved with “L.M.” (found clutched in the trembling hand of Ms. Lillian Moore, eighty-two, who’d wept when Cora dropped it into her open palm one Tuesday, landing on her sun-warmed garden bench).

People noticed. First, it was small things. Mrs. Gable, whose front door had jammed for three weeks, found her own key—cold and slightly damp—on her doormat one Thursday. No note. Just the key, lying flat, its teeth pointing east. Then came Mr. Hayes, the baker, who’d sworn he’d lost his bakery’s back-alley access key. He saw Cora perched on his chimney pot at dawn, watching him knead dough through the steam-fogged window. That afternoon, he found the key tucked into the flour sack beside the sourdough starter—dry, unblemished, impossibly clean.

“You’re not stealing them,” said Leo Chen, nine years old, standing barefoot on his porch one misty October morning, holding out a single, warm peanut. Cora tilted her head, one black eye fixed on him. “You’re… keeping them safe. Until they’re needed again.”

She didn’t take the peanut. She hopped once, twice, then flew low and slow past his ear, her wingtip brushing the air just inches from his temple. A soft *shush* sound, like pages turning.

Word spread. Not as rumour, but as quiet certainty. When old Mr. Croft passed away in his sleep, his widow, Agnes, found his master key ring—the one with the tiny brass owl—on her breakfast tray, nestled beside the sugar bowl. She didn’t cry. She held it to the light, tracing the owl’s beak with a trembling thumb, and murmured, “Ah. You remembered, Cora. You remembered where he kept it, even after the dementia took the names.”

One blustery afternoon in late November, a woman in a grey trench coat stood beneath the Whispering Beech, her shoulders hunched, staring at the fissure. Her face was pale, her knuckles white where she gripped a crumpled tissue. It was Dr. Anya Sharma, the new GP at the Ashwick Health Centre, who’d moved in only last month. She’d misplaced her office key—the one that opened the locked cabinet containing patient records—during her frantic first day. Security protocol demanded immediate replacement, a two-week wait, and a £120 fee. She’d searched her coat, her bag, her car, the waiting room floor. Nothing.

Cora landed on the lowest branch, silent as smoke. She watched the doctor’s breath plume in the cold air, watched her lower her forehead against the rough bark of the beech.

“Please,” Dr. Sharma whispered, not to the sky, but to the tree itself. “Just… just one more day. I need to get those files reviewed before the audit.”

Cora didn’t move. She waited. Three minutes. A robin hopped across the frost-rimed grass. A delivery van rumbled past, gears grinding. Then, with a soft *whirr* of feathers, Cora dropped. Not to the ground. To the fissure. She disappeared inside for precisely seven seconds. When she emerged, she carried nothing in her beak. Instead, she nudged something with her foot—a small, polished rectangle of dark wood, set into the moss-lined hollow. It was a shallow depression, barely visible unless you knew to look. And there, resting in it, was a single key. Chrome-plated, sleek, stamped with the Health Centre’s logo and the number “B-3”.

Dr. Sharma gasped. She reached in, her fingers brushing the cool metal. As she withdrew it, Cora lifted off, circling once, twice, high above the lane, her wings catching the weak, slanting sun. She didn’t caw. She didn’t pause. She simply flew west, towards the river, where the willows dipped their long fingers into the water, and where, if you stood very still at dusk, you could sometimes hear the faint, metallic chime of something small and precious, falling softly, perfectly, into place.

title: creation myth|how the northern lights were woven
text:
The northern lights weren’t *born*. Not like a calf in the barn, or frost cracking the creek ice at dawn. They were *woven*.  

I heard this first from Old Aino—Aino who smelled perpetually of dried lingonberries and pipe smoke, whose left earlobe had a tiny, perfect knot in it, like a snagged thread. She’d sit on her porch swing in Kautokeino, even in November, wrapped in a reindeer-hide shawl patched with blue wool so faded it looked like the sky just before twilight. Her hands—knuckles swollen, veins like buried roots—would rest in her lap, still. And then she’d begin, voice low, as if telling a secret to the wind itself:  

“There was no sky then. Just *tangle*.”  

She meant it literally. Not metaphor. Not poetry. *Tangle*. A great, breathing snarl of raw light—gold, yes, but also bruised violet, the green of foxgloves after rain, the sickly yellow of old birch sap—caught in the ribs of a dead whale that had washed up on the frozen shore of Sápmi, miles inland, somehow, impossibly. No one questioned how. You don’t question the whale. You question the *light*, and why it wouldn’t settle. Why it hummed—not a sound, but a vibration in your molars, a buzz behind your eyes. It made the ptarmigan go silent. Made the lichen on the rocks pulse faintly, like a slow, cold heartbeat.  

That’s when the Weaver came. Not a god. Not a giant. Just *her*: Márkka. Barefoot, even on snow that squeaked like broken glass. Wore a dress woven from dried river reeds, stiff and rustling, stitched with threads pulled from her own hair—black, yes, but shot through with silver, like moonlight caught in spider-silk. She carried no loom. No shuttle. Just her fingers. And a pair of shears. Not steel. *Antler*. Carved from the shed horn of a seven-year-old bull reindeer, its tip worn smooth and dark from decades of use. She didn’t speak. Not once. Just knelt beside the whale-rib tangle and began to *sort*.  

Ah—but here’s the thing people forget, or pretend isn’t true: she didn’t *create* the colours. She *rescued* them. The gold wasn’t sun-gold. It was the gold of a child’s first lost tooth, buried under the hearthstone. The green? That was the green of the moss that grows only on the north side of ancient pine stumps—the kind that smells like damp earth and forgotten promises. The violet? The inside of a crow’s wing, seen at exactly 3:17 a.m., when the world holds its breath. Márkka didn’t invent light. She gathered what had been *lost*, what had slipped loose from stories, from dreams, from the sighs of elders before they slept. She gathered the *almost*-remembered.  

Her weaving wasn’t neat. Not like the geometric patterns on a duodji knife-sheath. It was… hesitant. She’d pull a strand of pale blue—*that’s the colour of a grandmother’s voice when she tells you about the time the stars fell into the lake*—and loop it around a rib, then pause, frown, tug it back out. Too thin. Too sharp. Then she’d try again, twisting it with a filament of deep red—*the red of the berry you pick last, the one that tastes like cold iron and sweetness*—and *then* it would hold. A soft, warm shimmer. Not bright. Not loud. Just *there*, like breath on a windowpane.  

And the *sound*. Oh, the sound. Not music. Not silence. A low, continuous *shush-shush*, like wind moving through dry reeds, or the quiet rasp of a needle pulling thread through thick felt. Sometimes, if you stood very still, very close (but never too close—Márkka’s antler shears gleamed dully, and her gaze, when it lifted, held the weight of glaciers), you’d hear a single, clear note—a high, pure chime—like ice cracking *just so*, releasing trapped air. That was the moment a new arc caught fire. Not burning. *Unfolding*.  

It took three winters. Not calendar winters. *Real* ones. The kind where the cold gets into your marrow and stays. Where the snow doesn’t melt—it *subsides*, like a tired animal settling. By the third spring thaw, the tangle was gone. In its place, suspended between the highest peaks and the lowest clouds, hung the first aurora. Not a curtain. Not a ribbon. A *net*. Delicate. Trembling. Alive with the rescued colours, all humming softly, all holding their breath.  

Márkka stood. Brushed snow from her reed skirt. Didn’t look up. Just walked east, barefoot, towards the rising sun, leaving no footprints. Only a faint, lingering scent of crushed juniper and warm stone.  

The lights stayed. But they’re not finished. Never are. Every winter, when the air turns brittle and the stars seem close enough to bite, you’ll see it: a flicker, a hesitation, a sudden, sharp *pull* in the green—like a thread catching. That’s Márkka, still working. Still sorting. Still rescuing the light we’ve dropped, the colours we’ve forgotten how to name.  

So next time you see them—really *see* them—not just the spectacle, but the *texture*—look for the unevenness. The way one arc seems thicker, warmer, than the one beside it. The way the violet sometimes flares, then dims, like a memory surfacing, then slipping away. That’s not atmosphere. Not solar wind. That’s the antler shears. That’s the reed skirt brushing snow. That’s the quiet, relentless, human work of gathering what’s almost gone… and weaving it, stitch by trembling stitch, back into the dark.  

(And if you ever find a single, impossibly long strand of silver hair, caught in the bark of an old birch near the fjord? Don’t touch it. Just leave it. It’s hers. She’ll be back for it.)

title: memoir|a father's ledger found after his death
text:
...and there it was, nestled between old tax returns and a stack of faded photographs. The ledger, its cover worn and edges curled, seemed to carry the weight of years, much like my father had in his final days. I gently pulled it out, feeling an odd mix of reverence and trepidation. It was as if I were about to uncover a secret, a part of my father's life that he had never shared, even with us, his children.

I opened the ledger, and the musty scent of aged paper filled the air. The first pages were neatly labeled, "1975-1980," and I began to read. The entries were meticulous, each one a snapshot of our family's financial life: income, expenses, savings, and debts. But as I turned the pages, I realized that this ledger was more than just a record of money. It was a chronicle of our lives, a story told in numbers and brief, often cryptic, notes.

One entry from 1976 caught my eye: "Bought new bicycle for Tom. $45.00. Saw the joy in his eyes. Worth every penny." I remembered that bicycle, a shiny red Schwinn, and how proud I had been to ride it around the neighborhood. My father had worked extra hours at the factory that month, and now I understood why. It wasn't just a bike; it was a symbol of his love, a way to bring a smile to his son's face.

Further along, I found a note from 1978: "Mary's piano lessons. $20.00 per week. Her talent is blossoming. Proud of her dedication." Mary, my sister, had indeed become a talented pianist, and I recalled the countless hours she spent practicing, the sound of scales and arpeggios echoing through the house. Our father, despite his long workdays, always made sure to attend her recitals, beaming with pride from the audience. The ledger revealed the sacrifices he made, the choices he prioritized, to nurture her gift.

As I delved deeper into the ledger, I noticed a pattern. Every few months, there would be a significant withdrawal, always accompanied by a brief, almost poetic note. One from 1981 read, "Grandma's medicine. $150.00. Health above all." Another, from 1983, said, "Uncle Joe's funeral. $300.00. Said goodbye with dignity." These entries painted a picture of a man who was not only a provider but also a caretaker, someone who took on the burdens of his extended family without complaint.

There were moments of struggle, too. A particularly stark entry from 1985 read, "Lost job. Savings down to $2,500.00. Must find new work soon. Keep faith." That year had been tough, but my father had never let us see the full extent of his worry. He had always maintained a calm, reassuring presence, even when the future seemed uncertain. Reading these words, I felt a surge of admiration for his resilience and his unwavering commitment to our well-being.

But it wasn't all hardship. There were moments of celebration and joy, too. An entry from 1987, the year I graduated high school, read, "Tom's graduation. $100.00 for party. Proud of him. Future looks bright." I remembered that day, the sense of accomplishment and the overwhelming support from my family. My father had been there, a pillar of strength, encouraging me to reach for the stars. The ledger, in its own way, captured those fleeting, precious moments, preserving them in ink and paper.

The more I read, the more I realized that this ledger was a testament to my father's character. It was a document of his values, his priorities, and his love. Each entry, no matter how small, was a piece of the puzzle that made up his life, and by extension, ours. He had kept these records not just for himself, but for us, to show us the effort, the care, and the sacrifices that went into raising a family.

Tears welled up in my eyes as I reached the last page. The final entry, dated just a month before his passing, was simple yet profound: "Paid off mortgage. Home free and clear. Grateful for this life. Love to all." This was his legacy, a life lived with purpose and devotion, a life that had left an indelible mark on all of us.

I closed the ledger, holding it close, feeling a deep connection to the man who had been both my father and my hero. In his absence, this ledger became a bridge, a way for me to understand him more deeply, to see the world through his eyes, and to carry forward the values he had instilled in us. As I placed the ledger back in the box, I knew that it would be a cherished heirloom, a reminder of a life well-lived and a love that endures.

title: memoir|growing up above a family laundry in a northern English town
text:
The Humming Floor

The floorboards above the laundry didn’t creak. They *sang*. Not a melody—nothing so polite—but a low, insistent thrum, like the vibration of a plucked bass string held too long. It began at dawn, when Mr. Hargreaves, our neighbour and the laundry’s sole proprietor, unlocked the heavy steel door below us with a key that sounded like a dentist’s drill. Then came the groan of the industrial washer’s drum engaging, the hiss of steam escaping its valves, the rhythmic *thump-thump-thump* of the centrifuge spinning wet sheets into tight, damp fists. This wasn’t background noise. It was the architecture of my childhood: the bassline to every conversation, the tremor beneath every footfall, the reason the teacup on the windowsill sometimes developed a fine, slow tremor of condensation, even in winter.

We lived in a narrow, three-storey brick building on Sycamore Street, Hartlepool. The laundry occupied the ground floor and cellar; our flat—the ‘upper rooms’ as Mum called them, with a faint, persistent air of apology—was wedged above it, accessed by a steep, uncarpeted staircase smelling perpetually of damp wool and ozone. The walls were thin—not paper-thin, but *listening*-thin. You learned the acoustics: the sharp, metallic *clack* of the folding table being set up meant Mrs. Gable from the fishmonger’s was dropping off her husband’s aprons; the high, reedy whine of the steam iron’s regulator signaled a rush order for the hospital gowns; the sudden, muffled thud followed by a low curse was Mr. Hargreaves wrestling the heavy linen sack into the boiler room. Privacy was a theoretical concept, like gravity on the moon. Arguments, whispered confessions, even the soft, wet sound of a baby crying in the flat next door—all bled through the plasterboard, distorted but unmistakable. We learned to modulate our own voices, to swallow certain words whole.

The heat was another constant presence. Not oppressive, but deep and pervasive, radiating upwards through the floor like warmth from a sleeping animal. In winter, it made the flat unnervingly mild, forcing us to open windows wide despite the North Sea wind rattling the panes. In summer, it turned the upstairs into a slow, humid oven. The air tasted faintly of starch and bleach, a clean, sharp scent that never quite masked the underlying tang of damp cotton and machine oil. I remember lying on the lino in the hallway, pressing my ear to the warm floor, feeling the vibrations travel up my skull—not hearing the machines, but *feeling* their labour in my molars, in the hollow behind my eyes. It was the closest thing I had to a heartbeat that wasn’t my own.

Mum worked the counter downstairs, her hands perpetually red-raw from the water, her hair perpetually escaping its bun in damp tendrils. She knew the weight of every sheet, the exact shade of grey that meant ‘worn but serviceable’, the precise fold that satisfied Mrs. Thistlewaite’s exacting standards. Her world was measured in pounds of linen, minutes of cycle time, and the careful negotiation of stains—tea, gravy, engine grease, blood (always discreetly labelled ‘medical’). She spoke of fabric softener not as a luxury, but as a necessary buffer against the relentless abrasion of the wash. Her knowledge felt ancient, practical, rooted in the physical world in a way school lessons never did. I watched her fingers, knuckles swollen, move with unconscious precision over piles of towels, and understood, without ever articulating it, that competence could be a kind of quiet dignity, forged in steam and repetition.

I spent hours in the small, high window of our front room, looking out over the terraced roofs towards the grey smear of the sea. Below me, the laundry breathed. The rhythm was relentless, but not monotonous. It shifted: the frantic energy of Monday mornings, the slower, heavier pulse of midweek, the almost mournful sigh of Saturday afternoon when only the hospital linens remained, churning in the last cycle. Sometimes, I’d watch Mr. Hargreaves, a small, wiry man perpetually damp at the temples, methodically checking dials, adjusting valves, his face calm in the steam-haze. He never rushed, never seemed flustered. His authority wasn’t loud; it was the quiet certainty of knowing exactly how much pressure the boiler could hold, how long the wool needed to rest before pressing, how to coax stubborn ink from a child’s school shirt without dissolving the thread. It was a different kind of power than the one wielded in offices or council chambers—older, more elemental, tied to the physics of heat and water and friction.

There was no grand epiphany, no moment where the humming floor suddenly revealed some profound truth. It simply *was*. The damp patches on the ceiling that bloomed in winter, the way the light through the high window always held a faint, blue-tinged haze of suspended lint, the way the smell of hot ironing board covers clung to my school blazer… these weren’t metaphors. They were the texture of being. The laundry didn’t teach me resilience, exactly. It taught me the weight of routine, the quiet persistence of maintenance, the way life continues its essential, unglamorous work beneath the surface of things, humming, vibrating, generating heat that you learn, eventually, to live inside.

When we moved, finally, after Dad’s redundancy and Mum’s quiet decision to take the job at the library, the silence upstairs was the first shock. Not peace, but a vacuum. The floorboards were still. The air was cool, dry, scentless. I stood in the empty hallway, listening to nothing, and felt profoundly unmoored. The absence wasn’t relief. It was the sudden, startling loss of a fundamental frequency. The world felt thinner, less substantial, without that deep, resonant thrum beneath my feet. I didn’t miss the damp, or the smell, or the thin walls. I missed the sheer, undeniable *presence* of it—the proof, vibrating up through the soles of my shoes, that something vital, something necessary, was happening, right there, all the time, just below the surface of ordinary life. The floor was silent now. But the memory of its song, low and insistent, remains lodged in my bones.

title: literary novel|an elderly translator finishing her last book
text:
The rain in Kyoto fell in slow, silver needles, stitching the moss on the stone lanterns outside Chishaku-in’s eastern gate. Inside the small, paper-shaded room—Room 307 at the Kiyomizu Guest House, where she’d rented the same tatami chamber for thirty-seven springs—Eleanor Voss sat at a low lacquered desk, her left hand resting atop a stack of loose-leaf manuscript pages bound with faded indigo twine. Her right hand, knotted at the knuckles but steady as a metronome, held a Montblanc Meisterstück, its nib worn smooth by forty-two years of ink and intention.

She was translating *The Plum Rain Diary*—a fragmentary, fever-dream journal written in 1821 by a widowed courtesan named Yūko from the Shimabara district of old Kyoto. Not the polished, poetic version anthologized in university textbooks, but the raw, ink-blurred original: pages stained with tea, pressed plum blossoms, and one faint, rust-coloured smudge Eleanor had tested once—hemoglobin, not iron gall. She’d found it tucked inside a cedar box beneath the floorboards of a derelict machiya in Nakagyō, purchased for ¥3.2 million and half a bottle of aged Yamazaki single malt from the reluctant heir.

“Still at it, Miss Voss?” said Kenji Tanaka, leaning in the doorway, balancing two steaming cups of hojicha on a lacquer tray. He wore his usual cardigan—navy, slightly frayed at the cuffs—and carried the quiet deference of someone who’d watched her translate *The Tale of the Heike* into English while recovering from pneumonia in this very room in ’98.

Eleanor didn’t look up. “Kenji-san, you know I loathe ‘Miss.’ It makes me feel like a governess at a girls’ seminary in Bath.”

He smiled, placed one cup beside her wrist. “Then Mrs. Voss. Though you’ve never been married.”

“I’ve been married to syntax,” she said, turning the page. Her voice was low, gravelled by decades of reading aloud—first to herself, then to her late husband Robert, who’d listened in bed with his eyes closed, fingers tracing the braille dots on the spine of her Penguin Classics.

Kenji poured milk into his own cup—never hers; she drank it black, scalding, three times a day at precisely 10:15, 2:47, and 7:03 p.m., as if time were a stanza she refused to scan loosely. “The publisher called again. From New York. They want the introduction finalised by Friday. The galleys go to press Monday.”

She dipped her nib, paused over the word *kage*. Not “shadow.” Not “shade.” In Yūko’s context—*kage no naka de kimi o mitsumete iru*—it meant something else: the quiet, deliberate act of watching someone *within* their own absence. A presence held in suspension. Eleanor had rendered it, in draft six, as *“I watch you inside your leaving.”* Then crossed it out. Draft seven: *“I hold your departure in my gaze.”* Draft eight, still unfiled, read: *“I keep vigil where you are no longer.”*

She wrote it now, slowly, the kanji for *kage* dissolving into hiragana beneath her pen—*かげ*—then translated it aloud, softly: “I keep vigil where you are no longer.”

Kenji exhaled, long and quiet. “That’s the one.”

She nodded, turned the page. On the verso, in Robert’s cramped, looping hand—written during his last lucid week, before the hospice in Takarazuka—was a note in pencil: *“You’re not translating her grief, Ellie. You’re translating her grammar of survival. The commas matter more than the nouns.”*

She touched the pencil mark with her thumbnail. Felt the groove in the paper.

Later, after Kenji had gone—leaving behind the scent of sandalwood soap and the damp wool of his coat—she opened the bottom drawer of the desk. Not for the manuscript. For the small, brass-bound box containing Robert’s spectacles, a dried sprig of wisteria from their garden in Hampstead, and a cassette tape labelled *R.V. — 1983, Kyoto Station Platform*. She’d never played it. Didn’t need to. She knew the sound: the clatter of wooden geta, the high chime of the station bell, Robert’s voice saying, *“Listen—the way the train sighs before it moves. That’s the first line of your next book.”*

Outside, the rain softened. A lone temple bell tolled—not for prayer, but for the hour: 4:33 p.m. She checked her Seiko, the one with the cracked crystal Robert had glued with beeswax in ’79. Yes. Precisely.

She reached for the final page of Yūko’s diary. Not the last entry—Yūko had stopped writing on the seventh day of the fourth month, 1821—but the blank sheet pasted onto the back cover, where the courtesan had drawn, in sumi ink, a single, imperfect circle. No centre point marked. No radius indicated. Just the curve, trembling slightly at the northern quadrant, as if drawn with a breath held too long.

Eleanor picked up her finest brush—a sable no. 2, gifted by the calligrapher Sato-sensei in 1991—and mixed ink with a drop of plum wine from the bottle beside her, its deep violet pooling like congealed dusk. She did not replicate the circle. Instead, she painted, just beneath it, three characters in delicate, unbroken stroke:

*tsugi ni*

Next.

Then, below that, in English, in her own hand, smaller, almost apologetic:

*Not the end. The turn.*

She set the brush down. Closed the manuscript. Walked to the shōji screen, slid it open just enough to let in the cool, wet air—and the green, breathing hush of the maple grove behind the guest house. A single leaf, veined gold and russet, trembled on the lowest branch. Not falling yet. Not holding. Just there, suspended between wind and weight, catching the last light as it slanted through the clouds.

She watched it until the light changed. Until the leaf shifted, infinitesimally, on its stem.

title: myth retelling|the smith who forged the first bell
text:
In the heart of an ancient, sprawling forest, where the trees whispered secrets and the wind carried tales of old, there lived a humble blacksmith named Eamon. His forge, nestled at the edge of a bubbling stream, was known far and wide for the fine tools and weapons he crafted. But Eamon was no ordinary smith; he had a peculiar fascination with sound. He would often pause in his work to listen to the crackling of the fire, the soft hiss of metal cooling, or the distant songs of birds. It was said that Eamon could hear things others couldn't, like the whispers of the earth itself.

One evening, as the sun dipped below the horizon, casting long shadows across the forest, a stranger arrived at Eamon's door. He was a tall, gaunt figure, dressed in tattered robes, with eyes that seemed to pierce through the very soul. The stranger introduced himself as Aedan, a traveler from a distant land, and he bore a request that would change Eamon's life forever. Aedan needed a bell, not just any bell, but one that could call the spirits of the forest and bring harmony to the land. Eamon, intrigued and a bit skeptical, agreed to take on the task. He had never made a bell before, but the challenge excited him.

The first step, Aedan explained, was to find the right materials. The bell must be forged from a special ore, found only in the deepest part of the forest, near the sacred grove. Eamon, accompanied by his loyal dog, Finn, set out the next morning. The journey was arduous, and the forest seemed to shift and change around them, as if it were alive and trying to guide them. After hours of walking, they finally reached the grove, a place of eerie beauty, where the light filtered through the leaves in shimmering patterns. There, hidden beneath a pile of fallen leaves, they found the ore, a deep, rich red, almost pulsing with an inner light.

Eamon returned to his forge, his mind buzzing with ideas. He began to melt the ore, a process that took days, as the metal was stubborn and resistant. The heat in the forge was intense, and the air thick with the smell of molten metal. Eamon worked tirelessly, shaping the bell with his bare hands, guided by a vision that seemed to come from somewhere deep within him. The bell, when it was finally finished, was a thing of beauty: a perfect, gleaming sphere, with intricate carvings that told the story of the forest and its inhabitants.

But the real test was yet to come. Aedan had instructed Eamon that the bell must be rung at the stroke of midnight, on the night of the full moon, for its true power to be revealed. As the appointed night approached, Eamon felt a mixture of excitement and dread. What if the bell didn't work? What if he had failed?

When the moon rose, full and luminous, Eamon gathered all the villagers. They stood in a circle around the bell, their faces illuminated by the silvery light. Eamon took a deep breath and, with a steady hand, struck the bell. The sound that emerged was unlike anything anyone had ever heard. It was a clear, resonant tone that seemed to vibrate through the very air, reaching into the depths of the forest. And then, something miraculous happened. The spirits of the forest, creatures of myth and legend, began to emerge from the trees. They danced and sang, their voices blending with the sound of the bell, creating a symphony of harmony and peace.

From that day forward, the bell became a symbol of unity and protection for the village. Eamon, once a simple blacksmith, was now revered as a hero, a man who had brought the spirits and the people together. The bell, too, was cherished, and it was said that its sound could heal the sick, calm the troubled, and bring prosperity to the land.

Years passed, and Eamon grew old, but the memory of that night, and the magic of the bell, lived on. Even today, in the quiet moments, you can still hear the faint echo of the bell, a reminder of the power of sound, and the enduring connection between the earth and those who inhabit it.

title: creation myth|how the northern lights were woven
text:
The loom was already trembling.

Not with the shuddering of earth or the groan of ice, but with a deep, resonant *hum*, like the lowest note of a glacier calving into the sea—felt more than heard, vibrating up through the soles of her bare feet and into the hollows behind her ribs. She stood before it, barefoot on the frozen breath of the world, her fingers already stained indigo and silver where they’d brushed the first threads. The warp strands—cold, unyielding filaments spun from solidified starlight and the sigh of the first wind—stretched taut across the frame, glinting like frozen rivers under the bruised violet sky. They were silent, waiting. Not passive, but *attentive*, as if holding their breath for the first true note of song.

She did not sing with her throat. She sang with her hands.

Her left palm pressed flat against the central beam—the *Sky-Spine*, she called it in the quiet language of making—and she drew breath deep, drawing not air, but the raw, thin cold of the upper dark. Her right hand lifted, fingers splayed, and from the tips—not blood, but *light*—began to seep: liquid gold, warm and honey-thick, pooling in the hollow of her palm. It wasn’t fire; it held no heat, only radiance, the captured essence of the sun’s last kiss on the horizon, preserved in amber resin and memory. This was the first weft thread. She didn’t pull it from herself; she *unwound* it, a slow, deliberate release, like letting go of a long-held grief that had finally softened into something luminous.

As the golden strand touched the first warp filament, the loom *shivered*. A single, pure chime echoed—not from metal, but from the air itself—and the golden light flared, then settled, weaving itself *into* the starlight thread, not over it, not under it, but *through* its very substance. Where they met, the warp filament pulsed, softening from brittle silver to a warm, breathing copper-gold. A warmth, subtle but undeniable, bloomed in the air around them, melting the frost from the nearest tussock of moss, revealing emerald shoots beneath.

But warmth alone was not enough. The north demanded contrast. Depth. The hush before the storm. So she turned, knelt, and pressed her forehead to the frozen tundra. Not to pray, but to *listen*. Beneath the ice, she heard it: the slow, grinding pulse of the earth’s core, the ancient, slow song of basalt and magma, muffled and immense. She drew that sound—not as noise, but as *substance*—up through her bones, her spine, into her throat, and exhaled it not as breath, but as a thread of deepest indigo, shot through with veins of obsidian black. It coiled from her mouth like smoke, yet held weight, density, a tangible coolness that made the nearby air crackle with static. This was the second weft.

She wove it beside the gold, not touching it, leaving a hair’s breadth of charged silence between them. And in that space, something new ignited. Where gold met indigo, not blending, but *resonating*, the air shimmered. Tiny motes of pure white light—like frozen breath given consciousness—detached from the loom’s edge and spiraled upward, vanishing into the high dark. The hum deepened, thickened, becoming layered: the low thrum of the earth, the bright chime of the starlight, and now, beneath it all, a soft, sighing *hiss*, like silk dragged across ice.

She rose, her knees stiff, her breath pluming white and swift. Her fingers, stained now with gold and indigo, moved faster. She wove not in straight lines, but in spirals, in undulating waves, in sudden, sharp zigzags that mimicked the flight of the snow goose at dusk. Each movement was a gesture of memory: the curve of a caribou’s antler against the moon, the jagged tear of a crevasse, the slow, patient unfurling of a fern in spring melt. She wove the silence of deep forests, pulling threads of muted grey-green from the scent of pine needles crushed underfoot. She wove the laughter of children chasing foxes across the tundra, translating the bright, staccato joy into quick, darting threads of iridescent pearl that seemed to hover just above the surface of the weave. She wove the sorrow of the old ones who remembered the land before the great freeze, drawing threads of deep, sorrowful violet that bled softly into the indigo, creating shadows that held not emptiness, but profound, quiet dignity.

The loom grew heavier, not with weight, but with *presence*. The threads themselves began to breathe. The gold pulsed like a slow heartbeat; the indigo deepened, swirling with nebulae of trapped starlight; the pearl threads flickered, alive with reflected motion. The air above the loom thickened, became viscous, charged. Snowflakes, falling gently moments before, now hung suspended mid-air, glittering diamonds caught in an invisible current. A raven, circling high, tilted its wing and drifted sideways, carried by a breeze that hadn’t existed a moment ago—a breeze smelling of ozone and distant lightning and crushed mint.

She wove until her shoulders burned and her vision blurred at the edges, until the rhythm of her hands synced with the thrumming of the earth and the chime of the stars. She wove the memory of every aurora witnessed—the fleeting green ribbon over the fjord, the violent crimson rip across the winter sky, the ghostly, silent white glow that haunted the poles. She wove them not as separate events, but as variations on a single, vast, living phrase. Her fingers, now glowing faintly with their own inner light, moved with the certainty of a river finding its course. There was no mistake, only adaptation. When a thread of unexpected, fierce crimson flared from her palm—born of a sudden, sharp memory of blood on snow, of life fiercely defended—she didn’t reject it. She wove it *in*, letting it bleed into the gold, transforming it into a richer, more complex amber, a colour that spoke of both sacrifice and enduring warmth.

The final thread was not drawn from without, nor woven with intent. It came as a sigh, a release so deep it felt like the world exhaling. It was clear, almost invisible, yet it carried the scent of thawing earth and the first fragile crocus pushing through snow. She laid it across the entire width of the completed tapestry, a single, unbroken line of pure, distilled *possibility*. As it settled, the entire weave *lifted*.

Not physically. But the light within it surged, detached, and rose—not as smoke, not as flame, but as a living, breathing entity of pure, articulated light. It flowed upwards, stretching, thinning, arching across the dome of the night sky like a bridge spun from breath and starlight and memory. It pulsed. It rippled. It *danced*. Green rivers swirled into violet veils; gold ribbons tangled with indigo currents; pearl motes scattered like startled birds, only to reform into shimmering, geometric patterns that dissolved into soft, rolling waves. It was silent, yet it roared with the accumulated resonance of every thread, every memory, every breath she had poured into the loom.

She stood back, her hands empty, her body trembling not with exhaustion, but with the sheer, staggering *aliveness* of what she had released. The northern lights were not painted on the sky. They were not trapped spirits. They were *woven*. And the loom before her, its warp strands now humming with residual light, its beams etched with faint, glowing patterns, was not finished. It waited. For the next breath. The next memory. The next hand, steady or shaking, ready to take up the shuttle and begin again. The sky breathed with light. And somewhere, deep in the frozen ground, the earth sighed back, a low, approving rumble that vibrated up through the soles of her bare feet, into the hollows behind her ribs, and out, once more, into the waiting dark.

title: literary novel|an elderly translator finishing her last book
text:
The light in the study was thin and yellow, the kind that seeped through the tall, dusty window only between ten-fifteen and eleven-oh-four each morning, as if time itself had narrowed to a precise, fragile aperture. Eleanor sat at the desk—not the oak one she’d used for forty years, but the smaller, lighter maple table her grandson had brought up from the basement last winter, its surface worn smooth in patches by generations of elbows and ink blots. Her hands rested on the manuscript: sixty-three pages, bound in unbleached linen, stitched with waxed linen thread, no title page, no author’s name—just her initials, E.M., penciled faintly in the lower right corner of the first sheet. The original text lay beside it: a slender volume of early-twentieth-century Lithuanian poetry, brittle at the spine, its paper smelling of dried thyme and damp cellar stone. She had found it in a box of her father’s things, wrapped in oilcloth, tied with twine knotted in a sailor’s hitch he’d taught her when she was nine.

Her left index finger trembled—not the coarse, rhythmic shake of Parkinson’s, but a finer tremor, like the vibration of a plucked wire just before silence. She pressed it gently against the margin of page twenty-seven, where she had written *“tamsa nebuvo tuščia, ji buvo pilna balsų, kurie nekalbėjo žodžiais, bet kvėpavimu”* — darkness was not empty; it was full of voices that did not speak in words, but in breath. She had translated it three times already. First: *Darkness was not void, but crowded with voices speaking only in breath.* Too heavy. Second: *Darkness held no vacancy—only breath-voices, wordless and close.* Too lyrical, too eager. Third, penciled now in the margin: *Darkness was not empty. It hummed—not with sound, but with the hush between inhalations.* She underlined *hush*, then crossed it out, leaving the ghost of graphite. Not quite. Not yet.

She reached for the small porcelain cup beside her typewriter—the one with the hairline crack snaking from rim to handle, filled not with tea but with lukewarm water. She dipped the very tip of a sable brush into it, then touched the brush to the pad of her thumb, feeling the cool, fleeting drag of moisture. She did this every morning, without thought: a calibration of touch, a reminder that translation lived in the interval between intention and mark, between tongue and ear, between one language’s throat and another’s jaw.

Outside, a neighbor’s dog barked—three sharp, insistent notes—then fell silent. Eleanor didn’t look up. She heard the bark as a syllable, not noise: *krau! krau! krau!*—a Lithuanian onomatopoeia for sudden alarm, something her father had whispered once during an air raid drill, his hand covering her ears, his breath warm against her temple. She remembered the weight of his palm, the scent of pipe tobacco and cold wool, the way his voice dropped into a register lower than speech, almost subsonic. That was the voice she was trying to carry across—not the dictionary meaning, but the resonance beneath the vowel, the gravity in the pause before the verb.

She turned to page forty-two. A single line repeated six times, each iteration slightly altered in spacing, in punctuation, in the thickness of the ink. *Kai širdis sustoja, ji nepersta klausytis.* When the heart stops, it does not stop listening. She had rendered it as *When the heart ceases, listening remains.* Clean. Accurate. But clean felt like erasure. The Lithuanian carried the weight of a stopped clock—its gears frozen mid-tick, yet the casing still vibrating with residual motion. She tried again, whispering: *When the heart holds its breath, the ears stay open.* Too poetic. *When the heart stops beating, it keeps hearing.* Too blunt. She closed her eyes. Felt the hollow behind her own ribs, the slow, deliberate thud-thud-thud that had lately taken on the quality of a metronome set just below tempo. She opened them, picked up the pencil—her grandfather’s, brass-tipped, worn down to a nub—and wrote, lightly, in the margin: *When the heart pauses, listening leans forward.*

A draft stirred the papers. Not wind—no window was open—but the old house settling, a sigh through the floorboards, a release of pressure in the plaster walls. She watched a dust mote spiral down in the slanted light, catching fire for half a second before vanishing into shadow. She did not reach for the magnifying glass anymore. Her eyes blurred at the edges, yes, but the center remained startlingly clear—especially for texture: the tooth of the paper, the slight indentation where her fingernail had pressed while reading aloud, the faint blue halo around the ink where humidity had kissed the page last August.

At noon, her granddaughter appeared in the doorway, barefoot, holding two mugs. “Brought you ginger tea. And I made oat biscuits. Slightly burnt.” She placed one mug beside the water cup, the other on the windowsill, where the light caught the steam rising in a slow, translucent curl. Eleanor watched her granddaughter’s hands—long fingers, nails bitten short, a smudge of charcoal on the knuckle. She remembered those same hands, smaller, pressing clay into the grooves of a Lithuanian alphabet stamp set, spelling out *širdis*, *tamsa*, *kvėpavimas*, over and over, until the letters became shapes, not sounds.

“Did you finish the last stanza?” the girl asked, not looking at the manuscript, but at Eleanor’s face.

Eleanor lifted the page. Turned it slowly. The final line was blank except for a single comma, placed precisely where the poet had left it—after the word *šviesa*, light. Not a period. Not a dash. A comma, suspended, breathing.

“I’m waiting,” Eleanor said, her voice dry as the paper’s edge, “for the silence after the comma to settle.” She did not say that she had already typed the final sentence—twice—on the carbon copy beneath. That she had struck through both versions. That the comma was not hesitation, but threshold. That some translations are not made with the mind, but with the body’s slow unclenching, the way a fist opens not all at once, but in stages: first the wrist, then the heel of the palm, then the reluctant, trembling release of the smallest finger. She watched the steam from the mug thin, rise, dissolve. Then she reached—not for the pencil, not for the brush—but for the edge of the linen binding, and ran her thumb along the seam, feeling the tiny, deliberate bumps of each stitch.

title: memoir|learning to fish with a silent uncle on a Scottish loch
text:
In the summer of 1985, I was a gangly, awkward twelve-year-old with an insatiable curiosity about the world. My family had decided to spend our holiday in the Scottish Highlands, and it was there, on the shores of Loch Morar, that I met my Uncle Angus. He was a tall, broad-shouldered man, his face etched with lines that spoke of years spent outdoors, and he had a way of moving that was both deliberate and silent. I remember being struck by how little he spoke, but there was a warmth in his eyes that made me feel at ease.

We were staying in a small cottage near Mallaig, a fishing village perished against the rugged coastline. The cottage was old, with walls that seemed to breathe, and the air inside carried the faint scent of peat and sea salt. On the first morning, as the sun painted the sky in hues of orange and pink, Uncle Angus appeared at the door, holding a battered fishing rod. "Ready to learn, lad?" he asked, his voice low and gravelly. I nodded eagerly, and we set off down the narrow path that led to the loch.

The path wound through a dense forest, where the trees whispered secrets to one another, and the ground was carpeted with a thick layer of moss. As we walked, Uncle Angus pointed out the different types of birds that flitted between the branches, and the wildflowers that bloomed along the trail. He knew every inch of this land, and his knowledge was like a hidden treasure, waiting to be discovered.

When we reached the loch, the water was a mirror, reflecting the early morning sky. The silence was profound, broken only by the distant cry of a gull or the gentle lapping of the waves against the shore. Uncle Angus showed me how to cast the line, his movements fluid and graceful. "Watch the water, lad," he said, his eyes never leaving the surface. "It tells you everything."

I watched, mesmerized, as the line arced through the air and landed softly on the water. We sat side by side, the only sounds the occasional rustle of leaves and the soft hum of insects. The hours passed, and though I caught nothing, I felt a deep sense of peace. There was something meditative about the act of fishing, a connection to the natural world that I had never experienced before.

As the day wore on, Uncle Angus began to share stories of his own childhood, of long summers spent exploring the loch and the surrounding hills. He told me about the time he and his brother, my father, had built a raft and sailed across the loch, only to be caught in a sudden storm. They had huddled together, soaked to the bone, but laughing all the same. His stories were filled with a quiet joy, and I could see the light in his eyes as he relived those moments.

In the late afternoon, just as I was beginning to lose hope, I felt a tug on the line. My heart raced as I reeled in, and to my astonishment, I pulled out a small, shimmering trout. It was a modest catch, but to me, it felt like a triumph. Uncle Angus smiled, a rare and genuine smile, and patted me on the back. "Well done, lad," he said. "You’ve got the knack for it."

We cleaned the fish by the water’s edge, and Uncle Angus taught me how to prepare it for cooking. That evening, as we sat around the fire, roasting the trout over the flames, the smell of the fish mingled with the smoke, creating a rich, earthy aroma. We ate in silence, savoring the simple meal, and I realized that the day had been about more than just learning to fish. It was about the bond that had formed between us, a bond forged in the quiet moments by the loch.

Years have passed since that summer, and I have grown into a man with my own stories to tell. But the memory of that day, of the silent uncle and the tranquil loch, remains vivid in my mind. It was a lesson in patience, in the beauty of nature, and in the power of unspoken connections. And every time I find myself by a body of water, casting a line, I think of Uncle Angus, and the wisdom he shared with me on the shores of Loch Morar.

title: myth retelling|the smith who forged the first bell
text:
The bell wasn’t meant to be *heard*. Not really.  

Old Man Hemlock—yes, *that* Hemlock, the one whose left ear was permanently folded like a dried fig leaf from the time he leaned too close to the crucible in ’32—told me this while stirring a pot of turnip-and-duck-grease stew with a spoon that had once been part of a broken harp string. His knuckles were blackened not just by soot, but by decades of handling hot iron that hadn’t quite cooled. He paused, blew steam off the stew, and said: “People think bells are for calling. For warning. For weddings. Ha. First bell was for *silence*. Proper silence. The kind that settles in your molars.”  

So here’s how it went, more or less.  

It was late autumn, 1078—or maybe ’79; the monks at St. Elmo’s kept two different calendars, one for feast days and one for when the roof leaked worst—and the village of Bracken Fen had gone three months without rain. Not drought-dry, not dust-in-your-teeth dry, but that slow, thick dryness where the frogs stopped croaking at dusk and the willows wept sticky amber sap instead of water. The smithy stood on the edge of the fen, half-sunk into the peat, its thatch patched with river reeds and old prayer scrolls (donated, reluctantly, by Father Cuthbert after the third mouse ate his breviary).  

Hemlock’s grandfather—Bran the Unblessed, they called him, though no one knew why he’d been unblessed, only that he’d refused last rites twice—was the smith. He didn’t sing at the anvil. Didn’t whistle. Didn’t even hum. Said sound was “a thief that stole heat before you could shape it.” So he worked in near-silence, save for the *shush-hiss* of quenching, the *thunk* of hammer on iron, the occasional sigh of the furnace breathing like a tired badger.  

One evening, the air tasted metallic. Not like iron—like *before* iron. Like the inside of a wet cave where something ancient had just blinked. Bran had been trying to forge a hinge for the new chapel door—simple work—but the iron kept *refusing*. Not cracking. Not warping. *Refusing*. It would flatten under the hammer, yes, but then, as it cooled, it would subtly *recoil*, drawing itself inward, tightening like a fist. Three times he tried. Three times the hinge curled, unbidden, into a shallow, perfect bowl.  

He cursed—not loudly, just a low, gravelly exhalation—and tossed the fourth attempt into the ash pit. But the bowl-shaped lump landed *just so*, nestled between two half-buried river stones. And when the wind came up—cold, smelling of bog myrtle and drowned earth—it caught the curve just right. A single, pure note rose. Not loud. Not sharp. A low, warm *hum*, like a bee trapped in amber.  

Bran froze. Not because it was beautiful—though it was, in a way that made your sternum ache—but because it *stopped* things. The wind dropped mid-gust. A sparrow, mid-flight over the fen, dipped, hovered, then settled on a reed, head cocked. Even the furnace’s usual low growl seemed to… thin.  

He dug the bowl out. Cleaned it. Polished it with crushed snail shells and goose fat (the only polish he trusted—said lye made metal “nervous”). Then he hung it—not with rope, but with a twisted length of willow root, still green and supple—on the rusted iron hook above the forge door.  

First time the wind took it? The note lasted *eight seconds*. Eight full seconds where no cricket chirped, no water dripped from the eaves, no child coughed in the cottage next door. Just that tone—C-sharp, Hemlock insists, though I’ve never heard a C-sharp that smelled faintly of burnt honey and wet flint.  

Word spread. Not fast. Slow, like ink soaking into blotting paper. People came—not to pray, not to beg, but to *stand*. Farmers. Widows. The miller’s apprentice who stammered so badly he communicated by tapping rhythms on tabletops. They’d stand beneath the hanging bowl, eyes closed, breathing shallow. Some wept. Not from sorrow. From *recognition*. As if they’d forgotten what true quiet felt like—and here it was, ringing.  

Then came the night of the Black Frost. Ground froze solid at midnight. Frost climbed the walls like silver spiders. And the bowl *rang*—not from wind, but from the cold itself, contracting the metal with such sudden, precise tension that the note cracked the ice on the nearby duck pond.  

That’s when Bran knew. It wasn’t a bowl. It wasn’t a hinge. It was a *vessel for absence*. A shape carved into the world to hold the space *between* sounds.  

He never forged another. Took the tongs, the hammer, the anvil—buried them deep in the peat bog behind the smithy, wrapped in salted otter hide. Walked away barefoot, wearing only his leather apron and a necklace of river-polished quartz. Was seen once, years later, sitting on a mossy stone near the old standing stones, humming a tune no one else could hear. Or maybe he wasn’t humming. Maybe he was just *listening* to the silence he’d taught the world to make.  

The bell—well, the *first* bell—hung there until the great flood of ’12. Washed away, they say. But Hemlock swears he’s heard it, just once, on a still morning in March, when the mist hangs low and the world holds its breath: that same low, warm hum, coming not from the air, but *from the ground*, rising up through the soles of your boots.  

Funny thing? No one ever cast it again. Not properly. Too many try—brass, bronze, even silver—but they all ring *at* you. Loud. Proud. Demanding.  

The first one didn’t ring *at* anything.  

It rang *into* the hollow.  

And the hollow answered.

title: short story|a night bus driver and a passenger who never gets off
text:
The bus groaned as it leaned into the curve past the shuttered laundromat—*Spin & Rinse*, the sign’s neon letters long dead, leaving only a faint, ghostly phosphor-green afterimage on the retina. Leo kept his hands at ten and two, knuckles pale, breath shallow. He’d been driving this route—Route 7, the “Owl Run”—for seventeen years, and he knew the exact pitch of the suspension when the left rear airbag was low, the precise shudder in the floorboard when the transmission slipped just before third gear. But he didn’t know *her*.

She sat in seat 14B—the one with the torn vinyl exposing grey foam like exposed bone—and she hadn’t moved in forty-three minutes. Not to adjust her coat, not to check her phone, not even to blink quite right. Her eyes were open, yes, fixed on the rain-streaked window, but the light behind them wasn’t reflecting the sodium-orange glow of the streetlamps; it was deeper, older, like looking down a well where the water had gone still centuries ago.

Leo glanced in the rearview. She was still there. Always there. Not every night—no, that would be too easy—but often enough that he’d stopped counting after the fifth time. Once, he’d pulled over near the old rail yard, engine idling, and said, “Ma’am? You okay? This is the end of the line.” She’d turned her head slowly, so slowly it made his teeth ache, and said, “Is it?” Her voice wasn’t hoarse or tired. It was neutral. Like a thermostat reading ambient temperature. Then she looked back out the window, and Leo, heart hammering against his ribs, had driven on—not to the depot, but back onto the loop, the bus humming its low, resigned song.

Tonight, the rain had turned to sleet, tapping the roof like cold fingertips. The digital clock above the windshield blinked 2:47 a.m. The bus was empty except for her and the hollow echo of its own machinery. Leo’s coffee had gone cold hours ago, the dregs bitter and metallic in his mouth. His fingers tightened on the wheel. He’d tried everything. Asked if she needed help. Offered a blanket from the emergency kit. Even once, very quietly, asked if she was waiting for someone. She’d only murmured, “Waiting is what happens when time forgets to move forward,” and then smiled—not with her mouth, but with the corners of her eyes, which crinkled like old paper folding along forgotten creases.

He remembered the first time. A Tuesday. Fog so thick it swallowed street signs whole. She’d boarded at the corner of Elm and 9th, stepping up the metal stairs without a sound, her coat—a long, charcoal wool thing, slightly too large—swirling around her ankles like smoke. No bag. No umbrella. Just a small, worn leather satchel resting on her lap, its clasp shaped like a tarnished silver moth. He’d checked the fare box: no token dropped. No tap of a card. Yet the green light had flashed *Paid*. He’d watched her in the mirror as she settled into 14B, and something in his chest had gone very still, like a bird holding its breath mid-flight.

Since then, he’d started noting things. She never ate. Never drank. Never shifted her weight, not even when the bus lurched over potholes. Her coat never dampened, though the rain soaked through his own collar every time he stepped outside. And her reflection in the dark window—when he dared look—was always slightly *behind* her actual position, as if lagging by half a second, like a delayed broadcast.

At the next stop—Maple & 5th—he slowed, brake hissing. The sign read *MAPLE & 5TH – TRANSFER POINT*. Empty bench. Wet pavement gleaming under the lone working lamp. He paused, engine thrumming, the door sighing open. No one waited. No one boarded. He held the door for twelve seconds—the regulation minimum—then closed it with a soft, final *hiss-thunk*. In the mirror, she remained motionless. Her satchel rested on her lap, unopened. He’d never seen her open it.

The bus rolled on, tires whispering over wet asphalt. Leo’s radio crackled—dispatch, voice tinny and bored: *“Owl Seven, confirm status. Depot reports no inbound passengers scheduled. You’re clear for return.”* He keyed the mic, throat dry. “Owl Seven… confirmed. Returning now.” He didn’t say *except for one*. He never did.
